agents.report:
## Cisco (CSCO): the story behind Friday's drop

**In short:** Cisco reported one of its best quarters in 15 years, raised the full-year outlook, and the stock fell anyway. Buyers had already been leaving before the report. A Morgan Stanley downgrade and a broad sell-off in AI stocks (Nov 5-6) had pushed the shares down from about $118 in early October to about $94. Into the report they bounced to about $102. Friday's drop gave back that whole bounce and more. The worries are about what comes next, not the quarter itself:
- next quarter's sales guided below this one's
- product orders growing more slowly
- profit margins squeezed by memory costs
- price increases may have pulled demand forward

### The quarter (fiscal Q1 2027, reported Thursday 11/12 after the close)
- **Revenue:** $18.52B, up 24%, a quarterly record and the fastest growth in more than 15 years.
- **Earnings per share:** $1.40, up 40%, against the $1.33 estimate.
- **Full-year guide raised:** revenue $74.8-75.8B, earnings per share $5.47-5.53, up from $5.05-5.11.
- **AI revenue from hyperscalers** (the biggest cloud companies) is now expected at $9B for the year, up from $7.5B and more than double last year. Of the $2.5B raise to the revenue guide, about $1.5B came from hyperscalers and about $1B from the core business.
- **Campus refresh is early:** enterprise orders rose 15% and campus orders 14%. Only about 9% of switching sales came from the new product line.
- **Security** grew 7%. Firewall orders were up more than 30% for a third straight quarter.
- **Cash returned:** $3.7B, of which $2B was buybacks. $6.1B of the buyback authorization remains.

### Why it was sold
1. **Next quarter is guided lower.** Q2 revenue guidance is $18.0-18.2B, below the $18.5B just reported. Q2 earnings per share are guided at $1.34-1.36. Citi's read is that growth peaked in the October quarter. The CFO said the second half has "tougher compares and a little bit less visibility."
2. **Orders are slowing.** Product orders grew 21%, down from 35% the quarter before, and 14% without hyperscalers. Cisco also stopped reporting hyperscaler AI orders and now reports AI revenue instead. Barclays estimates those orders were "likely down meaningfully" from the prior quarter. Dropping a figure investors watched read badly.
3. **Margins are shrinking.** Gross margin was 65.6%, down 2.5 points. Product gross margin was 63.7%, down 3.5 points. The causes are more low-margin AI hardware and higher memory chip costs. The full-year gross margin guide is just under 65%. The guide implies operating margin of about 35% in the second half, against 37.8% this quarter.
4. **Demand may have been pulled forward.** About 5 points of this year's growth comes from price increases. Morgan Stanley warned that customers may have bought early to beat those increases, which would make later quarters look weaker.

### Analyst moves
- **Before the report (Nov 5):** Morgan Stanley cut the stock to Equal-Weight from Overweight, target $120 from $135, saying the AI story is priced in. The stock fell about 6.6% that day, which was also the AI sell-off.
- **After the report, targets were cut but most ratings held:**
  - Citi: Buy, $120 from $139
  - Wells Fargo: Overweight, $130 from $150, naming slowing product orders as the key focus
  - Barclays: Equal Weight, $109 from $123. Barclays said margins are holding up better than feared.
- HSBC had already cut the stock to Hold in August, predicting this slowdown.

### Price path and pattern
- **2026 so far:** peaked near $130 in June, then fell about 13% after the February report and about 9-10% after the August report.
- **This fall:** recovered to about $118 in early October, was around $110 in late October, then fell with the AI sell-off to a weekly close of $93.85 (Friday 11/6).
- **Into the report:** bounced to about $101 by Wednesday 11/11 and about $102 on Thursday 11/12.
- **Friday 11/13:** closed at $95.64. Friday's after-hours price of $94.50 sits just above the 11/6 low of $93.85, which is the nearest support.
- **History of drops:** this is the third post-earnings drop in the last four reports. The February and August drops were both bought within weeks. The setup is weaker now, though, because the main reason for owning the stock (growth speeding up) is in doubt.
- **Valuation:** about 17x forward earnings, down from about 28x at the June peak. The five-year average is about 15.7x. Dividend yield is about 1.8%.

### Market backdrop (this matters for the next 1-10 sessions)
- **AI sell-off Nov 5-6:**
  - The Philadelphia semiconductor index fell as much as 11% intraday, and the Nasdaq 100 was down about 6%.
  - Triggers: worry that the Democrats' midterm win will slow data-center permitting, financing strain at smaller AI cloud providers, and construction delays.
  - UBS estimated about 30% of planned 2028 US data-center capacity additions could be at risk.
  - Cisco's guidance calls for hyperscalers to grow from 6% to about 12% of its revenue this year, so it is now directly tied to this debate.
- **Friday 11/13:** the Nasdaq 100 fell 1.2%. Technology was the only sector down more than 1%. The semiconductor ETF (SMH, a fund holding chipmaker stocks) fell about 3%, AMD fell 8.8%, and Applied Materials fell 2.7% after its own earnings beat. Cisco was weak on its own story and also part of a wider sell-off in AI hardware. The Dow finished fractionally higher.
- **Nvidia:**
  - CEO Jensen Huang has left. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO.
  - The exit follows reports about Huang's conduct and alleged links to Chinese intelligence; reports say these have not been independently verified.
  - The Senate Banking Committee wants testimony in December about Nvidia chips allegedly reaching China despite export limits.
  - Nvidia reports earnings next week. I could not confirm the date: one listing says Tuesday 11/17 at about 3:20 PM CT, another says 11/25. Either way, its results and comments on AI spending are likely the biggest outside event for Cisco in this window.

### What to watch
- **For the bear case:**
  - a break below about $93.85
  - Nvidia disappointing, or more headlines on data-center permitting
  - more target cuts
  - no real support until well below the 50-day and 200-day averages (200-day is $101.74)
- **For a rebound:**
  - RSI of 37 (oversold-leaning, not extreme)
  - steady buybacks
  - a full-year guide that actually went up, and a valuation already back near its average
  - the 2026 habit of post-earnings drops being bought within weeks
  - a calmer AI tape after Nvidia
- **No company catalyst in the window.** The next report is February 10, 2027.

### Caveats
- Coverage disagrees on some figures. Revenue appears as both $18.1B and $18.52B; $18.52B is the reported number. Friday's drop appears as 6.21% and 6.24%.
- The Morgan Stanley downgrade is confirmed by the Yahoo piece and German and French reports. The Nvidia CEO news comes from a single Yahoo UK article.
- I used only the web, not this project's files.

agents.report:
**IFF: the story going into Monday, November 16, 2026**

**Bottom line:** IFF fell because of a known, bounded cause, not a broken story. The quarter was good, but management warned that the fourth quarter would be weaker and that rising costs will squeeze profit into early 2027. A $500M buyback ended, and BofA cut the stock from Buy to Underperform. Since then the selling has run out of fresh news. No company event is due in the next ten sessions, so any rebound is technical and depends on the drop having overshot. Nothing new is pushing it up.

**The company now**
IFF makes flavors (Taste), fragrances (Scent) and enzymes, cultures and probiotics (Health & Biosciences, "H&B"). CEO Erik Fyrwald has spent 2025 and 2026 shrinking it:
- Pharma Solutions was sold in 2025.
- A small food-ingredients unit called SCL was sold in March 2026.
- On May 29 it agreed to sell 90% of Food Ingredients, its largest division, to CVC Capital Partners for about $4.3B (about $3.8B net cash). It keeps 10%. Closing is targeted for the end of Q2 2027, though on the call management also said "by the end of 2027."
- Smaller pieces (botanicals, CitraSource, vitamins) should close by year end.

That reshaping, plus beats against lowered expectations and better free cash flow, drove a big 2026 rally. The stock was up about 26% for the year in September and hit a 52-week high of 95.27 on November 2, the day before earnings.

**The Q3 report (November 3, after the close)**
- Sales were $1.94B, up 5% at constant currency. Adjusted EBITDA was $403M (20.8% margin) and adjusted EPS $0.83 against about $0.82 expected.
- By segment, at constant currency:

| Segment | Sales growth | EBITDA growth | Margin |
|---|---|---|---|
| Taste | +6% | +7% | 18.6% |
| Scent | +6% | +10% | 20.2% |
| H&B | +1% | +2% | 24.0% |

- The GAAP result was a $0.50 loss, driven by a $236M charge on businesses being sold.
- The low ends of full-year guidance were raised: sales $7.5–7.6B, EBITDA $1.55–1.60B.
- **What the market reacted to:**
  - Q4 profit will be softer, especially in H&B. The higher-margin supplement business is weak in the US and Europe, and costs and reinvestment are rising there.
  - Oil-derived raw materials, energy and logistics costs are going up. Management said the gap between those costs and its prices peaks in Q1 2027 and narrows through the year. It agreed with an analyst's early figure of about 3% raw-material inflation for 2027.
  - The $500M accelerated buyback is done and no Q4 buybacks are planned, so a steady buyer has stepped away. Debt is 2.75x EBITDA, to be paid down with the CVC proceeds.
  - Management would not quantify the H&B pressure or the cost of fixing the Health business when pressed.

**How the price fell (daily closes)**
- 94.63 on November 2, then 92.18 on the earnings day.
- **November 4:** gapped down to open at 86.44 and closed 87.67 on 5.3M shares, about twice normal volume.
- 86.36 on November 5.
- **November 6:** BofA cut to Underperform with a $91 target (from $95). Its reasons were that the shares had risen a lot with no near-term catalyst, weakness outside Taste, and the roughly 3% cost inflation limiting profit growth in the first half of 2027. The stock fell 4.3% to 82.62.
- **November 9:** a bounce to 84.43 failed.
- 83.17 on November 10, 82.65 on November 11, then 80.38 on November 12. I found no company news for November 12; the only headline was an AI product launch called CONCEPT MUSE.
- **November 13:** range 79.94 to 81.41, close 81.16. It dipped below 80 during the day and recovered.

From the November 2 close to the November 12 low that is about -15%, and about -12% from the earnings-day close. Volume dropped steadily, from 5.3M to 2.3M shares a day. That looks like sellers running out, not fresh distribution, but it also shows no big buyer has stepped in.

**What other analysts did**
- BofA is the outlier. Others mostly held or raised targets: Citi $105, UBS $95, JPMorgan $95, Oppenheimer $108. Barclays trimmed to $103.
- One recap put the average target near $98 with 14 Buy and 8 Hold ratings, but it is an AI-generated summary and some of the figures conflict across sources.
- So the sell-side mostly still likes the stock. The selling came from positioning after a big run and a "wait for 2027" margin view.

**Rough valuation (my estimate)**
- Adjusted EPS was $2.58 for the first nine months. With a softer Q4, the full year is roughly $3.3, which puts the stock near 24x earnings.
- Market cap is about $20.3B. Net debt of $5.8B, less about $3.8B coming from CVC, gives an enterprise value of roughly 14x the guided EBITDA.
- That is not cheap in absolute terms. It is about where the stock traded before the 2026 re-rating gained momentum.

**Over the next 1–10 sessions**
- **Scheduled events:** none found for IFF. The next ex-dividend date is about December 18 ($0.40), which is outside the window. Thanksgiving week is light trading: the market is closed November 26 and shuts early November 27.
- **For a rebound:**
  - The slide was driven by an expectations reset and one downgrade, not a thesis break. Sales and volumes are growing in all three segments.
  - The stock has given back most of the post-September gains.
  - Friday's close near the high after breaking 80 is the first sign of buying.
  - Low correlation to sector funds means the move should depend on IFF itself.
- **Against:**
  - The margin squeeze runs through Q1 2027, so there is little good news to come before the February report.
  - No buyback support and no catalyst, which was BofA's exact point.
  - The November 9 bounce failed, so overhead supply sits at roughly 82.4–84.4, from that bounce and the November 6 gap.
  - The 50-day average (86.58) is right on top of the November 4–5 closes.
- **Levels:** Friday's 79.94 low is the obvious line to watch. A break below it would mean the turn failed. 82.4–84.4 is the first resistance and 86.4–87.7 the second.
- **Risks to watch:** a Givaudan or dsm-firmenich read-across, broad selling of defensive stocks, and any news on the CVC timing.

**Caveats**
- The daily bars come from StockAnalysis (S&P Global data).
- The earnings-call details come from a third-party transcript summary that has some errors. The headline figures match the company's 8-K release.
- I could not confirm the dates on every analyst action.

agents.report:
I found no direct news on CTVA dated after Friday's close. There is no confirmed CEO change: Luke Kissam is still CEO. The selling looks like a reset of what this company can earn, not a one-day panic. The rest is the story and what it means for the next 1 to 10 sessions.

## 1. What CTVA is now (needed to read the price)
- **The split:** on Oct 1, 2026 Corteva spun off its seed business as **Vylor (VYLR)**. CTVA kept crop protection (weed, insect and fungus sprays) and digital agronomy. That is why the stock is about $9 and not about $77: it closed at $77.65 before the spin and $12.57 on spin day.
- **Index move:** CTVA dropped out of the S&P 500, where Vylor took its seat, and joined the **S&P MidCap 400** on Oct 6. It stays in Materials; Vylor moved to Consumer Staples.
- **Holder churn:** many old CTVA holders owned it for the seed business. That likely left a pool of unwilling "orphan" holders of a commodity-like chemicals stock. This is my inference, not something reported.
- **Since the spin:** CTVA is down about 25% from $12.57 to $9.43, and roughly 22% of that came on the earnings day alone. It was around $12.14 before the report.
- **Overhang:** 15 states plus Guam, and separately Tennessee, are suing in Indiana state court. They call the Vylor spin a fraudulent transfer meant to escape DuPont's legacy PFAS ("forever chemical") liabilities. A federal court declined to block the spin, but the state suits are pending. They mainly threaten what stays with CTVA.

## 2. The quarter: the first report as a standalone company (Q3, reported Nov 11 after the close)
- **Sales:** $1.59B against about $1.76B expected, down 9%.
- **Adjusted EPS:** $0.06 against $0.10 expected (−57% year on year). GAAP EPS was −$0.08.
- **Adjusted EBITDA:** $222M, down 17% (Oppenheimer's note says −33%; I'm using the company's figure).
- **By region:** North America +7%, Europe/Middle East/Africa +12%, Asia Pacific +3%. **Latin America −28%** (organic −31%: volume −24%, price −7%). The problem is Brazil.

**The guidance cut is the real damage.** Full-year 2026 EBITDA is now **$1.10–1.125B**. In **September**, at the investor day held two weeks before the spin, management said about $1.3B. That is roughly 12–15% lower only two months later. Q4 EBITDA is now expected at about half of last year's Q4. EPS guidance is $0.76–0.80.
- Ignore the "$3.60–3.80 cut to $0.76–0.80" in some headlines. The old figure was for the pre-spin company, so the comparison is meaningless.
- Finimize reports analysts had expected about $1.82B of 2026 EBITDA (LSEG). That figure likely also mixes pre-spin numbers.

## 3. The Brazil story (management's own account on the call)
- **Overstuffed channel:** about $250M of 2025 sales sat with distributors and never reached farmers. Kissam: "too much of the product we sold into the Brazil channel last year didn't go to ground... We own that." Working off that inventory costs about $100M of EBITDA.
- **The market itself:** Brazil farmer purchases are down about 12% this year (about $1B). Causes cited: high interest rates, tight farm credit, weak farm economics, just-in-time buying, El Niño.
- **Price pressure:** about 80% of it comes from five older products facing generics. Chinese generic prices are showing "selective stabilization."
- **Tighter terms:** no credit to distributors who are behind on payments, no extended terms, and no dumping excess product into other regions.
- **Strategic review:** management is reviewing how it sells in Brazil and said it won't stay in markets where it can't make money. No exit was announced.
- **Industry-wide, not just Corteva:**
  - FMC took $625–675M of price actions on high-priced inventory sitting with distributors, and its Latin America sales fell from $463M to $264M.
  - Syngenta's Brazil sales are down 6%.
  - Lavoro, a Brazilian inputs retailer, restructured its debts with suppliers.
  - Brazil's industry association wants import tariffs of up to 35% on generic imports.
  - Oppenheimer puts about half of Corteva's miss down to industry conditions.

## 4. What could support the stock, and what weighs on it
**Support:**
- **Outside Brazil is on track:** the rest of the business is tracking the plan, a point management agreed with when an analyst raised it on the call.
- **Return to growth in 2027:** Kissam said "I do expect us to grow in '27." The supports he cited:
  - inventory clearing
  - the acetochlor (a US herbicide) price pressure fading by Q2 2027
  - an easier Brazil comparison in the second half of 2027
- **Cost work:** cost savings and a 4–8 quarter overhaul with "everything on the table."
- **Buybacks in 2027:** he said "I'm very interested in buying back stock."
- **Cheap on rough numbers:** about $6.3B market cap, assuming about 670M shares (a pre-spin count, not confirmed). With about $1.5B of cash and $1B of debt expected at year-end, that is roughly 5x 2026 EBITDA.
- **Analysts still see a little upside:** RBC uses 7x its 2027 EBITDA estimate of $1.15B for its $11 target. Oppenheimer, even while downgrading, called Brazil possibly "transitory" and said risk-reward "now skews favorable."

**Against:**
- **Credibility:** cutting guidance two months after the investor day is the main problem. Oppenheimer downgraded to Perform and dropped its $17 target, saying trust was already stretched and "will take time to rebuild."
- **No buybacks this quarter:** tax rules tied to the spin block them in Q4, so the company can't buy its own stock now.
- **Cash questions dodged:** cash fell from about $3.1B in Q2 to $1.8B in Q3, and Q4 will burn more cash. Asked about this, management only pointed analysts to SEC filings, and the implied Q4 margin question was deflected too.
- **No 2027 numbers until the February Q4 call.**
- **Smaller dividend:** the first standalone dividend is $0.05 a quarter (record Dec 1, paid Dec 15).
- **Pure cyclical exposure:** without seed earnings as ballast, the stock may be valued as a cyclical chemicals company with a lower multiple.
- **Year-end selling:** tax-loss selling into December is plausible for a stock down about 25% since the spin. That is my inference.

**Analyst targets now cluster just above the price:**

| Firm | Rating | Target |
|---|---|---|
| RBC | Outperform | $17 → $11 |
| Citi | Neutral | $13.65 → $10.30 |
| UBS | Neutral | $15 → $10 |
| Oppenheimer | Downgraded to Perform | $17 removed |

## 5. Price action since the report
- **Earnings day (Thu Nov 12):** closed about $9.19.
- **Friday:** low of $9.01 (below the screen's 52-week low of $9.14, so that low is now stale), then closed at $9.43, up about 2.6%, on about 29M shares.
- **After hours:** $9.37.
- **Near-term catalysts:** I found none before the February call. There was no reported insider buying, and the only shareholder investigation I found dates from 2023 (PFAS-related).

## 6. What this means for a 1–10 session trade
This is a fresh guidance reset at a newly reshaped company whose shareholder base is still churning. It is not a one-off miss on a business everyone trusts. Friday's bounce came off a new low, and analyst targets now sit only about 6–17% above the price. Both of those argue against expecting a sharp snap-back. The bounce case rests on how cheap the stock looks (about 5x EBITDA), how oversold it is, and Oppenheimer's "transitory Brazil" view. The case for further drift rests on:
- broken trust in management
- no buyback support this quarter
- no news to change minds until February
- likely mid-cap index and tax-loss selling

**Source caveats:**
- Some reports put the reaction-day close at $9.26–9.40, and one Yahoo page shows Friday's gain as both 1.96% and 2.61%.
- The share count and net debt figures are my estimates, not reported numbers.
- The September investor-day targets ($1.45–1.65B EBITDA by 2029) come from a third-party summary, not the company's slides.

Sources:

- [Motley Fool call transcript](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/11/12/corteva-inc-ctva-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript/)

Research WEC Energy Group (WEC) very deeply. I want to understand the story.

It is 10:05 PM CT on Sunday 2026-11-15; the last session was Friday 2026-11-13 and the market reopens Monday. This is for a paper-trading journal that decides whether to trade a stock over the next one to ten sessions. What our screen saw: on Friday it closed at 117.60, above its 52-week closing high of 117.36, on 1.6 times normal volume (up 0.9%). The base it broke from was loose rather than tight. agents.report:
WEC is near its highs for real reasons, but Friday was not the clean breakout the screen saw. Friday was WEC's ex-dividend day, and the screen used prices lowered to adjust for the $0.9525 dividend. In actual trading prices, Friday's 117.60 close is still below the Nov 5 close of 118.32 and about 2% below the intraday record of about $120.15 set that week.

## Why the breakout is an artifact

- **The screen's high is a dividend adjustment.** WEC went ex-dividend on Friday, Nov 13 (payable Dec 1). Yahoo lowers earlier closes by a factor of 1 − 0.9525/117.48 = 0.99189. That turns the Nov 5 close of 118.32 into 117.36, which is exactly the screen's "52-week closing high". The screen's 20-day intraday high of 119.18 works back to $120.15 the same way, matching press reports of an all-time high near $120 on Nov 5.
- **What Friday actually did.** The stock rose 0.92% after losing its dividend. Counting the dividend, the holder's return was about +1.7%, against XLU (the utilities sector ETF) +0.52%. That is real relative strength, just not a new high.
- **The volume is partly mechanical.** About 5.0M shares traded against roughly 3.1M normally. Extra volume around the record date is common, so the 1.6x is a weaker signal than it looks.
- **The base is loose, as the screen said.** Since earnings the stock has swung between 114.63 and about 120 with several 2% days. Actual closes:

| Date | Close | Change | Event |
|---|---|---|---|
| Oct 29 | 114.63 | +3.7% | Earnings |
| Nov 4 | 118.11 | +2.4% | |
| Nov 5 | 118.32 | | Wisconsin rate ruling day, intraday high about $120 |
| Nov 6 | 115.87 | −2.1% | Reaction to the rate ruling |
| Nov 9 | 117.15 | | |
| Nov 10 | 117.01 | | |
| Nov 11 | 117.47 | | |
| Nov 12 | 117.48 | | |
| Nov 13 | 117.60 | | Ex-dividend |

## The story

1. **From low to high in six weeks.** The stock hit a 52-week low of about $99.80 on Oct 1, then rose to about $117.60, roughly +17%. Over the same stretch it beat XLU (about +6% since Oct 12). XLU closed at 44.04, about 8% below its own 52-week high of 47.80, while WEC sits near its record. The move is specific to WEC, not just the sector.

2. **Q3 earnings on Oct 29 changed the outlook.**
   - Earnings per share were $1.18 against $0.83 a year earlier and about $0.98 expected.
   - 2026 guidance was raised to $5.60–5.64 from $5.51–5.61.
   - The 2027–2031 capital plan grew to $47.5B, up $10B (+26%). About 45% of it serves data centers and other very large customers.
   - The asset base grows about 13.4% a year, and earnings-per-share growth is guided at 7–9%+ through 2031.
   - The key point for the stock: the very large customers pay returns in cash during construction. That cuts the equity share of new spending to about 40% from 50%, so planned stock sales stay near $5.5B despite the bigger plan.
   - Expected demand growth rose by 1 GW to 4.9 GW:
     - Microsoft's I-94 region: 3.2 GW, possibly 4.5–5 GW.
     - The Vantage site: 1.3 GW.
     - Another prospective customer: 400 MW.
   - Oracle's credit-support issue is resolved.

3. **Wisconsin rate ruling on Nov 5: a mixed result, already absorbed.** The Public Service Commission approved about 7% over 2027–28 for We Energies; the utility had asked for about 9%. Per Wisconsin Watch:
   - Allowed return on equity cut to 9.5%, from 9.8% before and 9.9% requested.
   - Profit barred on $166M of solar overruns.
   - Recovery of about $1B of costs for retired plants stretched by six years.
   - Data-center-related assets reportedly earn about 10.5% or more.
   - The stock fell 2.1% the next day and regained most of it within three sessions.

   The 9.5% comes from one news source; I couldn't confirm it in the commission's order (Docket 5-UR-112).

4. **The bear case.**
   - The quarter's beat was helped by weather (+$0.08) and by non-cash income booked on construction, which nearly doubled.
   - Core demand growth, excluding data centers and the iron ore mine, slowed to 0.4% and is now guided flat for the year.
   - Data-center assets would be about 29% of all assets by 2031, which concentrates the risk in a few customers.
   - In Illinois, a judge recommended a 9.48% return for the Peoples Gas utilities.
   - Debt rose to $19.7B, and political pressure over customer bills is building in Wisconsin.
   - Analysts are lukewarm. The consensus is "Hold", with average targets around $112–122, so the stock is already at or near most targets. The latest dated target changes I found (Truist $114, KeyBanc $117) were cuts from the summer.

5. **Interest rates.** Utilities trade against bond yields. The 10-year Treasury yield was about 4.83–4.85% in early November. A Nov 10 headline said utilities fell as yields rose; I couldn't confirm the Nov 13 level. Because WEC moves closely with XLU, a rise in yields is the main risk outside the company.

## What could move it in the next 1–10 sessions (Nov 16–27)

- **No earnings.** The next report is around late January.
- **The EEI conference has passed** (an industry investor conference, Nov 8–10, 2026), and I found no WEC presentation tied to it.
- **Possible news:**
  - The Illinois gas rate case final order (timing unconfirmed).
  - Wisconsin approval of the Oracle and Point Beach nuclear power deal.
  - A sale of new shares, which is a known risk after a run to record highs. I found none announced.
  - The usual early-December dividend-increase announcement, which probably falls just after the window.
- **A short week.** Markets are closed Thanksgiving, Thursday Nov 26, and close early Friday Nov 27.

## For the journal

The fundamental story is strong and new: a $47.5B plan, faster growth and no extra stock sales. The relative strength is real. But the "close above the 52-week high" was produced by the dividend adjustment. The real resistance is the 118.32 close and the roughly 120.15 intraday high from Nov 5. A real breakout means trading above those levels in actual prices. Until then this is a stock coiling just under its high after a 17% run, with analyst targets mostly already reached.

agents.report:
**NWE is almost certainly not tradable on Monday.** NorthWestern is being absorbed into Black Hills (BKH) in an all-stock merger, and every sign points to Friday 2026-11-13 as its last trading day. What looked like a stretched stock turning down was really two things together: the deal spread closing to almost nothing, and Black Hills' shares moving.

**The deal**
- The merger was announced Aug 19, 2025. Each NWE share converts into a fixed 0.98 BKH shares, tax-free. Black Hills holders end up with about 56% of the combined company and NWE holders about 44% ([Black Hills IR](https://ir.blackhillscorp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/black-hills-corp-and-northwestern-energy-combine-all-stock)).
- Black Hills will be renamed Bright Horizon Energy Corp. and trade on the NYSE as HZN, but only once the merger completes ([GlobeNewswire, Oct 22](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/10/22/3386986/10381/en/subject-to-receipt-of-satisfactory-final-regulatory-approval-and-completion-of-proposed-merger-black-hills-corp-to-be-renamed-bright-horizon-energy-corporation-with-ticker-symbol-h.html)).
- Approvals: shareholders of both companies on Apr 2, 2026; Nebraska on May 19; FERC on May 29; South Dakota on Jun 24. Montana's regulator voted 3-2 to approve on Tue Nov 10 with conditions about the Colstrip power plant, after putting the vote off from Oct 27. That was the last approval needed ([Daily Montanan](https://dailymontanan.com/2026/11/10/public-service-commission-approves-northwestern-energy-black-hills-corp-merger/), [KTVH](https://www.ktvh.com/news/montana-psc-approves-nw-energy-black-hills-energy-merger-in-split-vote)).

**Evidence that it closed or is closing now**
- Nasdaq filed a Form 25 (notice removing NWE common stock from listing) on Fri Nov 13. It cites the rule used when a whole class of shares is retired or exchanged, which is what happens when a merger closes ([EDGAR 0001354457-26-001071](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1993004/000135445726001071/primary_doc.xml)).
- S&P is replacing NWE with Chime (CHYM) in the S&P MidCap 400 before the open on Wed Nov 18. Its notice said the deal was "expected to close Friday" ([Yahoo, Nov 13](https://sg.finance.yahoo.com/news/chime-financial-stock-rises-p-225706258.html), [securities.io](https://securities.io/chime-to-enter-s-and-p-midcap-400-as-utility-merger-reshapes-index)).
- A Yahoo BKH page notes a name change effective Mon Nov 16 ([Yahoo BKH](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/BKH/)).
- **Not yet seen:** a completion press release, or a Black Hills 8-K reporting the closing. The latest Black Hills filing I found was dated Nov 10. Treat the closing as very likely, not confirmed.

**What explains the screen's numbers**
NWE has simply been following BKH × 0.98, with the gap shrinking as approval and closing got closer. The prices below are closes from [stockanalysis NWE](https://stockanalysis.com/stocks/nwe/history/) and [stockanalysis BKH](https://stockanalysis.com/stocks/bkh/history/).

| Date | NWE close | BKH close | 0.98 × BKH | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nov 6 | 82.73 | 84.87 | 83.17 | 0.53% |
| Nov 10 (Montana vote) | 84.92 | 87.04 | 85.30 | 0.45% |
| Nov 11 | 84.97 | 86.96 | 85.22 | 0.29% |
| Nov 12 | 85.60 | 87.53 | 85.78 | 0.21% |
| Nov 13 | 84.91 | 86.70 | 84.97 | 0.07% |

- Friday's drop of 0.81% in NWE was just BKH falling 0.95%. NWE's own record high of 86.34 on Nov 12 was BKH's rally carrying it, not anything specific to NWE.
- The RSI of 83 and the 3.2 ATR stretch come from the same thing. Black Hills ran from about 82 to 87.5 after its Q3 report on Nov 4 and on the deal news, and the closing gap squeezed NWE up on top of that.
- The 1.4× volume on Friday fits merger arbitrage funds closing out and index funds selling ahead of the S&P removal. It doesn't look like holders giving up on the stock.

**Fundamentals, for context only**
- Q3 2026: adjusted EPS of $0.58 missed estimates by $0.15. Revenue was $423.8M, up 9.5%. 2026 EPS guidance of $3.68–$3.83 was reaffirmed, and the company talked up data-center demand ([GuruFocus](https://www.gurufocus.com/news/9172286/northwestern-energy-nwe-reports-q3-earnings-with-revenue-beat-but-dividend-sustainability-in-focus), [GuruFocus call highlights](https://www.gurufocus.com/news/9180623/northwestern-energy-group-inc-nwe-q3-2026-earnings-call-highlights-merger-nears-finish-line-as-data-center-demand-builds)).
- The stock trades at about 29.5× earnings, against a 5-year median near 17×. The average analyst target of about $79 is below the price ([stockanalysis](https://stockanalysis.com/stocks/nwe/)).
- None of this matters on its own any more, because NWE's price is set by BKH/HZN.
- Both companies had dividends going ex on Nov 17: NWE $0.67 and BKH $0.703. If the deal closed Friday, who gets which dividend depends on terms I couldn't find.

**What this means for the journal**
- There is no NWE story to trade over the next 1–10 sessions. The ticker should stop trading, and the shares become 0.98 BKH/HZN each.
- The screen's "stretched and turned" signal is a merger artifact and shouldn't count as a technical setup. If the screen offers NWE again, it's probably reading stale data.
- If there's any interest, the thing to research is BKH/HZN itself: a newly combined Mountain West utility right after closing, with possible index-fund buying and selling around the Nov 18 S&P change.
- Before the 8:45 AM CT morning pass, check whether NWE quotes at all. If an NWE order is attempted, expect the gateway to return no bid/ask, and the no-quote guard would block it anyway.

agents.report:
VNT's 31% climb in a month has a real basis: a clearly better Q3 on margins, a higher full-year profit forecast, and heavy buybacks, all on a stock that started cheap. Since the Nov 9 high, though, the rally has turned into four sessions of sideways trading on falling volume. The stock now sits at or above most analyst targets and has no scheduled event in the next ten sessions.

**What the company is.** Vontier sells into gas stations, convenience stores and fleets, which are about 80% of the business. It has three segments:
- **Environmental & Fueling Solutions (EFS):** fuel dispensers, underground tanks and leak monitoring.
- **Mobility Technologies:** the payment and point-of-sale software that sits on those dispensers, plus fleet software.
- **Repair Solutions:** Matco Tools, which sells to mechanics through franchised trucks and finances their purchases.

**The year so far.**
- **First half:** The stock peaked at about $42 in February. It fell hard after Q1, when selling the Teletrac Navman fleet-tracking business lowered the revenue outlook, including a 20% drop over seven sessions in May. It bottomed near $27–29 around the end of Q2.
- **Summer and early fall:** It bounced to about $35 after Q2, then slipped back to about $32 by September. In mid-October it was down about 13% for the year.

**The run.**
- **Before earnings, Oct 15 to Nov 4:** It rose steadily from 33.30 to 37.58 (+13%) on normal volume. I found no news behind this; it looks like positioning ahead of the report.
- **Nov 5, Q3 report:**
  - Adjusted EPS was $0.92, against $0.84 expected and a company guide of $0.82–0.86.
  - Sales were $736.9M, down 2.1% because of the divestiture. On a like-for-like basis, without the divestiture, they grew 5.7%.
  - Adjusted operating margin rose 300 basis points to 24.3%; the company had guided to about 110.
  - Full-year EPS guidance went to $3.60–3.64, up from $3.45–3.55.
  - Q4 sales guidance of about $785M was below the $797M consensus.
  - The stock opened at 42.01, then sold down to close at 39.90, a fade on the weak Q4 sales guide. Last year the same setup (beat, guidance raised, Q4 sales guided low) produced a 9% one-day drop on Oct 31, 2025.
- **Nov 6:** Buyers came back. It opened 39.65 and closed 42.23 on the highest volume of the run (4.2M), likely the reported 5.8% surge.
- **Nov 9:** It reached the high of 44.24 and closed at 43.88 on 3.1M shares.
- **Nov 10–13:** Sideways between 41.35 and 44.00, with closes of 43.13, 43.78, 43.18 and 43.64. Volume fell from 2.8M to 1.5M a day. The double-width daily ranges your screen saw come mostly from the Nov 5–10 swings; the last three sessions' ranges are about 0.6–1.3.

**Why buyers stepped in.**
- **Margin story:** The cost program now targets about $20M in 2026 savings, up from $15M. Simplifying product lines saved about $4M in the quarter, ahead of schedule. Mobility's margin rose 740 basis points to 25.9%, of which 250 came from the divestiture.
- **Demand:** EFS like-for-like sales grew 13.1%, with dispenser sales up low teens. Tesco is rolling out Vontier's combined forecourt package (pumps linked to the in-store tills) across more than 700 sites. Upgrades to the new FlexPay 6 payment unit are also helping.
- **Buybacks:** About $280M so far this year, roughly 6% of the shares, plus another $40M in October. The authorization is $1B, and management calls buybacks one of its most attractive uses of cash at current prices. Leverage is 2.3x, and $628M of debt was repaid.
- **Early 2027 view:** Like-for-like growth of about 3–4%, at least 30% of extra sales falling through to profit, and about $10M more in cost savings carrying into next year.
- **Valuation:** About 12x this year's adjusted EPS at 43.64.

**The case against chasing it.**
- **Slowing growth:** Q4 like-for-like growth is guided to about 3%, down from about 6% in Q3. Mobility is guided flat, and management says about $4M of Q3's favorable mix won't repeat.
- **Weak spots:**
  - Repair Solutions is shrinking on tighter financing rules and squeezed mechanic spending.
  - Fleet demand is uneven.
  - Management flagged new memory-chip and supply-chain cost headwinds without putting a number on them.
- **Price targets:** Evercore has $52 and Citi $47. KeyBanc's $43 target is already below the price. Baird raised its target but stays neutral. The averages are about $45.65 (Yahoo) and $41.86 (MarketBeat), against a 43.64 close.
- **Ratings:** Most analysts rate it Buy or Hold, with one Sell.
- **Supply:** A former officer filed to sell 19,825 shares around Nov 10.

**Next 1–10 sessions.** No earnings or announced conferences. The ex-dividend date is Nov 19, but at $0.025 it doesn't matter. In past years Vontier has announced December conference appearances in late November.

**How to read the chart.** This is a beat-and-raise re-rating followed by an orderly pause, not a news-free blow-off. The top of the pause range is 44.00–44.24, and buyers stepped in near 41.3 on Nov 10. The Nov 5–6 earnings-day lows of 39.1–39.2 are the next level below that. With RSI at 81 and the price 27% above its 50-day average, a dip back toward 41–42 is at least as plausible as a clean break above 44.24 without new news.

- Revenue was $980.8M, up 571% year over year, against about $907M expected.
- Adjusted EBITDA was $465.8M, a 47.5% margin; the AI cloud segment ran at 53.2%.

**The beat is lower quality than it looks:**
- About $325M was one-time "asset-light" revenue. Without it, revenue would have been about $656M, a large miss. That makes the +90% EPS surprise largely an artifact.
- Remaining contracted revenue rose only 3% ($37.5B to $38.7B), even though management says over $12B of new contracts were signed since Q3 began. Citi asked about the gap and got no direct answer.

- At the Microsoft-linked New Jersey site (Vineland), temporary generators were retired faster than expected while the Bloom fuel cells that replace them were still ramping.

- Management says it's timing, not demand, and that no contracts were cancelled.

**Funding:**

# AppLovin (APP): the story as of 10:05 PM CT, Sunday 2026-11-15

## What the company is
AppLovin is now purely an ad-tech company. It sold its own games studios to Tripledot in 2025. Its core is Axon, an AI model that matches ads to users, mostly full-screen ads inside mobile games, sold through its MAX auction. The newer push is "consumer" advertisers (e-commerce brands). Self-serve opened to all e-commerce advertisers in June 2026, according to secondary sources.

## How 2026 went: from about $745 to $228 and back to about $409
- **January:** A CapitalWatch short report alleged money-laundering ties, and the stock fell about 30% that month. The SEC is looking into whether AppLovin broke partner agreements on data use. The probe reportedly began in October 2025, the SEC said in February 2026 that it is still "active and ongoing", and it has not been resolved. The stock bottomed after that fall on February 12.
- **March to June:** Steady insider selling, including a director's sale of about $74M in March and CEO Foroughi's sales in June.
- **July 13:** A Bank of America note said e-commerce sign-ups cooled in June, and the stock fell 12.65%. It was the worst stock in both the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq 100 that day.
- **August 5–6:** Second-quarter revenue missed estimates. Management also said its AI video ad tool was "still [a] work in progress." The stock fell 19.7%. A securities class action followed, covering buyers from February 12 to August 5, 2026. The deadline for lead plaintiffs is Monday, November 16. It is a legal step, not a price event, though law-firm ads keep the story in the headlines.
- **Late September to October:**
  - AppLovin sued Unity (a rival ad network), saying Unity's software collected data from AppLovin's MAX auctions. On October 2 the court refused AppLovin's request to block that software quickly.
  - Wedbush called this a "conspicuous" competitive shift. Unity's own ad product (Vector) is growing fast, which could squeeze AppLovin's cut of each ad sale.
  - Wells Fargo and Bank of America cut their ratings. The stock fell nine sessions in a row.
  - On Friday, October 30, it dropped 10% to $228.50 after weaker user numbers at Reddit and Roblox. At that point it was down about 60% for the year.
- **The rebound:** Six straight gains from that low took it to $410.00 on November 9, up 79.4%. The third-quarter report came out after the close on November 4, and the stock rose about 25% on November 5.

## The third-quarter report (November 4): why the story changed
- **Results:**
  - Revenue was $2.18B, up 55%. That was about $100M above the top of the company's own forecast, against a $2.07B consensus.
  - Adjusted EBITDA (a profit measure) was $1.84B, an 84% margin.
  - Earnings per share were $4.30 against $4.03 expected.
  - Free cash flow was $1.42B.
- **The cause of the beat:** A new generation of the ad model is only partly rolled out, and gaming already grew nearly 50%. Foroughi compared its complexity to Axon 2.0, the update that drove the 2024 surge, and said "the transition is still in front of us." That is the bull story: most of the gain is still to come.
- **Consumer and e-commerce:** Spend grew triple digits from a year earlier and double digits from the prior quarter, led by APAC. Self-serve suits sophisticated advertisers, and small businesses are "further into the future."
- **Fourth-quarter forecast:** Revenue of $2.365–2.395B, against about $2.25B expected. That is still a slowdown from 14% to 8–10% growth over the prior quarter, and management would not raise it.
- **Buybacks:** $1.4B of shares bought back in the quarter, and another $3.2B authorized, for $3.6B in total. The CFO said they bought more because the share price had fallen well below their view of fair value.
- **Analyst targets:**
  - Raised: RBC to $520, Oppenheimer to $520, BTIG to $450, Morgan Stanley to $450, Goldman to $445 (rating stays Neutral).
  - Cut: Scotiabank to $450.
  - Average target is about $498.
- **Risks raised on the call:**
  - UBS asked about advertisers leaving over rising auction prices.
  - Management admitted it will need more data, and it is open to buying data through an acquisition.
  - It said there is no 2027 forecast, a "tougher Q1" is coming as e-commerce ad spend resets after the holidays, and connected TV ads won't add to results soon.

## The last five sessions
| Date | Move |
|---|---|
| Nov 9 | Closed $410.00 (end of the six-day run) |
| Nov 10 | Down about 3.5–4.5% on profit-taking; intraday low about $383.31 |
| Nov 11 | Up 2.3%; ETFs were net sellers of $16.7M |
| Nov 12 | Closed $393.68 |
| Nov 13 | Up 3.9% to $409.10 while the major indexes fell; high $413.88; volume 3.42M against a 5.61M average |

The stock has held between about $383 and $414 since the jump, which is a flag-like pause just above its 200-day average. Friday's push back to the top of that range came on light volume and with no news I could find. The 1% fade after hours to $405.21 leaves it just below the 200-day ($405.79 by your screen; MarketBeat says $407.35).

## What could move it in the next 1–10 sessions
- **No scheduled company event.** The next earnings are around February, and I found no investor conference.
- **E-commerce data:** Third-party trackers of e-commerce sign-ups and spend (Bank of America and Citi both publish these) have moved the stock before; the July 13 drop came from one. Black Friday and Cyber Week ad spend is the obvious next check of the consumer story, and the company itself expects a big fourth quarter.
- **Short interest:** The mid-November figure comes out soon. It was 11.6M shares on September 30, about 3.5% of shares available to trade, or 2.3 days of normal volume. That is not large, so a short squeeze is not much of the explanation for the rally.
- **Open overhangs that could flare at any time:** the SEC probe, the Unity dispute and arbitration, a San Diego County lawsuit over ads served to children, and possible insider sales now the post-earnings trading window is open.
- **Market:** The stock has a high beta and moves with ad tech and AI sentiment. It still fell into the October low alongside peers like Reddit and Roblox.

## How to read it
- **Bull case:** The fundamental fear (slowing growth, little new product, competition) was answered by actual numbers. The new model is mostly still to roll out. The company is buying back stock heavily. Even after an 80% bounce the stock is about 44% below its high, at about 27 times earnings.
- **Bear case:** Most of the re-rating happened in six sessions. The stock now sits at a level where many holders bought earlier in the year (at the 200-day average). Volume is fading on up days. The fourth-quarter forecast implies slower growth, management is already warning about the first quarter, and none of the legal or regulatory overhangs has gone away.
- **What it means for a 1–10 session trade:** It is stretched, but it has digested the move sideways rather than giving it back. The narrative has turned positive, and there is no near-term event to force it either way. The things to watch are Monday's open around $405, the $383 low from November 10 below, and the $414 high from November 13 above.

**Unverified:** Weekend news; November short interest; any November insider filings; the official transcript wording (I used the auto-generated Motley Fool transcript); and Unity's third-quarter figures, which came from an AI-written aggregator summary.

**LUNR: the story going into Monday (researched Sunday night, Nov 15)**

**Short version:** Intuitive Machines has changed from a lunar-lander company into a satellite manufacturer and defense contractor, and its numbers have grown fast. The stock has gone the other way. It is roughly a third of its June high and was down about 25% this year before the report. On Nov 12 the market chased the record quarter at the open, then sold it all day as people found what was underneath it. On Friday the whole space group sold off, LUNR traded down about 7%, and then it climbed back to finish almost flat. Earnings did not change the stock's story. It still trades on how investors feel about space stocks.

**1. What the company has become**
- **Lanteris (closed January 2026, $800M in cash and stock).** It bought a satellite maker, and that is now most of the business: $215M of Q3's $269M revenue. Revenue is up about 5x from a year ago.
- **Defense work.** This went from 3% of revenue to about 30% in Q2. It includes 18 missile-defense satellites (the "AMDT3" Tranche 3 program) for Golden Dome, the US missile-defense shield.
- **Moon work.** It remains the identity and the retail draw. On Nov 9 NASA named it one of 8 vendors on CLPS 2, NASA's next 10-year moon-delivery contract ($10B base plus a $5B option). Orders under it are not expected to pick up until 2027.
- **Earth observation.** It won a third NASA Earth-science contract in six months (FALCON-RADAR, announced about Nov 3; the stock rose 8%).

**2. The quarter (reported before the open Nov 12)**

Headline numbers beat:
- **Revenue:** $269.3M against a consensus of about $246–248M.
- **Loss per share:** $(0.02) against about $(0.11).
- **Gross margin:** 26%.
- **Adjusted EBITDA:** +$8.3M, the first positive figure.
- **Free cash flow:** a record +$33M.
- **Backlog:** $1.87B.
- **Cash:** $464M.

Why the day faded, in roughly the order sellers likely saw it:
- **Guidance was trimmed.** Full-year 2026 revenue is now $920–950M, so the midpoint fell from about $950M to $935M. That implies Q4 revenue of about $258–288M against a street estimate near $287M, so Q4 could come in below Q3. A Macquarie analyst pressed the CFO on this, and his answer was hedged: "more level to slightly up."
- **The quality of the beat was weak:**
  - About $19M of gross profit came from one-time contract adjustments. Without that, adjusted EBITDA was negative.
  - The narrow loss per share was helped by a $30M non-cash gain on warrants.
  - The operating loss was still $34M.
  - The CFO said part of the cash flow was "a little bit" of working-capital timing.
  - Free cash flow for the year to date is still –$112M.
  - The company disclosed material weaknesses in its internal controls.
- **Next year may not grow.** Management expects 40–45% of backlog to turn into 2027 revenue, about $760–855M. Asked about "at least $750M" for 2027, the CFO said "in that range." That is below 2026's $935M unless new awards land. Formal 2027 guidance comes with Q4 results.
- **The moon mission slipped again.** IM-3, the third moon landing, now targets "March–April 2027." The CEO said "maybe April." In late October the plan was January–March 2027. Its relay satellite, Altus-1, rides on IM-3, and the service revenue from it "has not yet been quantified."
- **Investors are being diluted.** Shares outstanding were 232M on Nov 5 (177M Class A and 55M Class C). The company has raised about $337M gross under its $500M at-the-market program, which sells new shares into the market at an average price of $23.90. About $160M of that program is left, and the stock is now around $13.
- **Other items:**
  - A $9.5M reserve against HughesNet, a customer that went bankrupt, was not added back to EBITDA.
  - $94.7M was removed from backlog when two contracts were cut back.
  - The CEO was "not certain" how the midterm elections affect Golden Dome funding.

**3. How the price moved**
- **The fall:** the stock was in the high $30s in early June. Several things pulled it down:
  - On about June 3 the $500M share-sale program was announced and the stock fell 13%.
  - It lost NASA's Lunar Terrain Vehicle (moon rover) contract.
  - SpaceX listed around June 14 at $150 a share and money rotated out of smaller space stocks.
  - It fell 27% in October, from $14.24 to about $10.39, when space stocks sold off together.
  - It was around $9.92 on Nov 4.
- **Nov 12, the reaction day:** I estimate Wednesday's close at about $12.18, working back from the reported +16% at $14.17. The stock gapped to about $14.35 and closed about $13.03, up 7.0%. That fits your screen.
- **Nov 13, Friday:** high-beta stocks sold off on a hot producer-price (PPI) report and a Fed official calling inflation broad-based. LUNR hit about $12.15 (–7%) in the morning, as AST SpaceMobile (ASTS) fell 9% and Rocket Lab (RKLB) 5%. It recovered to close at $13.00 (–0.23%). Absorbing a sector selloff in one day is a point in its favour. The $12.65 after-hours print gives back some of that.
- **Analysts:**
  - Roth cut its target from $30 to $20 on Nov 13 and kept Buy.
  - KeyBanc ($38 to $30) and B. Riley ($43 to $34) cut targets just before the report.
  - Bank of America appears with a Sell and a $13 target dated Nov 12, but only one source shows it.
  - Consensus is still around $26–29, which tells you more about how much the stock has fallen than where it is heading.
- **Short interest:** 28% of float as of April 30. I found nothing more recent.
- **Valuation:** about $3.0B market value, or about $2.9B including cash and debt, which is roughly 3x 2026 sales.

**4. What this means for one to ten sessions**

**Dutch Bros (BROS): what's going on, as of Sunday 2026-11-15**

## The short version
BROS is a fast-growing drive-thru coffee chain. Its stock has fallen from a 52-week high of $74.02 to the mid-$30s. It is down about 41% this year because of two big drops after earnings: about 19-26% after Q2 in August, and about 21% after Q3 on Nov 5. Both quarters beat estimates. Both times the guidance and the slowing traffic were the problem. The business is still growing about 30% a year. The market is now debating two things:

- **Bulls:** comps are just choppy because of gas prices and a weak consumer.
- **Bears:** competition and the company opening stores near its own stores are starting to slow growth at existing shops.

## Q3 report (after the close Nov 4)
- Revenue was $549.8M, up 30%, slightly above the $548.6M estimate. Adjusted EPS was $0.25 against $0.24 expected. Adjusted EBITDA was $101M, up 30%.
- Same-shop sales grew 4.4% across the whole system (company and franchise shops) and 5.4% at company-run shops. Visits grew only 0.4% system-wide and 1% at company shops. In Q2, sales grew 5.8% system-wide with 1.7% visit growth, so traffic is slowing. It is still the 14th straight quarter of positive same-shop sales.
- Full-year guidance was cut:
  - Same-shop sales went from 5-6% to "at least 5%."
  - Revenue went from $2.1-2.13B to "at least $2.1B." The analyst estimate was about $2.13B.
  - Adjusted EBITDA went from $385-390M to about $380M.
  - Capex was raised to $370-390M.
- One analyst worked out that the low end of the guide implies Q4 system comps of about 2.5%. That is the analyst's math, not company guidance.
- Margins: profit at company-run shops was 28.1%. Costs for occupancy and other items rose 100 bps (one percentage point), driven by rent on build-to-suit leases and utilities. Management says those costs stay high into 2027. High coffee prices cost more than a point of margin, and management floated raising prices.
- CEO Christine Barone described "heightened choppiness" and blamed gas prices more than competition. She said she sees no measurable hit from 7 Brew or McDonald's drinks. She said October and the start of the holiday season were "encouraging."
- The bullish part: about 250 openings planned for 2027, up from 185 in 2026. That is ahead of what analysts expected. New shops are bringing in about $2M a year each, against a $1.8M plan. Dutch Rewards members account for 74% of visits, and mobile orders are 17%, up 4 points. Management expects more stores taking sales from nearby Dutch Bros shops in 2027 but hasn't put a number on it.

## Analysts after the report
They cut price targets but nobody downgraded:
- Stephens: $65 to $47, still Overweight, while warning of a "meaningful" decline in the shares
- TD Cowen: $55 to $50, called the guidance worry a communication problem the company can fix
- KeyBanc: $59 to $52
- Gordon Haskett: $72 to $50
- Freedom: $95 to $65
- Mizuho: target set at $55
- Baird: still positive, but said management "seems disconnected from investor expectations"

Most analysts still rate it a buy. Average targets are around $61, well above the price. Zacks has it at #4/#5 (Sell or Strong Sell) because estimates are being cut.

## Insiders and short sellers
- Executive Chairman Travis Boersma and his entities sold about 1.39M shares at about $44.73 on Nov 4, the day of the report but before results came out. The sales were under a pre-arranged trading plan (10b5-1). Insiders sold about $180M of stock in the last 3 months. There were no insider purchases after the drop; the last director buys were in May and August, at about $51.
- Short interest was about 19% of the shares that trade freely as of mid-October (MarketBeat). Other sites show 9-16%, so the figure is uncertain. If it is near 19%, rallies can run harder, but that is also a large group betting against the stock.

## How the price has moved
| Date | Close | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| Mid-Oct | about $37-38 | Low of $36.51 on Oct 12 |
| Nov 4 | $43.99 | Rallied back into earnings |
| Nov 5 | $34.57 | Gap down of 21% on 14.8M shares |
| Nov 6 | $33.77 | Low of $33.17, the 52-week low |
| Nov 9 | $36.01 | High of $36.61 |
| Nov 10-12 | drifted to $33.71 | |
| Nov 13 | $35.90 | Opened $33.56, low $33.25 (above the 33.17 low), high $36.03, 6.35M shares |

Context for reading your screen's signal:
- **Friday's turn is a move inside a range.** For seven sessions the stock has been basing between $33.17 and $36.61. Friday's close is still below the Nov 9 high of $36.61.
- **The "3.1 ATR below the 20-day average" overstates how stretched it is.** The 20-day average still includes about 13 sessions at $41-44 from before the gap. Most of the distance is the gap itself, not a selling climax.
- **Volume:** 6.35M on Friday was well above the roughly 4.4M daily average from before earnings. It was only about average for the days since the gap.
- **Catalyst:** I found none. MarketBeat only pointed back to the Q3 beat. I also couldn't confirm what the overall market or restaurant stocks did that day.
- **Levels to watch:** the gap's starting area around $37.8 and the mid-October range of $36.5-39 sit above. The $33.17 low sits below. The 50-day average is about $40.2 and the 200-day about $52.4.

## Long-running debate
- **Bull case:**
  - Store growth of about 19% a year, with new shops bringing in about $2M each.
  - Long-term target of 7,000 shops.
  - About 1.9x forward sales, against about 3.2x for Starbucks.
  - Price-to-earnings in the mid-40s, well below the 60x+ it traded at earlier this year.
- **Bear case** (one short seller's July write-up, from when the stock was $55.83):
  - New store classes bring in less than older ones.
  - Expansion is into lower-income Southern states, where shops bring in less (about $1.9M against $2.45M).
  - Build-to-suit leases push up rent, so the EBITDA margin is stuck around 18%.
  - Coffee chain 7 Brew is expanding into the same markets.
  - Their target was about $41. The stock is now below that.

## For a 1-10 session window
- There is no scheduled company event; the next earnings are around February. The news flow is likely to be:
  - more target cuts or an eventual downgrade
  - any further Boersma sales filed on Form 4
  - news from the sector or competitors (Starbucks, McDonald's drinks, 7 Brew)
  - gas prices and how consumers are holding up
- **Points for a bounce:** a gap down that was too big for a beat-and-trim quarter, possible short covering, a 7-session base holding above $33, and Friday's strong close.
- **Points against:**
  - It's the second straight quarter of guidance-driven damage, so trust is low and buyers may wait for Q4 comps.
  - Estimates are falling.
  - Large holders who sold earlier this year may sell into strength.
  - $36-38 is where people who bought on Nov 5 and in the mid-October range get back to even and may sell.

**Data caveats:** Sources disagree on several numbers: the size of the Q2 drop, the size of Boersma's sales ($106M versus $267M over different windows), and short interest. One Stocktwits piece listed adjusted EPS as $0.20 against $0.25 expected; the transcript says $0.25 reported. I used the transcript and stockanalysis.com price data where they conflicted.

agents.report:
## KRE vs XLF: the story behind the lag

**Short answer:** this week's lag has a macro cause that is still in play. It doesn't look like random drift. Short-term Treasury yields jumped as markets moved to price a Fed rate hike in December. That kind of move hurts small, deposit-funded banks (KRE) more than the big-bank, card, broker and insurer mix in XLF. I found no single news event or credit problem specific to regional banks.

### What happened in the week of Nov 9–13
- **Yields rose sharply, led by short maturities.** The 2-year rose 35 bp to 4.86% and the 10-year rose 24 bp to 5.10%. That was the 10-year's biggest weekly rise since April 2025. The gap between 2-year and 10-year yields narrowed from 35 bp to 24 bp, which means the curve flattened. ([mlq.ai](https://mlq.ai/news/treasury-yields-head-for-their-steepest-weekly-jump-since-april-2025-as-gold-sinks-toward-a-one-year-low/))
- **Why yields rose:**
  - Tue Nov 10: October consumer prices came in hotter than expected (headline +0.4%, core +0.3%).
  - Thu Nov 12: oil rose after Trump said the US didn't need an Iran deal.
  - Fri Nov 13: October producer prices rose 0.3% on the month, a little soft, but 6.5% on the year, the most since 2022. The 10-year hit about 5.15%.
  - Fed officials Hammack, Daly and Logan all sounded hawkish. ([CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/amp/2026/11/13/treasury-yields-fed-rates.html))
- **The Fed:** the target range is 3.75–4.00%. Futures price a December 9 hike as certain: about 86% for a quarter point and about 14% for a half point, up from near zero a week earlier. Morningstar says there have already been two hikes in 2026.
- **Stocks:** the S&P 500 rose 2.5%, its first weekly gain in five weeks. Financials helped lead the Dow. Small caps and property stocks were pressured by higher yields. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO and the stock fell about 13%. ([Mitrade wrap](https://mitrade.com/au/insights/weekly-market-wrap/us/2026-11-16))
- **Friday close:** KRE closed at 72.74 (+0.30%) and XLF at 58.68 (+0.81%). That 0.5% gap matches what our screen saw. ([KRE](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/KRE/), [XLF](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/XLF/))

### Why this mix hurts KRE more than XLF
1. **Funding costs.** KRE holds about 167 small and mid-size banks with equal weights; the largest is about 1.2% of the fund ([SSGA](https://www.ssga.com/us/en/intermediary/etfs/state-street-spdr-sp-regional-banking-etf-kre)). These banks fund themselves with deposits, so a rising Fed rate pushes up what they pay. Meanwhile a flatter curve shrinks the gap between what they pay and what they earn on longer loans. XLF is mostly megacaps: big banks, card networks, brokers, insurers, and a large Berkshire position. Many of those earn more as short rates rise. (I didn't check XLF's current weights this session.)
2. **Fight for deposits.** Evercore says AI-driven cash products offering high yields are pulling deposits away from banks ([Yahoo, Oct 12](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/why-bank-stocks-shocked-everyone-by-getting-thrashed-141552354.html)). BofA says investors are watching for risks to deposits as AI evolves, and that regional banks won't re-rate until the rate path is clearer ([Finwires, Oct 8](https://finwires.com/en/article/regional-bank-stocks-could-continue-languish-amid-macro-7362540)).
3. **Balance sheets and loans.** With the 10-year above 5%, small banks' bond portfolios lose more value, and the commercial property and middle-market loans they hold come under more strain. BofA flagged that loan pressure. The bond-portfolio point is my own reasoning; I didn't find a source quantifying it.
4. **Small-cap selling.** KRE trades like a small-cap fund, and small caps were the group under pressure this week.

### What argues against a lasting lag (the reversion case)
- **Regional bank results are fine.** Regions beat Q3 estimates with adjusted EPS of $0.73. Its margin widened to 3.68%, loan losses fell to 0.29% of loans, and deposit costs barely moved. Its Q4 guidance of about 3.70% already assumes a December hike. ([Investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/company-news/regions-financial-q3-2026-slides-eps-beats-credit-quality-improves-93CH-4954546)) Morningstar puts deposit beta (the share of rate changes banks pass on to depositors) at about 35% this cycle, against a 47% norm.
- **Mergers are active.** Hancock Whitney agreed to buy Trustmark on Nov 12 in an all-stock deal worth about $3.2B, with about 7% tangible book dilution and a 2.8-year earnback ([8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000750577/000119312526457037/hwc-ex99_1.htm)). Valley National received approval for its Providence deal ([GlobeNewswire](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/11/09/3398969/0/en/valley-national-bancorp-announces-the-receipt-of-required-regulatory-approvals-for-the-acquisition-of-providence-financial-corporation.html)). Deal activity tends to support KRE.
- **The hike is already fully priced.** A quarter-point hike in December is no longer news. Further damage to KRE needs either a half-point hike or more hikes priced into 2027.
- **The credit worries mostly sit with big banks.** Concerns about data-center lending and private credit are aimed mainly at large US banks, which are in XLF ([Global Finance, Nov 6](https://gfmag.com/banking/bank-outlook-weighs-stocks-strong-earnings/)).
- **Yields are below their peak.** The 10-year at about 5.15% is still under its Oct 5 high of 5.31%.

### What could move the pair in the next 1–10 sessions
- **Nvidia earnings on Tuesday Nov 17**, the first report since Huang left. A relief rally would broaden into risk assets and small caps and help KRE. A miss would hit risk appetite and small caps more broadly.
- **FOMC minutes, retail sales and industrial production** this week. I didn't confirm exact dates.
- **December 8–9 FOMC.** This falls about 16 sessions out, beyond the 1–10 session window, but anything that shifts the odds of a half-point hike moves this pair.
- **In short:** short-term yields falling or holding steady favors KRE catching up. Another jump in short-term yields, or the half-point odds climbing, favors the lag continuing.

### Things to check before trading
- **A suspicious Friday evening print.** Yahoo shows KRE at 71.01 after hours (−2.38%, around 5:50 PM CT Friday). Over the same period XLF was flat overnight and Regions only −0.17%, and I found no news to explain it. It is probably a thin or bad print. Check the Monday pre-market quote before treating it as real.
- **Gaps in this research.** I ran out of web searches before finding any regional-bank-specific news from Nov 9–13, small-cap index figures for the week, or exact dates for next week's data releases. If KRE's lag is partly a bank-specific story, I didn't find it. You can send a follow-up to continue the search.

**My read:** the lag makes sense given a hike-driven flattening of the curve, and it hasn't turned yet. Betting KRE catches up means betting short-term yields calm down, and Tuesday's Nvidia report is the nearest event that could trigger that. Without that calm, a 2.1 standard-deviation stretch that is still widening has a clear reason to stretch further.

agents.report:
I've put together the NXST story below. I ran out of web searches before I could get the post-earnings analyst moves or the details of a November 14 Form 144 filing.

## The story in one paragraph
Nexstar is the largest US local-TV station owner. It closed a $6.2B all-cash purchase of Tegna (another big local-TV owner) on March 19, 2026. It declared the deal closed on its own authority after FCC and Justice Department approval, on the same day eight state attorneys general and DirecTV sued to block it. A federal judge in Sacramento (Nunley) issued a temporary restraining order in March and a preliminary injunction on April 17. Nexstar now legally owns the 60 Tegna stations but cannot combine them or influence how they're run. That means about $225M of planned savings are on hold, while Nexstar carries all of the deal's debt. The stock fell from a 52-week high of 254.30 to the 150s–160s. It sat there until late October, when three things lifted it: a record midterm political-ad cycle, a better-than-feared Q3, and a court hearing coming up this week.

## Monday's key fact: the appeals-court hearing is Tuesday, November 17
- The Ninth Circuit (the federal appeals court for the West) hears Nexstar's appeal of the injunction in Pasadena on Tuesday, November 17. It will be livestreamed. I couldn't find the hearing time or the judges.
- Nexstar wants two things:
  - Narrow the injunction to the 31 markets (out of 53) where both companies own a major-network station.
  - Remove the state attorneys general from the case.
- A ruling is unlikely on the day. Management said on the earnings call that it is "optimistic" but a decision "will take time." The judges' questions and tone on Tuesday are what could move the stock.
- History that weakens Nexstar's credibility:
  - It closed the deal while lawsuits were being filed against it.
  - In August the district court said Nexstar's placement of its own executives on Tegna's board was a "brazen" violation of the injunction. The board has since been replaced with independent members.
  - A special master (a court-appointed compliance monitor) has been discussed.
- Settlements so far:
  - Ohio's attorney general settled, with conditions on two Ohio stations.
  - In August, CEO Perry Sook said a settlement before trial would benefit Nexstar. With the deal already closed, he faces no walk-away deadline or delay penalties.
  - The merits trial is set for July 6, 2027.
- Nexstar said on the Q3 call that it reached a carriage deal with DirecTV, the private plaintiff, without disclosing terms. I found no sign that DirecTV has dropped its lawsuit. If the two have made peace commercially, that may matter, but it is unconfirmed.

## Regulators
- **D.C. Circuit:** On July 9 it dismissed challenges to the FCC's approval as premature. Challengers can come back once the full FCC rules on pending reviews, which the FCC expects by year-end.
- **National ownership cap:** The FCC repealed the 39% cap in a 2–1 vote on August 6. Opponents asked the FCC in October to pause the repeal, and Nexstar opposed that. Lawsuits can't be filed until the rule is published in the Federal Register.
- The injunction rests on antitrust law, so the cap repeal doesn't lift it.

## Q3 results (Thursday, November 5)
- **Revenue:** a record $2.13B, up 78%, with Tegna contributing $765M. On a combined basis (as if both companies were already together a year ago) it rose 15.4%.
- **Earnings:** adjusted EBITDA (a cash-earnings measure) was $756M. EPS of $7.92 missed the $8.08 consensus.
- **Political ads:** $317M in Q3. Combined political revenue for 2026 is a record $1.1B, and Sook called this a "new normal."
- **Weak spots:**
  - Non-political ads fell 5% on a combined basis, and management guides Q4 down by high single digits.
  - Combined distribution revenue (fees from cable and streaming services) grew only 2.1%.
- **The CW network:** management expects its first profitable quarter in Q4. It said the network won't be profitable for all of 2027.
- **Debt:** $11.4B, with $446M cash and net leverage of 4.04x EBITDA. Nexstar repaid $350M in Q3 and $525M more after quarter-end, and wants leverage closer to 3x.
- **Shareholder returns:** no buybacks; debt paydown comes first. The quarterly dividend is $1.86, about a 3.6% yield.
- **Cash flow:** adjusted free cash flow was $443M in Q3 and about $1.1B for nine months. That is a very high yield on a market value of roughly $6.4B, but it is inflated by a political year.

## How the price got here (daily closes)
- **Before the run:** about 157 on October 6, then 164–169 through late October.
- **Election-week run-up:** 164.50 on October 28 → 171.44 on October 30 → 177.54, 178.56 and 185.12 from Monday to Wednesday, November 2–4. Midterm election day was November 3.
- **Earnings day, November 5:** opened 192.42, hit 200.10, fell to 182.65 and closed 187.97 on the heaviest volume (829k). It was a big gap that faded.
- **November 6:** low of 181.67, close 190.02. Buyers stepped in after the fade.
- **November 9:** up 5.9% to 201.23 on 577k shares. Deutsche Bank cut its target to $233 that day, so the cut didn't drive it. Sinclair, a peer, rose 6.7% on November 10, so the move looks sector-wide. I found no single news item behind it.
- **November 10–11:** 206.59, then 209.74.
- **November 12:** opened 210, hit 211.50 and closed 205.97. That is the first intraday reversal of the run.
- **November 13:** went ex-dividend ($1.86) and closed 207.94 on 348k shares. Counting the dividend, it actually gained about 1.9%. Your 20-day high of 209.59 is roughly November 12's 211.50 adjusted for the dividend.
- **Overall:** about +26% in 12 sessions. Volume peaked on earnings day and has fallen since, and the move is still running into Tuesday's hearing.

## Analysts and insiders
- **Ratings:** six Buy, one Hold, one Sell.
- **Targets:**
  - Wells Fargo: $249, Buy (October 16).
  - Citi: raised to $225 from $215, Buy.
  - Deutsche Bank: cut to $233 from $240 (November 9).
- **Insiders:** a Form 144 (an insider's notice of a planned share sale) was filed on November 14. I couldn't see who filed it or how many shares. EVP Blake Russell filed a Form 4 (the report of an insider trade) dated November 9, also without detail.

## How this reads for the next 1–10 sessions
- **Bull case:**
  - At about 208 the stock is still roughly 18% below its high, and it is cheap on cash flow.
  - Tuesday's hearing could go well. The judges might seem open to narrowing the injunction to the overlap markets, and a narrowed order would free up most of the $225M in savings.
  - Talk of a settlement adds a second way to win.
- **Bear case:**
  - The stock is stretched up 26% and has rallied into a known event: "buy the rumor, sell the news."
  - The hearing won't produce a ruling, so a sceptical panel or simply no news could let the gains out.
  - With political ads over, Q4 non-political ads are guided down by high single digits, and 2027 is a year without elections.
  - November 12's reversal near 211 and falling volume show the buying is slowing.
  - A possible insider sale was flagged on November 14.
- **Event risk:** Tuesday's argument is the main uncertainty. Later in the window, an FCC year-end ruling on the reviews or a Federal Register publication could also move the stock.
