agents.report:
I'd lean against a long on AVEX for the next 1–10 sessions, or at least wait. The business is doing well, but Friday gave back about two-thirds of the post-earnings gain on normal volume. The "bad news bought" signal is weaker than it looks: the EPS miss was mostly a one-time tax accounting charge, and revenue beat estimates by a wide margin.

I hit the web search limit for this turn before checking two things. Nothing in this report covers how the drone and defense group traded on Friday, or anything that came out over the weekend.

**The company.** AEVEX makes military drones and unmanned systems and is based in Solana Beach, CA. Its products include the Phoenix Ghost loitering munition, one-way attack drones and long-range strike aircraft, and since September, unmanned boats. Madison Dearborn, a private equity firm, controls it and the board. About 83% of revenue comes from the US government. It listed on the NYSE on April 17, 2026 at $20, raising $320M. Shares outstanding are about 127M across two share classes. At $12.51 that is roughly a $1.6B market value, or about $1.68B once you add $172.5M of debt and subtract $78.6M of cash. That is about 13 times this year's adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization) at the guidance midpoint.

**How it got from $42 to $9.**
1. **Spring:** the stock ran from the $20 IPO to a high of $42.34.
2. **Early June:** a secondary offering of 8M shares at $27, about 41 days after the IPO, was made possible by waiving the IPO lock-up early. The stock fell 16% on June 2 and 7% on June 5. A class action filed August 20 claims the waiver was planned all along; that case is consolidated and stayed.
3. **The core worry:** a large share of revenue was Ukraine-related (Phoenix Ghost and an EUCOM Deep Strike program), and it is winding down. That was $167.7M in Q1, $52.5M in Q3 and an expected $36.3M in Q4.
4. **September 8:** AEVEX bought BlackSea, which makes unmanned boats. It paid $279M in cash plus 12.7M new shares, with an earnout of up to $50M in shares that only pays if the stock averages $28 over 30 days.
5. **October 21:** Bloomberg reported that the Navy had stopped buying BlackSea's drone boats (called GARC) after an independent review, having spent about $137M on them. The stock fell 32% from 14.34 to 9.68 on 13M shares. The company said no orders were stopped: it had already delivered all 325 boats under its contract and is now funded for upgrades. Analysts cut targets on October 22: RBC to $22, and Piper Sandler and UBS to $13.
6. **November 4–6:** another slide of about 14% and then 11%, which I could not explain from any source. It made the 52-week low of 8.95 intraday on November 6.
7. **November 10:** AEVEX announced a contract worth up to nearly $400M for unmanned aircraft from an unnamed US customer, its largest since listing. It is a ceiling, not funded orders.

**Q3 results (November 11, after the close).**
- **Revenue:** $189.7M against an estimate of about $149M, up 56.5% from a year earlier.
- **The EPS miss:** the GAAP loss of $0.40 per share came from a one-time $37.9M deferred tax charge tied to the BlackSea deal. Without it, net income would have been about $21M. This is what the screen read as a 328% miss.
- **Adjusted EBITDA:** $30.8M, a 16.2% margin. The drone segment's margin rose to 22.6%.
- **Guidance raised:**

| FY2026 | Before | Now |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $700–720M | $820–840M |
| Adjusted EBITDA | $105–111.5M | $128–132M |

About half the revenue raise is from the core business and half from adding BlackSea. Consensus had been about $753M.
- **The key turn:** revenue outside the Ukraine programs ("core" revenue) rose from $49M in Q1 to $137M in Q3, with $185.5M implied for Q4. Q3 was the first quarter where core revenue was bigger than Ukraine revenue.
- **Orders:** Q3 bookings were $250M, about 1.3 times revenue. Funded backlog is $444M, with another $1.1B awarded but unfunded. The sales pipeline is $16.6B, and $4.9B of that came with BlackSea. Management expects about $150M of maritime revenue this year and says GARC upgrade work continues. No 2027 guidance was given.
- **Analysts:** Needham cut its target to $30 from $45 but put the stock on its Conviction List. Piper Sandler stayed Neutral and raised its target to $15 from $13. The consensus target is about $25–28, with 11 Buy, 2 Hold and 1 Sell.

**What the price did.**

| Date | Close | Move | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nov 11 | 12.13 | +4.6% | Before the report |
| Nov 12 | 13.76 | +13.4% | High 15.53, 5.95M shares, closed about 11% off the high |
| Nov 13 | 12.51 | −9.1% | 2.1M shares, about normal volume |

Friday's after-hours price was 12.32. Overhead, the October 21 gap runs from about 12.4 to 14.3, and the 50-day average is about 14. Support is around 11.4–11.6 (the November 9–10 range), then the 8.95 low.

**For the trade decision.**
- **For a long:** the "Ukraine cliff" fear has largely played out, the revenue beat and raise were large, almost all of this year's guidance is covered by funded backlog, the valuation is modest for a drone company growing this fast, and analyst support is strong.
- **Against:** two-thirds of the earnings pop was gone within a day, and Monday looks set to open slightly weaker. Investors still distrust the company over the lock-up episode, the lawsuit and the Navy report. The stock moves 5–15% a day, with repeated unexplained drops. 12.7M BlackSea shares could be sold at some point; I couldn't find any lock-up on them. Q4 depends on task orders under the new contracts arriving on time, and management named a stopgap budget (a continuing resolution) as a timing risk.

The stronger setup would be a long only if it holds 11.4–11.6 and then closes back above about 13.8. Without that, the evidence leans toward a pass.

## What the company is
- It makes solar panels at its G1_Dallas plant. That plant came from a 2024 deal with Trina Solar, a Chinese solar maker that is still a related party and a creditor (Trina also has an anti-dilution right).
- It is building G2_Austin in Rockdale, Texas, a 2.1 GW factory for solar cells. Making cells in the US is what lets its panels count as domestic.
- The bull case is US-made solar panels and cells protected by tariffs and the Section 232 trade rules, plus the 45X manufacturing tax credit (a federal credit per unit of solar parts made in the US). Long-term targets are $375–450M a year of adjusted EBITDA once the first phase of G2 is running, and $650–750M at full build-out.
- There is also a side story: turning its old Norwegian site, Giga Arctic, into a data center. That is only a non-binding letter of intent so far.

## What happened last week
**Thu Nov 12, Q3 results (released before the open)**
- Revenue was $196.6M, against a consensus of about $270M. It was also down 6% from a year earlier.
- Gross margin was 8.5% and adjusted EBITDA was –$16.4M.
- Net loss to common shareholders was $41.6M, or $(0.14) a share.
- The company says part of the weakness came from deliberately building 326 MW of panel inventory for 2027 deliveries. Inventory is now $335M, up from $116M at year-end.

**The G2 financing**
- G2 is still not funded. The company is in exclusive talks with institutional investors on a package it says will be mostly debt, but nothing is signed.
- It says the package may include new shares or securities convertible into shares, and "there can be no assurance" it closes.
- First cell production has slipped to around April 2027, previously Q1. On the call the CEO admitted the promised financing "didn't happen."
- A $50M convertible note issued on Sept 30 was described as a bridge to that financing.

**The SEC probe (in the quarterly filing, after Thursday's close)**
- In September the SEC's Fort Worth office told the company it is investigating its public statements about qualifying for the 45X credit, plus "other accounting matters."
- This matters because the company has booked $155.3M of 45X credits and has not yet sold them for cash. The finance chief said buyers have been slow for companies without an investment-grade rating.
- The filing also mentions a material weakness in internal controls that still has to be fixed.
- Separately, since Nov 2025 there is a Justice Department grand jury subpoena about a 2023 sale of company stock by an executive who is also a board member.
- A plaintiff law firm, Block & Leviton, is now soliciting shareholders for a possible lawsuit.

**Guidance and orders**
- Dallas panel output for 2026 is now 4.0–4.2 GW, the top of the old range. The preliminary 2027 plan is 5.3 GW.
- More than 3.5 GW of 2027 output is under contract, with new deals signed in October including Avantus. Panel prices are said to be firm, around $0.35/W with imported cells and $0.45/W with domestic cells.
- One thing to check: the 10-Q shows $617M of the $624M nine-month revenue as related-party sales.

## Balance sheet and share supply
- **Cash:** $59.5M unrestricted, $137M including restricted cash. Operating cash flow was –$176M over nine months.
- **Debt:** about $944M in total, including about $495M of convertible notes. Enterprise value is about $1.46B against a market cap of about $574M.
- **Going concern:** management says it has enough money for 12 months and is in compliance with its loan covenants.
- **Shares:** 300.6M outstanding. The company has chosen to pay the rest of an Evervolt patent purchase with about 18.9M new shares. 7M were issued in November and the rest are held back by an ownership limit, so more stock is waiting to be issued.
- **Encompass:** funds run by Encompass Capital agreed on Wed Nov 11 to buy up to $15M of stock at the company's option. The offer expires Mon Nov 16, and I found nothing saying it was used or extended.
- **Short interest:** about 79M shares, 39% of the float, about 4.5 days to cover.

Short version: TXNM isn't trading on its own business right now. It's a pending buyout. Blackstone Infrastructure agreed to pay **$61.25 per share in cash**, and the stock moves on how likely that deal looks. Friday's "new high on 2.9x volume" is the gap to the deal price closing a little, not a breakout.

## The story

- **The company.** TXNM Energy (the former PNM Resources) owns two regulated electric utilities: PNM in New Mexico and TNMP in Texas. Together they serve more than 800,000 homes and businesses.
- **The deal.** Announced May 2025, valuing the company at about $11.5B including debt. Shareholders approved it in August 2025.
- **Approvals already in hand:** Texas regulators (February 2026), FERC (February 2026), the FCC, the antitrust waiting period, and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (August 21, 2026).
- **The one approval left:** the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission. This is the commission that turned down Avangrid's attempt to buy PNM in 2021.

**What went wrong in 2026:**
- Blackstone had bought $400M of TXNM stock directly from the company without New Mexico's prior approval.
- In June the commission's hearing examiners called that illegal. On July 2 the commission voted 2-1 to void the sale and fined the companies $300k.
- The sale was unwound, and Blackstone returned $13.3M in dividends it had kept after being criticised.
- In July the companies moved the merger's walk-away date to **May 31, 2027**. Expected closing slipped from late 2026 to the first half of 2027.

**The fix:** a revised application (motion filed September 15) offering about $300M of benefits to New Mexico customers, up from about $175M. That includes $220M of credits on customers' bills. The commission accepted the revised application on October 16.

**Why the stock firmed last week:** on **November 10** the hearing examiners denied the opponents' emergency motion to hold the hearings in abeyance. That keeps the hearings on schedule. The stock closed at 58.10 that day, then rose 1.3% to 58.83 on November 11, its biggest move in weeks, and held 58.82 and 58.87 after that.

I found no news for Friday itself. The 2.9M-share volume moved the price by only 5 cents. It looks like traders betting on the deal adding shares, or a block trade, not new information.

## Context the screen doesn't see

- **The "52-week high" is distorted by the dividend.** The stock went ex-dividend ($0.4225) on October 23, dropping from 58.73 to 58.27. Since October 5 it has closed between 58.10 and 58.87. On a dividend-adjusted basis Friday's close is a new high, but only by a few cents.
- **Upside is capped.**
  - The gap to $61.25 is $2.38, or 4.0%.
  - Two more quarterly dividends (paid around February and May) would add about $0.85, assuming the deal closes around mid-2027.
  - That works out to roughly 5.5% over about 7 months.
  - In 1 to 10 sessions, a realistic gain is a few tenths of a dollar, about 0.5 to 1%.
- **The risk is lopsided.** If the deal fell apart, the stock would drop toward where it traded before the announcement. That could mean $5 to $8 or more, though utilities have rallied since 2025, which helps. I couldn't confirm the pre-deal price; I ran out of web searches.
- **Upcoming dates:**

| Date | Event | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Nov 30, 2026 | Commission staff and opponents file testimony | About the 10th session from Monday, at the edge of the window. Staff supporting the revised deal would likely narrow the gap; staff opposing would likely widen it sharply. |
| Dec 18, 2026 | Companies' reply testimony | |

| Undated | New Mexico Supreme Court ruling | It agreed, in an appeal over a separate gas-utility takeover, to decide whether the commission must require a "net public benefit" for utility sales. A ruling could change the bar this deal has to clear. |

- **Open political risk.**
  - The New Mexico Department of Justice and the state Attorney General have raised concerns.
  - Advocacy groups, including New Energy Economy and Prosperity Works, are fighting the deal.
  - Opponents argued TXNM could have collected a $350M termination fee from Blackstone; TXNM says it had no legal basis.

- **The business is fine but doesn't drive the price.** Q3 ongoing earnings were $1.62 per share against $1.33 a year earlier, helped by rate increases in both states. The company gives no guidance while the deal is pending.

I researched HALO on the web. The search limit for this turn ran out near the end, so a few points rest on a single source; I flag those below.

**HALO (Halozyme Therapeutics): the story as of Sunday 10:05 PM CT, Nov 15, 2026**

## What the company is
Halozyme earns royalties. Its ENHANZE technology (an enzyme, rHuPH20) lets IV antibody drugs be given as a quick injection under the skin. Partners pay a royalty on every sale of those versions. The main earners are J&J's Darzalex SC, argenx's Vyvgart Hytrulo, Roche's Phesgo, BMS's Opdivo Qvantig and Roche's Ocrevus Zunovo. It is building two newer technologies, Hypercon (bought with Elektrofi in Nov 2025) and Aerocon (from Surf Bio). Merck's under-the-skin Keytruda (Keytruda Qlex) uses a rival enzyme from Alteogen, and Halozyme is suing Merck over its MDASE patents.

## What broke the chart
This was a gap down on news, not a slow slide. Daily closes:

| Date | Close | Volume | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Oct 30 | 130.91 | 1.4M | Near the 52-week high of 134 |
| Nov 4 | 130.34 | 1.6M | |
| Nov 5 | 122.96 | 2.9M | -5.7% in the session, before earnings came out after the close |
| Nov 6 | 103.63 | 6.2M | -15.7%, low 102.52 |
| Nov 9–13 | 102.92 → 100.27 | 1.4–2.9M | Five-session range of 99.26–105.64 |

The low reading on our screen (RSI 27, 4.4 ATR below the 20-day average) mostly comes from that one two-day gap. Since then the stock has held a tight 99–105 range. Friday's low of 99.26 matches Wednesday's 99.27. The 99.48 after-hours price sits at the floor of that range, not below it.

**Why it fell (three things in two days):**
1. **Medicare drug-price rule, Nov 5.** CMS finalized a rule that treats an under-the-skin version made with hyaluronidase (the enzyme type behind ENHANZE) as the same drug as its IV parent when Medicare negotiates prices. That closes the "new formulation buys years of price protection" argument behind much of the long-term royalty case. The fall during the Nov 5 session, before earnings, fits this news. I could not confirm that link directly.
   - On Nov 6 Halozyme said it expects "zero to minimal impact" on royalties through at least 2035. Its biggest earner, Darzalex SC, is exempt because all its uses have orphan (rare-disease) status. The market seems not to have believed the company.
2. **Q3 beat and a small raise, Nov 5 after the close.** Revenue was $493M (+39%), royalties $341M (+44%), adjusted EPS $2.39 against about $2.30 expected. Full-year EPS guidance went to $8.75–9.05 from $8.65–9.00, a raise the market had already priced in.
   - Investors may also have disliked parts of the call:
     - US patent reviews keep going against Halozyme. Merck's filing says 11 of 11 final decisions found every challenged claim invalid, and appeals could run to 2028.
     - There are no settlement talks with Merck.
     - Opdivo Qvantig has reached only about 17% of patients against a 30–40% target.
     - BMS handed back some targets.
     - Royalty rates step down in 2028–2030, starting with Darzalex. Management gave no sizes.
   - 2027 guidance and the long-range update come with Q4 results in February. The next earnings date is about Feb 16, 2027.
3. **Downgrades.**
   - **Leerink, Nov 6:** cited limited long-term growth tied to Keytruda royalties and moved its target to $117 from $110. This comes from GuruFocus only. Leerink's earlier underperform call in May 2025 was also about Medicare rules.
   - **Morgan Stanley, Wed Nov 11:** cut the stock to Equal Weight on valuation with a $109 target. It still calls Halozyme a top-quality royalty compounder, says the stock now matches its base case, and points to the royalty step-downs.
   - **Citizens JMP:** raised its target to $149 (Outperform).

## Setup going into Monday
- **Valuation:** about $11.4B market cap, roughly 9.5x forward earnings, EV/EBITDA about 12. That is cheap for a business with royalties up 44%. The bear case is about what happens after 2029, not the next few quarters.
- **Short interest:** 12.1% of the float, 6.2 days to cover (as-of date not given). Enough to fuel a squeeze if good news lands; it also shows that bears hold the narrative.
- **Buyback:** $400M bought so far this year, Q3 at an average of $79.47. About $1.08B in cash after a $1.5B convertible note sale. No buyback was announced after the drop, and the call summary did not mention one.
- **Insiders:** directors sold under pre-set plans in Aug–Sep at $103–108. No buying has been reported.
- **Analysts:** average target about $120, mostly Buy. The two notes since the drop were both downgrades.

## Known event inside the 1–10 session window
- **Thursday Nov 19:** Merck's appeal of the German preliminary injunction against Keytruda SC is heard, according to Merck's Q3 10-Q. That injunction came from the Munich court in Dec 2025. A related hearing is set for Dec 2.
  - If Halozyme wins (injunction upheld), it backs up the Oct 7 Dutch win and the "Merck will have to pay" story.
  - If Merck wins (injunction lifted), it adds to the US patent losses and supports Leerink's view.
  - German appeal courts often announce their decision on a later date, so the result may not come out on Nov 19.
- There is no scheduled earnings or company event before February.

## How to read it
- **Bull:**
  - A strong royalty business is down about 23% in six sessions.
  - Most of the drop came from a Medicare rule the company says doesn't touch its money for nine years, plus a downgrade on long-term growth.
  - The stock has held about $99–100 for three sessions with no further damage.
  - It trades at a single-digit forward P/E, with lots of cash and shorts in place.
- **Bear:**
  - This is a re-rating, not an overreaction to one bad print.
  - The Medicare rule shortens the long-term royalty story at the root. US patent claims keep failing, and the step-downs are real.
  - Each new analyst note since the drop has cut a rating, and none has defended the stock.
  - There is no turn yet: closes went 102.98 → 101.68 → 100.67 → 100.27, and after hours slipped to 99.48.
  - A close clearly below 99.26 breaks the base. With no support marked until the high 80s / 200-day average (about 85), there is room to fall.
- **What would change the picture:**
  - A buyback announcement or insider buying.
  - Analysts defending the Medicare-rule math.
  - The German appeal result.

## Gaps
- The Nov 6 Leerink details come from GuruFocus only.
- The tie between the Medicare rule and the drop is my inference from timing.
- The Nov 19 hearing date comes from Merck's filing as relayed by search; I could not read the filing's text.
- I found no news dated Nov 12–13.

The web search limit for this turn ran out partway through, so I didn't get to why the chip group sold off on Friday, the options market's current earnings bet, or the full FT report. Several pages also refused to load (Bloomberg, CNN, Invezz). Everything below comes from the sources listed at the end. Where sources disagree, I say so.

## The story

This is no longer a story about the business. It's about who runs the company, and about a security and export scandal, landing two days before earnings.

**Timeline (2026):**
- **Oct 5–6:** record high. The 52-week high is 243.37 and the company was worth about $5.75T.
- **Early November:** the stock was already sliding, down about 20% this month. Worries were AI spending and how it is financed, Nvidia funding its own customers (it invested in buyers like CoreWeave and Nebius), and higher yields. Inflation came in hot, and markets now expect the Fed to raise rates again.
- **Sat Nov 8:** Jensen Huang admitted an affair. The woman is reported to be Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore cloud company that is a Nvidia customer. The NYT reported US officials believe she is a Chinese spy. The Attorney General said the Justice Department has not concluded that. Megaspeed is under US criminal investigation for allegedly routing about 240,000 banned chips to China. It denies wrongdoing and says she left in August 2025.
- **Mon Nov 9:** a shareholder lawsuit alleges the company hid material information. The board opened an independent probe. Nvidia says it has "no reason to believe" its secrets or US national security were compromised.
- **Wed Nov 11:** the NYT reported a second relationship, with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell. The board met that night and moved to remove Huang.
- **Thu Nov 12:** Huang resigned as CEO, president and director, effective immediately. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO and keeps the CFO job. Harvey Jones became the first-ever board chair. A third affair, with another employee, was reported. The Manhattan US Attorney is reportedly looking at Super Micro smuggling through Alice Huang's companies. The stock fell as much as 13% during the day and closed down about 4.3%. Retail traders bought heavily: Robinhood customers bought about twice as much Nvidia as every other stock combined.
- **Fri Nov 13:** closed at 162.85 (down 2.0%), range 158.39–170.00. The 52-week intraday low is 148.80. HSBC cut to Hold with a $170 target, down from $375 (one source says $365). Its reasons: the stock struggles until a permanent CEO is named, and about 11% of revenue is at risk of tighter export rules. At least ten analysts have cut to Hold; Wedbush stays bullish. The week was down about 13%, the worst since April 2025, and the stock is more than 30% below its high. It was not only Nvidia: AMD fell 8.8%, the chip index fell 3.4%, CoreWeave fell up to 10.8% and Nebius up to 12.1%. Hot inflation also hit the group.
- **Sun Nov 15 (new since Friday's close):** the FT reports Huang is discussing a comeback as CEO with allies, who are lobbying the White House. CNN reports pressure on Commerce Secretary Lutnick over what he knew about Megaspeed. Treasury Secretary Bessent says much of the administration favors blacklisting Megaspeed. Also in play: the CEO search (Arm CEO Rene Haas reportedly approached; insider Ian Buck at about 40% on prediction markets; Trump has floated Tim Cook), and Huang has hired the law firm Paul Weiss.

## The business going into earnings

Results come out Tuesday Nov 17 after the 3:00 PM CT close, with the call at 4:00 PM CT. It is Kress's first report as interim CEO.
- **Last quarter (Q2 FY27):** revenue $96.2B (up 106% from a year ago), data center $89.0B, gross margin 75.0%, adjusted EPS $2.22.
- **Q3 guidance:** $108B ±2%, assuming no China data center sales, and gross margin of 74% ±0.5 points.
- **Q3 consensus:** about $109.2B and EPS of about $2.47.
- **Weak spots investors will look at:**
  - Free cash flow fell to $21.3B from $48.6B the quarter before.
  - Inventory rose to $31.6B from $25.8B, which the company tied to the Vera Rubin launch.
  - Q2 GAAP profit included a $7.8B gain on equity investments.
  - Margins are expected to drift lower as Rubin ramps.
- **What decides the reaction:** the Q4 guide and the call. An in-line quarter could still disappoint.
- **Valuation (my own arithmetic, not from a source):** at 161, the price is about 16 times $2.47 a quarter annualized. That is very low for this company and is what the dip-buyers are relying on.
- **Expected earnings move:** options priced about ±7.9% as of Nov 3, before the scandal. It is almost certainly wider now, but I couldn't confirm a current figure.

## For a 1–10 session trade

**For a bounce:**
- The board says operations, customer commitments and the product roadmap continue without interruption.
- The quarter is guided and the consensus sits only just above the guide, so a beat is plausible.
- Selling looks exhausted by the numbers (RSI 25, 3.6 ATR below the 20-day average, heavy volume), and retail is buying hard.
- The valuation is the cheapest in years.
- The comeback talk could swing sharply either way.

**Against:**
- The situation is still breaking: new revelations arrived every day last week.
- Several things are still to come:
  - Nvidia's promised statement on its probe.
  - The Justice Department and Manhattan smuggling inquiries.
  - The shareholder lawsuit.
  - Congressional pressure that could tighten export rules.
  - A possible Megaspeed blacklisting.
- An interim CEO who is also the CFO may guide cautiously.
- Cash flow, inventory and customer financing are open to attack.
- The selling was sector-wide (rates and AI-capex doubts), so a good print may not be enough.
- Nothing about the CEO question gets settled in the window, and the comeback talk adds to that uncertainty.

**Key points:**
- Tuesday's report is the main event. Any trade opened on Monday is a bet on the report.
- Friday's close broke the 52-week closing low (164.79). The next nearby level is the 52-week intraday low of 148.80.
- Things not settled:
  - **Friday's volume:** sources say about 360M shares against a 144M average, which is about 2.5 times normal, not the 1.9 times our screen shows.
  - **Thursday's drop:** one source puts the 4.3% decline on Nov 9, not Thursday.
  - **The FT comeback report:** I saw it only through a headline and a search summary, not the article itself.

I found six stories moving prices right now. Mostly they are one argument: whether the AI trade still holds now that rates are rising, Nvidia has no CEO and a record IPO is about to soak up money. The research ended because my web-search allowance for this turn ran out. A few threads go unchecked, listed at the end.

## Where things stood at Friday's close (Nov 13)
- **Indexes:** S&P 500 7,561.67 (−0.4% Friday, +2.5% on the week), Nasdaq 25,136.27 (−0.9%, +2.3%), Dow 52,347.55 (+0.1%, +2.1%), Russell 2000 2,790.49 (−0.3%, +1.3%).
- **The week:** it ended four losing weeks in a row for the S&P and Nasdaq. All 11 sectors rose, led by energy (+5.4%), industrials, communication services and tech. Monday Nov 9 alone was a roughly 2.3% S&P rally on falling oil.
- **Friday was split:** tech was the only sector down more than 1% (−2%). The equal-weight S&P (RSP, an ETF holding every S&P stock at the same weight) rose, and 314 members rose against 185 that fell.
- **Other markets:**
  - VIX 19.30.
  - 10-year Treasury 5.15%, up about 30bp on the week, its biggest weekly rise since April 2025.
  - 2-year 4.87%, 30-year 5.47%.
  - Dollar index 103.4, its highest since April 2025.
  - Brent $95.84, WTI $88.56.
  - Gold $3,886, near 52-week lows.
  - Bitcoin about $68k, its sixth straight down week.
- **Chart levels:** the S&P closed below its 50-day average (about 7,667), with the 200-day near 7,340. The Nasdaq sits right on its 200-day. SOXX (a semiconductor ETF) is about 13% below its 50-day.
- **Sunday night futures:** slightly up, with Nasdaq-100 futures +0.4% to +0.6% depending on the snapshot. Asia was weak Monday:
  - Advantest −10%, Tokyo Electron −5%, SoftBank −4%.
  - Japan's Q3 GDP unexpectedly shrank (−0.1% annualized).
  - China's October data missed.

## The six stories

**1. Nvidia without Jensen Huang: is the AI leader still the AI leader?**
- **What happened:** Huang resigned on Nov 12, effective immediately. It followed reports of affairs, one with a woman US surveillance reportedly suggested was passing information to Beijing. The FBI and Congress are investigating.
- **Who runs it:** CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, and the board named its first-ever chair, Harvey C. Jones. The FT reported the board approached Arm's CEO, Rene Haas; Nvidia says it is still choosing a search firm. Arm fell about 5% Friday. Other names floated: Ian Buck, Lisa Su, and Palo Alto's Nikesh Arora.
- **The stock:** NVDA lost about 12–13% on the week to roughly $161, below a $4T market value. That is its sixth straight weekly decline and about −20% for November, its worst month since late 2022. CNBC says Huang is reportedly considering a comeback.
- **Analysts:**
  - HSBC cut to hold and its target to $170 from $365.
  - Truist cut to hold.
  - Morgan Stanley cut its target to $267.
- **The bear case:** Nvidia funds and partners with much of the AI ecosystem, so a weaker Nvidia may mean less customer financing. Tighter Washington export controls are likely. One bank says the stock struggles until a permanent CEO is named.
- **The bull case:** demand for chips doesn't depend on the CEO. Taiwan's market rose Friday on that view.
- **Earnings:** Tuesday Nov 17, call at 4:00 PM CT.
  - Consensus: revenue about $109B, EPS $2.47. Company guidance was about $108B and a 74% gross margin, excluding China.
  - The key question is whether Nvidia keeps its forecast of about 70% revenue growth for fiscal 2028.
  - Also watched: export-control exposure, the buyback, how Kress handles ecosystem financing, Blackwell and Rubin timing, and Q4 guidance.

**2. Rate hikes are back, with the 10-year above 5%.**
- **How we got here:** under Chair Kevin Warsh the Fed hiked in September to 3.75–4.00%, its first hike since 2023. It held on Oct 28 with two dissents in favor of a hike (Cook and Hammack).
- **The data since:**
  - October CPI rose 0.4% (0.3% expected); core rose 0.3%, its third straight month at that pace. There is no year-over-year figure because the 2025 shutdown left a hole in the data.
  - Payrolls rose 165k against about 65k expected, and unemployment fell to 4.1%. U-6 (the broad underemployment rate) rose, though, and wages (+3.1%) are trailing inflation.
  - PPI was a bit cooler than expected for the month but up 6.5% on the year.
- **Fed speakers:**
  - Waller said 50bp "should be considered" if core runs at 0.3%.
  - Logan sees at least two more hikes.
  - Collins and Daly lean toward tighter policy.
- **Pricing:** a December 9 hike is about 100% priced, with roughly 10–14% odds of 50bp. Goldman sees another hike in March 2027.
- **The argument:**
  - Whether the move is 25 or 50bp.
  - Whether the long end (10-year 5.15%, high 5.31% in early October) breaks higher and pulls stock valuations down.
  - Housing names, banks and gold are trading off it.
- **This week:** Warsh speaks Monday at 11:00 AM CT, though the conference is about AI and productivity and he avoids giving guidance. Retail sales come Tuesday at 7:30 AM CT, and the October FOMC minutes Wednesday at 1:00 PM CT.

**3. Can the AI capex boom survive the midterms, high rates and negative cash flow?**
- **Election:** Democrats won both chambers on Nov 3; one outlet disputes the Senate, so check that against AP. Markets rallied Nov 4.
- **The crash:** on Nov 5 the SOX (the Philadelphia semiconductor index) fell 12.2%, its worst day since April 2025.
  - Moves: Nvidia −9%, AMD −17%, Micron −17.5%, Broadcom −10%, Tesla −11%, neoclouds (companies that rent out AI computing) −10% to −17%.
  - Causes: weak Qualcomm results, worry that a Democratic Congress slows the data-center buildout, and wins for anti–data-center candidates and local moratorium ballot measures in Texas and Georgia.
- **The backdrop:** in late-October earnings, Alphabet, Meta and Amazon showed negative free cash flow. Alphabet fell about 11% on its report. Big-four 2026 capex is about $720–745B, increasingly paid for with debt, share sales and leases. The SOX is still about 23% below its Oct 6 peak.
- **Bulls** (Barclays, Goldman's $7.6T AI-capex estimate): local opposition makes building more expensive but doesn't stop it.
- **Bears:** big-tech results were "an overall disappointment," Dan Ives now sees capex peaking in 2027, and Barclays calls the race a "war of attrition."
- **The tape:** money keeps rotating away from AI infrastructure (memory, optics, servers, power and cooling, neoclouds) into staples, energy and Apple. Apple hit a record $360.80 as a haven. Dip-buying is still heavy: about $37.5B went into big equity ETFs in five days, and $2.1B into SOXL (a 3x leveraged chip ETF) before $2.25B left it Friday.

**4. The Anthropic IPO: a confidence test, and a large new supply of shares.**
- **Terms:** prices Wednesday Nov 18 and trades Thursday Nov 19 on Nasdaq as ANT. The range is $70–78 for 825M shares, a raise of more than $60B plus a $26B private placement. That implies about $1.3–1.45T fully diluted, down from about $2T talk in September.
- **Demand:** reports say about 6x oversubscribed, and bankers are weighing pricing above the range. I didn't find a primary source for the demand figure.
- **The question:** does a strong debut revive the AI trade, or does the money needed to buy it come out of other AI and megacap holdings?
- **The S-1 numbers:**
  - Q3 revenue $17B, though quarter-over-quarter growth slowed to 47% from 144%.
  - Committed compute spending of nearly $1T.

**5. Iran, Hormuz and oil: is the war premium leaving?**
- **Background:** the US-Iran war began Feb 28. A ceasefire was reportedly agreed in June and collapsed in July; the sources disagree on that history.
- **This month:** Brent is about −20% in November, briefly near $90 on deal hopes.
- **The twist:** on Nov 12 Trump said the US doesn't need a deal ("we've got their Strait"), and Brent rose 3.3%. Tankers hit mines Friday, and attacks on shipping continue. The IEA says the market is returning to surplus.
- **Why it matters:** oil is the main lever on inflation and Fed expectations. Monday's rally came on falling crude, and energy led last week.

**6. Lower-priority threads to track**
- **Trump-Xi at APEC in Shenzhen, Thursday Nov 19,** plus a Trump-Xi-Putin meeting. Officials expect a truce extension, not a deal. The US says export controls aren't negotiable, and China has threatened rare-earth retaliation.
- **Government funding runs out Dec 11.** Prediction markets put a shutdown at about 38%, and Democrats want to use the talks to limit Iran war funding.
- **The consumer:** Home Depot reports Tuesday before the open, with 10-year rates central to its story and CEO Decker on leave. TJX, Target and Lowe's report Wednesday (Stifel cut Lowe's to sell). Walmart reports Thursday at 7:00 AM CT. Retail sales come Tuesday.
- **Crypto weakness:** Bitcoin is below its 200-week average. MSCI plans to remove MSTR from its indexes, and the Democratic sweep stalls crypto legislation.
- **Prediction markets:** DraftKings, Flutter and Robinhood dipped Friday on reports that Meta is testing a prediction-market app. The DOJ and CFTC sued Arkansas over its enforcement against Kalshi.
- **Deals:** Modine jumped about 28% on reported takeover talks with Samsung.
- **Unconfirmed:** a report of an FAA nationwide ground stop late Friday weighed on airlines. My one search for it found nothing, so treat it as unconfirmed.

## The week's calendar (CT)
| Day | Event |
|---|---|
| **Mon Nov 16** | Empire State survey 7:30 AM; Williams 8:05 AM; Warsh 11:00 AM; earnings from Baidu, Tyson, XPeng |
| **Tue Nov 17** | Retail sales 7:30 AM; Home Depot and Disney before the open; Nvidia after the close (call 4:00 PM) |
| **Wed Nov 18** | TJX, Target, Lowe's before the open; housing starts; FOMC minutes 1:00 PM; Palo Alto after the close; Anthropic prices that night |
| **Thu Nov 19** | ANT starts trading; Walmart and Alibaba before the open; jobless claims; Philly Fed; Trump-Xi; Intuit and Ross after the close |
| **Fri Nov 20** | Final UMich sentiment and inflation expectations; monthly options expiration |

## Caveats
- Several sources are newsletters or aggregators, and some figures differ between them; I cited the majority figure. Where they disagree:
  - Nvidia's weekly loss: 12% versus 13%.
  - The odds of a 50bp hike.
  - The size of the Senate majority.
  - The Iran ceasefire history.
- Big outlets (WaPo, Bloomberg, CNN) blocked fetching, so I relied on the AP-style syndicated recaps and CNBC.
- **Not covered because the search allowance ran out:** a deep Nvidia preview (export-control and customer-financing detail), consensus for retail sales, and any weekend Iran news. You can send a follow-up to continue on those.

agents.report:
I found what moved YETI (YETI Holdings, maker of premium coolers, drinkware and bags) through its Q3 report and how it traded through Friday. The search limit ran out before I could explain two moves in the run-up (see the end).

**The story in one line:** profit came in well ahead of forecasts, mostly thanks to lower tariffs, but sales missed and the company said shoppers are hunting for deals, more so at the start of the holiday quarter. Investors sold because sales growth is slowing, and the profit beat didn't matter.

## The report (Thursday 2026-11-12, before the open)
- **Sales:** up 4% to $509.4M, against about $523M expected. Excluding a charge for a 2023 soft-cooler recall, sales rose 6% to $517.9M.
- **Earnings per share (adjusted):** $0.91, up 49% from $0.61, against $0.84 expected. That is the 8% beat your screen saw.
- **Gross margin (adjusted):** 59.0%, up 3.1 points. About 2 of those points came from lower net tariff costs, and the quarter also booked a $4.7M tariff refund. So the beat came from lower costs, not stronger demand.
- **Channels:**
  - Selling to stores rose 19%.
  - Selling direct to customers fell 6% (3% excluding the recall charge). The drop was in YETI's own US website and US Amazon sales. Management blamed Amazon's Prime Day moving from Q3 into Q2 and YETI taking part less, and said direct sales would have been about flat without that.
  - US website traffic fell, but the share of visitors who buy rose.
- **Drinkware:** up 8%. A small group of fad-driven cups and bottles that have gone out of style cut about 5 points from its growth, with similar pressure in Q4. Management expects that drag to end in Q1 2027.
- **Coolers and equipment:** up 4% excluding the recall charge, and expected to return to double-digit growth in Q4.
- **International:** up 19%, with Europe, the UK, Japan and Australia strong and Canada weak. The full-year international outlook was cut to growth in the mid-teens, mainly because of Canada.
- **Full-year guidance cut:**
  - Sales growth: about 6%, down from 7–8%.
  - Operating profit growth: 7–9%, down from 10–12%.
  - Earnings per share: $2.90–2.95, down from $2.94–3.00.
  - Gross margin (57.5–58%), operating margin (about 14.9%) and free cash flow ($200–225M) were left unchanged.
  - The implied Q4 gross margin of about 57.5% sits below Q3's 59%. Management put that down to channel and country mix, not discounting.
- **What management said about demand:** shoppers are "increasingly deal motivated." The higher-priced products are under the most pressure, while the cheapest hard coolers (Roadie 8 and 15) are holding up. Demand "moderated" early in Q4 and was "more acute" as the holiday season ramped up, though the CFO stressed that most of the quarter is still ahead. YETI says it isn't discounting more than in past years, but expects the market to stay heavy with deals into 2027.
- **2027:** no guidance yet. Management expects sales growth within its long-term target of mid-to-high single digits.
  - Helping: last year had an extra (53rd) week that won't repeat, the drinkware drag ends, and new products are coming.
  - Hurting: tariffs that started in late February 2026 will cost more in early 2027, plus higher costs for plastic resin, steel, magnets and fuel.
  - A $100M cost-saving program is meant to offset this; details come next quarter.
- **Balance sheet:** inventory up 22%, but up only 6% over two years because last year's level was unusually low. Cash of $74M roughly matches debt of $71M, and the $300M credit line is unused. YETI has bought back $150M of shares this year, with $350M of authorization left. At about 75M shares and $39.42, the company is worth roughly $3.0B.

## What analysts did
- Piper Sandler downgraded to Neutral and cut its target from $58 to $39, which is almost exactly where the stock is now.
- KeyBanc cut to $49 from $57 and stayed positive.
- Stifel cut to $48 from $50 and kept Buy. Its target is 14.6 times its 2027 earnings estimate of $3.28 (down from $3.42).
- Search results also mention Citi cutting to $50 and kept Buy, and Baird cutting, but I couldn't open those pages.
- Before the report, 12 of 16 analysts rated it Buy, with an average target of about $55.

**Paylocity (PCTY) — the story as of the 3:00 PM CT close, Monday 2026-11-16**

Paylocity sells payroll and HR software to mid-sized US employers. It fell hard this year when investors feared AI would hollow out software that charges per user, then recovered as its results kept holding up. Today's rise was the payroll group being bought as a safe place during an AI and chip sell-off, and PCTY led that group. I found no company news today.

**Today**
- **Price:** closed at $184.46, up 3.50% from $178.22. It opened at $180.06, ranged from $178.38 to $185.88, and closed near the high. That high is a new 52-week high.
- **Volume:** about 995k shares against an average of about 653k, roughly 1.5 times normal.
- **After hours:** flat at $184.46, but on a delayed quote taken seconds after the close, so it says little.
- **Market:** the S&P 500 fell 1.9% and the Nasdaq about 2.5%; the VIX (Wall Street's fear gauge) jumped about 19%. Nvidia fell about 4% on tighter US limits on chip sales abroad. The market is waiting on Nvidia's earnings Tuesday night and Anthropic's IPO, expected Thursday at a reported $1.4T valuation, which may pull retail money out of other AI stocks.
- **The payroll group all rose on the red day:** Paycom (PAYC) +2.4%, Paychex (PAYX) +1.8%, ADP +1.1%. PCTY's +3.5% was the best of them.
- **Why the group fits a day like this:**
  - Low beta, about 0.43, meaning it usually moves much less than the market.
  - No exposure to chips or AI infrastructure.
  - It earns interest on the payroll cash it holds for clients ("float"). That income grows when rates rise, and the 10-year Treasury yield is about 5.1%.

**The bigger arc**
- **The fall:** early 2026 brought a sell-off in seat-priced software, nicknamed the "SaaSpocalypse." The worry was that AI would do more of the work, so customers would pay for fewer users. The software index fell more than 26% from late January to its low in April. PCTY's 52-week low is $92.99, so it has roughly doubled since; Investing.com puts the six-month gain at about 66%.
- **Management's answer:** on the August call it said it had seen no AI disruption. It points to the parts that are hard to copy: service, payroll tax-filing complexity, and capital-heavy operations.
- **The climb into earnings:** about $146 on Oct 6, then $178.53 on Oct 26, a pullback to about $168, and $170.96 just before the report.
- **The report (fiscal Q1 2027, Nov 5, after the close):**
  - Revenue $451.7M, up 10.7% and above the $443M estimate.
  - Recurring revenue up 12.0%.
  - Adjusted earnings per share $2.09 against $1.91–1.93 expected.
  - Full-year revenue guidance raised $30M at the midpoint, to $1.910–1.925B (about 8% growth).
  - Q2 revenue guidance $452.5–457.5M (about 9% growth).
  - Bought back $152.5M of stock (1.1M shares).
- **Reaction:** the stock dipped late on Nov 5. On Nov 6 it opened at $162, swung up to $180.88 and closed at $173.15. It then crept up through $178–180 for a week before today's breakout.
- **Analysts after the report:**
  - Price targets raised: BTIG to $210, Truist to $200, Citizens JMP to $200, Citi to $214.
  - Barclays raised to $176 but kept Equal Weight, a neutral rating.
  - The older consensus target, about $178, is now below the price.
  - Wall Street Zen, a ratings site, downgraded to Hold on Nov 15.

**The bear case**
- **Interest income did much of the raise.**
  - Expected float income went from about $103M to about $118M after the Fed's September hike replaced the two cuts the company had assumed.
  - That is roughly half of the $30M raise.
  - One analyst called the beat in earnings excluding float the smallest in the company's history.
- **Growth is guided to slow:** recurring revenue from 12% in Q1 to about 10% in Q2 and about 9% for the year.
- **Weaker details:**
  - Adjusted gross margin fell year over year.
  - Quarterly free cash flow fell to $56M from $67M.
  - Buybacks were partly paid for with credit-line borrowing ($131M, up from $81M).
- **Valuation:** about 36 times past earnings (P/E), at a 52-week high.
- **Steady insider selling under pre-set trading plans:**
  - About $26.5M sold over 90 days, including founder and director Steve Sarowitz.
  - Sarowitz sold at about $180 on Nov 11 and Nov 13.
- **The AI worry hasn't gone away:** a November fund letter sold out of Paycom because it thinks AI coding tools lower the barrier for new competitors. The Anthropic listing could bring that argument back this week.

**What could move it in the next 1–10 sessions**
- **Nvidia's earnings (Tuesday night):** if the AI trade recovers, money may rotate out of defensive names like this one. If the sell-off deepens, the group could keep getting bought.
- **The Anthropic IPO (Thursday):** a reminder of the AI threat to software, or just a draw on cash.
- **Rates:** a December Fed hike was widely expected after September. Higher rates help float income.
- **No company catalyst:** next earnings are expected around Feb 4, 2027.
- **Levels:** today's breakout at about $181.6–185.9; the old resistance zone at $178–181 should now act as support. The 50-day average is about $158 and the 200-day about $128, so the stock is well extended above both.

## BDX (Becton Dickinson): the story behind the run and today's turn

**In short:** BD is a more profitable, slower-growing medical-supplies company than it was a year ago, and the market likes it more. The stock rose about 23% in six weeks, from roughly $178 on Oct 7 to $220.36 today, and is up about 38% this year. The fundamental news was good, but the price has now overshot what analysts think the shares are worth. Today's turn is real but small, and on light volume.

### What BD is now
- **A pure medical-supplies company.** In February 2026 BD split off its lab-instruments and diagnostics business and combined it with Waters, receiving a $3.9B cash distribution. What's left: needles, syringes and catheters (Medical Essentials), infusion pumps led by Alaris (Connected Care), drug-delivery devices such as prefilled syringes and injection pens (BioPharma Systems), and surgical and vascular products (Interventional).
- **A management turnaround story.** Under the "Excellence Unleashed" programme, organic growth reached about 4.4% in fiscal Q3 and 5.6% in Q4, against a street expectation of about 3%. That beat is the core of the bull case.

### How the run built up
1. **Oct 6: tariff deal.** BD agreed with the U.S. government to invest $19B in the U.S. (including $3B in factories) in return for relief from future Section 232 tariffs. It was the first big medical-device company to do so. The stock jumped intraday, then faded and closed at $180.30. This started the move from the ~$178 low.
2. **Oct 7 – Nov 3: steady climb** to about $198 on modest volume. Zacks upgraded to Strong Buy on Oct 21.
3. **Nov 4: +5.6% to $209.19 on 4.46M shares**, the day before earnings. That is roughly 2.5 times normal volume. I found no specific news for it; Benzinga attributes it to positioning ahead of results.
4. **Nov 5: fiscal Q4 results** (BD's fiscal year ends Sept 30). The stock closed at $213.55 on 4.0M shares.
   - Revenue was $5.27B, up 5.6% excluding currency. Adjusted EPS was $4.15, up 27%, against a $4.07 estimate.
   - Q4 adjusted operating margin rose about 280bp to 28.6%. Free cash flow for the year rose 42% to $2.9B.
   - BD bought back $2.4B of stock in fiscal 2026, added a 10M-share buyback authorisation and raised the dividend for the 55th year in a row.
5. **The fiscal 2027 guide was soft, and the stock ignored it.**
   - Revenue growth is guided to low single digits (Evercore pressed on a roughly 2–2.5% organic figure). Adjusted EPS is guided to $13.10–13.30; the midpoint is a touch below the $13.25 FactSet consensus. One aggregator cites a $12.67 consensus, which looks stale.
   - Q1 adjusted EPS is guided to **$2.32–2.37 against a street figure of $2.71**, a large gap. Management blames a tough Alaris comparison (about 250bp off Q1 revenue and about 500bp off full-year EPS) and a cautious approach to a new internal operating-system cutover.
   - The guide assumes no tariff relief. Management calls it "responsible" and says it can "even exceed" it.
   - The market read it as deliberately low, so it can be beaten.
6. **After the results:** Wells Fargo upgraded to Overweight and lifted its target from $170 to $242. Citi raised its target to $241 (Buy), RBC to $225 (Sector Perform), JPMorgan to $202 (Neutral) and Piper to $200 (Neutral). Barclays raised to $195 but kept its Underweight (sell) rating. The CEO sold about $629K of stock at $210 on Nov 5 under a pre-set trading plan, which is routine.
7. **Nov 6–13: a slow grind higher**, with volume back to 1.6–2.2M, ending with a record close of $218.03 on Nov 13.

### Today, Monday Nov 16
- Open 219.45, high **220.36 (new 52-week high)**, low 215.64, close **216.47 (−0.7%)**. The close sits about 18% of the way up the day's range.
- Today's high was above Friday's and today's low was below it, a bearish reversal shape.
- Volume was 1.50M, the lightest since earnings. That makes it a weak reversal, not a distribution day.
- I found no company news today.

### Where the stock stands
| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| 20-day average close (my calculation) | about $204.7, so the stock is about 5.7% above it |
| 50-day / 200-day average | about $191 / about $171 |
| Average analyst target (18 firms) | **$197.47, about 9% below the price**; 8 hold or worse |
| Adjusted P/E on fiscal 2027 guidance | about 16.4x |
| Beta | 0.22 (defensive, moves little with the market) |
| Gap left by the Nov 4 jump | about $198–200; no support below $209 until that zone |

### The case for a short over 1–10 sessions
- The shares already price in the "guide is too low" view. Most targets are below the price, and Barclays' sell call stands.
- A reversal at a new high after a roughly 23% move is a clean place to define risk. A stop just above $220.36 is close.
- The Q1 guide ($2.32–2.37 against $2.71) is a real cut to near-term estimates. Finimize flags the risk that the valuation multiple shrinks once forward estimates come down.
- The pre-earnings jump left a gap in the high $190s that the stock has never retested.

### The case against
- No news has broken the story. Every update since October has been positive: tariff deal, better growth, margins, upgrades.
- The buyback is large. Fiscal 2026 repurchases were $2.4B, about 4% of the company's market value, and the guide assumes about 273M shares.
- With a beta of 0.22, the stock tends to drift rather than drop sharply. It pulled back only twice in the run (Nov 6 and Nov 10), and both times shallowly.
- Today's reversal came on the lowest volume since earnings.
- **Investor Day is Dec 10, about 17 sessions away**, just outside the trading window. Funds that want to own the stock into the event may buy dips. Wells Fargo explicitly expects capital-return news and longer-term targets there. The $1.06 dividend goes ex on Dec 10, so a short closed within 10 sessions would not have to pay it.
- No short-interest data turned up.

### Read for the journal
A short is reasonable but not strong. It is a valuation call against a stock that is above most targets and reversed at a new high, with the stop just above $220.36. The realistic downside is a pullback to the 20-day average around $205, or at most the $198–200 gap. The main risks are steady buyback support and investors buying ahead of the Investor Day.

One thing could not be confirmed: the exact cause of the Nov 4 jump.

I found no single headline that explains today's move. TSCO closed at **$37.95, up 4.1%**, on about 15.3M shares, against a 20-day average of about 13.4M. After-hours was flat at $37.93 to $37.95. On a day the S&P 500 fell 1.9%, this looks like money rotating into a beaten-down, low-beta, mostly-essentials retailer. That rotation is layered on a small piece of good news (a Baird target raise this morning) and a bounce that has been building since the October 22 earnings report.

## The big story: a broken stock trying to base

- **2026 collapse.** The stock started the year near $50 and fell to a 52-week low of $28.36 around July.
  - **Q1, April 21:** earnings missed and customer transactions fell 1%. The stock fell about 11% in a day, from $44.81 to $39.57.
  - **Analyst reaction to Q1:** Piper Sandler downgraded the stock, pointing to structural weakness in pet adoptions.
  - **Q2, July 23:** comparable-sales guidance was cut from +1–3% to −1% to flat. The company took a $66M charge on its Petsense chain and withdrew its long-term financial targets. Management blamed a weak May, fuel prices and drought.
- **Q3 on October 22 was the turn.** The stock gapped down to $29.90 and then reversed to close at $34.73.
  - Sales of $3.91B (+5.1%) and EPS of $0.43 both beat estimates. EPS was still down from $0.49 a year ago.
  - Comparable sales were only +0.4%, but they improved each month: July negative, August modestly positive, September solid.
  - Management said comparable sales and customer transactions were positive for the first three and a half weeks of Q4, and credited share gains rather than a better market.
  - The 2026 guidance was kept, and it assumes positive Q4 comparable sales. Gross margin fell 90 basis points in Q3; Q4 is guided down only 10 to 30 basis points.
  - For 2027, management plans more than $75M of cost cuts, fewer new stores (85 to 90), capital spending below 4% of sales, and $425M to $450M of buybacks this year. Management said it is "not comfortable" with an operating margin below 9%.
  - Full 2027 guidance and a new long-term framework come with Q4 results in late January.
- **Since then, a steady uptrend.** The stock went from $31.61 on October 28 to about $37.50 by November 9 to 10, and today made **its highest close since April 23**.
  - It is now above the 200-day average (about $37.2 to $37.5) for the first time since April.
  - The 50-day average is about $33.6.

agents.report:
I researched Church & Dwight (CHD) on the web. Monday's close at $114.74 is a record. The stock has risen without much of a pause from about $94 on October 1, a gain of roughly 22% in six weeks. Three things are behind it: investors moving out of tech into consumer staples, real gains in sales volume at the company, and a small new deal announced this morning.

## What happened today (Mon 11/16)
- **The deal.** At 6:00 AM CT CHD agreed to buy 45% of BALI Treatment GmbH, owner of the BALI CURLS and BALI GENTS hair-care brands, for about $225M. That values the whole company at about $500M, roughly 5x its ~$100M of sales.
  - BALI was founded in 2022 and is growing fast, mainly in curly and textured hair.
  - The deal closes in Q1 2027. CHD can buy the other 55% two years after closing.
  - The company says it will add to cash earnings in 2027.
  - It is small next to a $27B company. It feeds the "buy fast-growing brands" story but doesn't change the numbers.
- **The market.** The S&P 500 fell 1.92% to 7,416.59, its third losing day in a row, and the Nasdaq fell 2.49%.
  - The selloff was led by AI and chip stocks. Nvidia fell about 4% after a report that its board is not discussing bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO.
  - The VIX (Wall Street's fear gauge) jumped as much as 25% to 24.05.
  - Consumer staples was the only S&P sector that rose. XLP (the consumer staples sector fund) hit a record at midday, and PG rose about 2%.
  - CNBC listed CHD and Colgate (CL) as hitting 52-week highs "as investors sought safer sectors."
- **The volume** was 3.40M shares against about 1.4–2.0M on a normal day. The day's high was about $115.42, so the stock closed a little below it.

## The bigger story
1. **This is a record, not just a 52-week high.** The previous record close was about $112.84 on March 10, 2025. Friday's $113.00 already beat it, and today's $114.74 is another record. There is no old price level overhead where earlier buyers might sell. The 52-week low was about $81.49, and the stock is up about 40% from it.
2. **The business is genuinely improving.** Q3 results came out October 30:
   - Organic sales (sales from businesses owned in both years) rose 5.1%, against an outlook of about 3%. Almost all of that was volume (+4.6%); price and mix added only 0.5%.
   - Adjusted EPS was $0.92, up 13.6%, against an outlook of $0.89.
   - Gross margin was 46.8%, up 170 basis points (1.7 points), helped by tariff refunds and productivity.
   - The full-year organic sales outlook rose to about 5%. Q4 is guided to about 4% organic growth and adjusted EPS up 17–19%.
   - The board approved a new $1B buyback. CHD bought back only $37M of stock in the first nine months, against $600M a year earlier, so there is plenty of room to buy.
   - Market share is rising. TheraBreath mouthwash gained 3.5 points to a record 26.8%, ARM & HAMMER cat litter gained 0.6 points to 24%, and laundry and Waterpik also gained share.
   - Reported sales growth is small because of the businesses sold in 2025 (vitamins and others), which cut about 6 points off reported growth.
3. **The money moving into staples matters more than the company news.** XLP reportedly gained about 11% in October, its best month since it launched in 1998. CHD's run since October 1 tracks that move.
   - The price path: about $94 → $108.86 on October 22 (3.1M shares) → $107.23 after earnings → $109–112 for two weeks → $113.00 → $114.74.
   - So CHD is riding the sector move, with its own fundamentals adding to it.

## Risks over the next 1–10 sessions
- **The rotation could reverse.** If Nvidia's results on Tuesday after the close, or the Anthropic IPO, steady the AI trade, money could flow back out of defensive stocks. Commentators have called staples crowded and richly valued since February, and a MarketWatch piece warned the bubble "may have shifted from artificial intelligence to soap."
- **It is expensive.** The trailing P/E is about 35 and the forward P/E about 29. The consensus price target of about $110 is below the current price; Morgan Stanley's highest-noted target is $117 with an equal-weight rating. Further gains rest on the move continuing, not on analysts being behind.
- **Input costs.** CHD's guidance assumes crude oil at about $100 a barrel and about $150M of inflation for the year. Brent is $96 after reports of tankers hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz, so a further oil spike would put pressure on costs. Markets are also pricing a Fed leaning toward another rate hike.
- **Events this week.** PG holds its investor day on Thursday 11/19, which will rub off on CHD in either direction. CHD has no earnings until about late January. It went ex-dividend on November 13, so no dividend falls in the holding window.
- **Touchland is flat for 2026.** Competitors moved into its stores. Management expects growth in 2027.

## Bottom line
- **For:** a record close on 1.7x volume against a falling market, backed by real volume growth, a raised outlook, an unused $1B buyback and a fresh deal headline.
- **Against:** the stock has run 22% in six weeks, sits above consensus targets, and its next move is closely tied to whether the AI selloff keeps going. Nvidia on Tuesday after the close is the event that decides that.

Some numbers came from secondary sites and were not checked against the company's filings:
- The 52-week range, P/E figures, the $110 consensus target and the daily price history are from stockanalysis.com.
- The Q3 market-share figures are from MarketBeat's summary of the earnings call.

agents.report:
EW is stretched, but nothing in the news says the move is breaking. It is a fundamentally driven re-rating that has gone quiet near its highs rather than climaxed. The next real catalyst is the investor conference on December 4, after a 1–10 session window ends. That leaves a fade short leaning on a "nothing new" stall against a story that is still being upgraded. I'd call it a weak short, not a clean one.

**Price path (StockAnalysis daily bars)**
- **Base:** EW traded around $88–92 from Oct 20 to Oct 30, and closed Oct 30 at $92.01.
- **Nov 2 (PROGRESS trial data at the TCT heart conference, plus an Edwards investor event):** It fell intraday to $87.90, about 5% down, then closed up 1.4% at $93.26. Volume was 12.2M, the heaviest of the period. That reversal is where the run started.
- **Nov 3–9:** It closed higher every day. Nov 4 was +4.4% into the evening earnings report. Nov 5 traded 9.2M shares and closed at $100.82. Nov 9 closed at $104.71, a one-year high.
- **Nov 10–16:** It flattened. Closes were $104.01, $105.81, $105.80, $107.15 and $107.11.
  - Today's open was $107.00. It set a new high of $108.00, dropped to $104.94 (about -2% from Friday), then closed flat.
  - The intraday dip was bought, so today shows no sign of a turn.
- **Run size:** Up about 16% in 11 sessions.
  - The close is about 10% above the 20-day average of closes (about $97, my calculation from those bars).
  - It is about 18% above the 50-day average ($90.42) and about 24% above the 200-day ($86.32), both per MarketBeat.
- **Volume:** It has faded from 9–12M shares to about 4M, below the roughly 4.8M average. The buying pressure is gone, but nobody is distributing heavily either.

**Why it moved: real news stacked over about eight weeks**
1. **Medicare coverage rule (CMS, Sep 10).** TAVR is a catheter-delivered replacement aortic valve and Edwards' core business.
   - CMS dropped the study-participation requirement and hospital volume thresholds for symptomatic patients.
   - Asymptomatic severe stenosis is covered only inside CMS-approved studies. The American College of Cardiology says none exist yet, so in practice that coverage is not live.
   - Management calls the effect "gradual."
2. **PROGRESS trial (Nov 2, NEJM).** It tested TAVR in moderate (not yet severe) aortic stenosis with risk features.
   - Death or heart-failure events were 16.7% with TAVR versus 23.9% with monitoring, a 33% risk reduction.
   - This could greatly enlarge the treatable population. But there is no approval for it and no filing timeline, and management admits these patients are hard to identify in community practice.
   - Stifel had warned beforehand that a positive result was priced in. The stock still ran.
3. **Q3 results (Nov 4): beat and raise.**
   - Sales were $1.72B, up 10.5%. Adjusted EPS was $0.80 versus about $0.74 expected.
   - The mitral and tricuspid valve line (TMTT) grew 44%.
   - Full-year guidance went to about 11.5% sales growth, 9–9.5% TAVR growth and $2.97–3.05 adjusted EPS.
   - GAAP EPS was $0.53 after a $220M write-down of an R&D asset.
4. **Analysts keep raising targets.**
   - Nov 5: Baird upgraded to outperform ($116). UBS went to $118, Barclays to $120, RBC to $115 and Mizuho to $120.
   - Around Nov 11: TD Cowen raised to $121.
   - Today: Wells Fargo raised to $121 (overweight).
   - The consensus average target is about $110, now only about 3% above the price. That gap is where the stretch shows.

**The bear side**
- **Valuation:** About 60 times trailing earnings, versus roughly 33 for the healthcare median (Trefis). Reported EPS has fallen for three years because of one-off charges, and buybacks are shrinking.
- **Growth mix:** The CEO said share gains have "reached a plateau," so TAVR growth now has to come from a bigger market.
  - Boston Scientific's 2025 exit from Europe has stopped flattering the comparisons.
  - Edwards expects to lose some share over 10 years.
- **Q4 guidance:** It implies a sequential dip in TMTT dollars.
- **Competition:** The FTC blocked the JenaValve deal in January 2026. One unconfirmed source says JenaValve got FDA approval and launched on its own.
- **Insiders:** About $5.5M sold over 90 days, all small and routine (one under a 10b5-1 plan).
- **Context:** Trefis found no new catalyst for the six-day streak and noted the S&P fell over the same stretch. The move is stock-specific and has had no fresh news since Nov 5 apart from target raises.

**What matters for a 1–10 session short**
- **The key date is just outside the window.** The investor conference is Dec 4 at the NYSE, from a single secondary source; Edwards' events page wouldn't load to confirm it. 2027 guidance and the moderate-stenosis plan are due there.
  - That event can keep holders in a "run into investor day" mood.
  - There is no known scheduled catalyst inside the window to force a reversal.
- **Thanksgiving week (Nov 23–27) falls inside the window.** Thin trading tends to favor drift over sharp reversals.
- **For the short:** Valuation is extreme, the stock sits on the consensus target, volume is fading and progress has stalled for about four sessions.
- **Against the short:** No turn yet (today's dip was bought), the upgrades are still arriving, the story is fundamental with fresh data and a raise, and the beta is low (0.85).
- **Not found:** Short interest, options positioning and any explanation for the Nov 2 intraday drop.

agents.report:
BBWI (Bath & Body Works, the mall chain selling candles, body care and soaps) dropped 9.9% today with no company news I could find. The bigger fact is that **it reports Q3 results before the open this Thursday, November 19**, two sessions from now. Any trade held one to ten sessions will go through that report.

## What happened today
- **Price:** it opened at $21.20, which was also the day's high, sold off all session, and closed at $19.27, near the low of $19.19. Friday's close was $21.39. Volume was 6.37M shares against a usual 3 to 5M, and after-hours was $19.41.
- **No company headline.** Two outlets said the same thing: pre-earnings caution across retail and "without a specific confirmed company catalyst." Their own price figures ($19.95, $20.19) were mid-day snapshots, not the close.
- **The analyst news was positive.** On Friday UBS raised its target from $17 to $22 (Neutral) and Morgan Stanley from $20 to $22. TD Cowen trimmed from $25 to $24, and BMO raised from $20 to $24 on November 3.
- **The whole market sold off.** The S&P 500 fell 1.9% and the Nasdaq 2.5%, led by chip stocks and Nvidia ahead of its report. BBWI's beta (how much it usually moves with the market) is about 1.3, so most of the 9.9% is specific to BBWI.
- **This happened last quarter too.** On August 25, the day before the Q2 report, BBWI fell 8.3% on 8.4M shares. It beat the next morning and rose 7.5%.

## The price path
- From about $19 to $19.67 in mid-August it slid to a low of $15.92 on September 30.
- It then rallied about 48% to $23.54 on November 5. I couldn't confirm what drove the rally because the search budget ran out.
- On November 6 it fell 6.2% to $22.08, the same day it declared its dividend. It held between $21 and $22 until today.
- Today gave back about half of the October–November rally. The 52-week range is $14.27 to $24.94.
- Around Friday the 50-day average was about $19.21 and the 200-day about $19.82, so today's close sits right around the 50-day.

## The business story
- **A shrinking mall retailer in a turnaround.** CEO Daniel Heaf's plan is called the "Consumer First Formula." Sales are still falling: full-year guidance is down 4% to 2.5%.
- **Q2 (reported August 26) looked like a big beat, but mostly wasn't.**
  - Adjusted EPS was $0.62 against roughly $0.21–0.24 expected. About $80M of that was a one-time tariff refund; without it EPS was $0.31, below the $0.37 of a year earlier.
  - Gross margin without the refund was 40.4%, down about 0.9 points.
  - Store sales fell 5.4%, while online sales grew 3% for the first time since 2021. International rose 25%.
  - Body care was down mid-single digits and candles down low-single digits.
- **Q3 guidance was weak.** Sales down 5% to 2.5%, and adjusted EPS of $0.07–0.12 against $0.35 a year ago. About 70% of a ~$35M extra marketing spend falls in Q3, ahead of the holidays.
- **The full-year raise was mostly the refund.** Adjusted EPS guidance went from $2.40–2.65 to $2.60–2.80. Free cash flow guidance went to about $650M, and no buybacks are assumed.
- **Expectations for Thursday:** consensus is about $0.11 EPS on about $1.54B in sales, near the top of guidance, so there is little room above it. The fourth quarter brings 45–50% of yearly operating income, so holiday trends and Q4 guidance will matter more than Q3 itself.
- **Management:** the CFO left in June to join Cencora. Tom Javitch is interim CFO and a search is under way.
- **Balance sheet:** cash $794M, long-term debt about $3.37B and coming down, inventory down $94M year over year.

agents.report:
## ARWR: the story behind the selloff (as of 3:40 PM CT, Mon 2026-11-16)

**In short:** A falling knife. The fundamental story is mostly intact, but the stock is being re-rated. The market has decided that Arrowhead's main near-term product will sell more slowly than hoped. Today's close was the low of the day, and there is no turn yet. The bounce case depends on that fear having been fully priced in. The case against is that the overhang won't lift for months.

### Price path
- July peak about $95.49 (52-week high). Mid-August about $87, when two directors sold. Early October about $61.
- **Nov 9: about -15% to -18%**, on 8.1M shares (normal is 1–2M). Closed $49.24, down from $58.16.
- Nov 10–13: drifted between $47 and $49. **Today (Nov 16): -7.5% to $44.21, closing at the day's low of $44.08**, on 1.86M shares. No company news explained today's drop.
- 50-day average about $63, 200-day about $71. The 50-day fell below the 200-day on Oct 27. The 52-week low is $37.06. Market value is roughly $6.2B.

### What drove it
1. **Mid-September, sell-the-news.** Early results for ARO-DIMER-PA (a cholesterol drug in early trials) cut LDL by about 54%. That looked no better than existing PCSK9 drugs, and patients had frequent injection-site and immune-type reactions. The stock had run up hard into the data, then sold off.
2. **Nov 7–9, the Ionis shock (the main driver).** Ionis sells Tryngolza (olezarsen), the closest competitor to Arrowhead's drug. On Nov 9 it more than halved its 2026 sales guidance, from $100–110M to about $50M, because sales in severe high triglycerides (sHTG) were growing slowly. Ionis had Q3 US sales of only $9M. Arrowhead's plozasiran (REDEMPLO) targets the same sHTG market, which Arrowhead sizes at $3–4B a year in the US, so the market read this as a warning about the whole category. ARWR fell even though biotech funds (XBI, IBB) rose about 3% that day. The same week, Novartis's pelacarsen failed a large heart-outcomes trial (HORIZON), which also hurt the broader Lp(a) cholesterol theme. Arrowhead's only Lp(a) exposure is milestone payments on olpasiran, now run by Amgen. Piper Sandler puts that at under 3% of its price target.
3. **Nov 12, fiscal-year results.** The headline reaction was "falls on earnings miss": quarterly revenue of $37.8M against $61M expected, and EPS of -$3.00 against -$1.52. The full-year loss of $724M includes a one-time $215M charge for buying a priority review voucher (a pass that speeds up an FDA review).

### The bull case
- **sHTG approval is close.** The application went in on Nov 2 under the FDA's STAR fast-track program, which aims for a 6-month priority review and possibly an earlier decision. That points to a decision around Q2 2027. A formal decision date (PDUFA) was expected within about 50 days of filing, so roughly late December. Its announcement is a possible catalyst inside or just past our trading window.
- **The data is strong.** In the SHASTA-3/4 trials, triglycerides fell 79–81% and pancreatitis attacks fell 78%. In patients who had pancreatitis before, attacks fell 91%, and only 3 patients needed treatment to prevent one attack. Management called Ionis's problems a matter of how Ionis sold the drug, not demand, and said Ionis's slow launch "doesn't affect our expectation in sHTG at all."
- **The current FCS launch is growing**, in the rare genetic form of very high triglycerides that REDEMPLO is already approved for. About 1,250 cumulative prescriptions, up from 950 at Sept 30. Weekly prescriptions run 50–60, up from 20–30 earlier in the year. More than 860 doctors have prescribed it. List price is $45,000 a year. Fiscal 2026 product revenue was only about $6.6M.
- **The balance sheet is solid.** About $1.19B in cash and investments. The voucher is no longer needed and could sell for $180–220M, though no deal exists yet. The old loan at 15% was refinanced into a $400M loan at SOFR + 5.5% maturing in 2031. There are also $700M of 0% convertible notes due 2032. Partners paid real money this year: Sarepta $317M, and Novartis a $200M upfront payment received in October.
- **Most analysts are still positive.** Average target is about $99. H.C. Wainwright $120, Piper $126, RBC $100, Stifel $96 (cut from $104). Goldman is Neutral at $74. Short interest is about 10.8M shares, roughly 10–11% of tradable shares and about 5.7 days to cover, which could fuel a short squeeze.

### The bear case
- **Ionis's results are the only hard evidence on sHTG demand, and they're bad.** Arrowhead's own FCS numbers are small, and management gave no guidance. The next real test of sHTG sales won't come until 2H 2027. Nothing near-term disproves the fear.
- **Execution flags.** Management called turning prescriptions into paid shipments a "choke point." Plozasiran also has a glycemic-control warning: blood sugar control worsened in 14.3% of patients versus 8.7% on placebo.
- **The price action is still weak.** Today closed at the low of the day, on lower volume than the Nov 9 capitulation. There are no buyers showing up yet. The 50-day has crossed below the 200-day, and the stock has fallen about 40% in six months. The rally after Nov 9 failed between $49 and $50, so that area is now resistance.
- **Leftover pressure.** Ionis is still trading at 52-week lows. Wall Street Zen cut the stock to "strong sell" on Nov 14. If Ionis or the sector weakens further, ARWR likely follows.

### Events in or near the 1–10 session window
- **The FDA decision date (PDUFA)** for sHTG could be announced. That is a likely positive headline, possibly around late December.
- **Obesity updates** (ALK7 alone and combined with tirzepatide) are promised "by end of 2026." The timing is uncertain and the outcome could go either way.
- Investor conferences were announced Nov 9; I couldn't confirm the dates. A sale of the priority review voucher could come anytime but has no timing. Amgen's OCEAN(a) trial completes around Dec 29, 2026, which is minor for ARWR.
- No earnings inside the window. The next report is a transition-quarter 10-QT, because the fiscal year is moving to calendar years.

### For the journal
The selloff is about a market-wide worry, not anything wrong at Arrowhead. Its own data, regulatory timing and balance sheet all improved this month. That makes a mean-reversion bounce believable, and with roughly 11% of shares sold short a squeeze could add to it. But the stock closed on its low with no turn, and nothing scheduled in the next few sessions clearly reverses the Ionis read-through. Natural downside levels are the $37 52-week low; on the upside, about $49–50 (where the post–Nov 9 bounce stalled) is resistance.

I couldn't find today's XBI close. I also didn't confirm the conference dates or a current short-interest figure, because the web search budget ran out before those checks. Price figures are from stockanalysis.com (S&P Global data); a few secondary sites gave conflicting quotes.
