agents.brief:
Research the evidence on positioning, flow, analyst and attention signals as predictors of short-horizon (1 to 5 trading session) stock returns in US small caps.

Context: this feeds the design of a candidate screen for a discretionary long/short swing book. The book trades US companies worth $250M to $1B (no biotech, banks or REITs, about 425 names; median 3 analysts, about 35% have two or fewer), long and short against IWM (the Russell 2000 ETF), holds 1 to 5 sessions, enters in regular hours only, pays roughly 1% round-trip in spread, and can only short when the broker (Interactive Brokers) shows shares to borrow. The bet is that thin analyst coverage means news is priced slowly.

Objective: a dense, sourced account of which of these signals have real evidence at a 1-5 day horizon (and separately at a 1-month horizon), with effect sizes, cost and borrow considerations, and recent-period validity (2015-2026), and how each could be used either as a screen trigger (an event that puts a name on the list) or as a ranking/conditioning variable.

Key questions:
- Analyst events in thinly covered names: coverage initiations (Irvine; Demiroglu & Ryngaert), upgrades/downgrades, estimate revisions, price-target changes — size of announcement return and of the 1-5 day drift afterward; is drift larger in small/low-coverage names (Gleason & Lee; Womack; Kecskés/Michaely/Womack; Loh & Stulz "influential" recommendations)? Has it decayed (Altınkılıç & Hansen; post-Reg FD)? Coverage drops/terminations.
- Short interest level and changes (Boehmer/Jones/Zhang; Rapach/Ringgenberg/Zhou; Diether/Lee/Werner daily shorting flow): predictive power at 1-5 days; the bi-monthly FINRA short-interest release as an event; days-to-cover (Hong et al.); borrow fee / utilization as the stronger signal (Engelberg/Reed/Ringgenberg "Short selling risk"; Drechsler & Drechsler "shorting premium"; Muravyev/Pearson/Pollet). Does FINRA daily short-sale volume predict anything?
- Short squeezes: can high short interest + positive news be screened for, with evidence?
- Index events: Russell reconstitution (June; preliminary lists), S&P SmallCap 600 additions/deletions — announcement-to-effective drift and post-effective reversal in recent years (Chang/Hong/Liskovich; Greenwood & Sammon "The disappearing index effect"). Relevance to a $250M-$1B book.
- IPO lockup expiries, secondary/insider unlocks (Field & Hanka; Brav & Gompers): pre/post expiry returns, still present?
- Institutional/13F and 13D/13G filing signals at short horizon; ETF flow pressure in small caps.
- Retail attention: Robinhood/retail order flow (Barber/Huang/Odean/Schwarz "Attention-induced trading and returns"; Boehmer/Jones/Zhang/Zhang retail order imbalance), social media (Reddit/StockTwits/X) attention spikes — reversal or continuation in small caps over 1-5 days? Google/Wikipedia/EDGAR search volume (Da/Engelberg/Gao; Drake et al. EDGAR downloads).
- Options-market signals are OUT of scope (the owner excluded option data) — skip.
- Which of these are stronger precisely in low-coverage small caps (the book's bet), and which are crowded/arbitraged away?

Suggested sources:
- Academic papers (SSRN, NBER, JF, JFE, RFS, JAR, Management Science). Read the papers or their abstracts/tables, not blog summaries; check surprising claims against a second source.
- Practitioner summaries (Quantpedia, Alpha Architect, S3 Partners, Ortex, S&P Global research on index effect).

Constraints:
- US equities; focus on small caps ($250M-$1B) and 1-5 session horizons, noting longer-horizon results separately. Give effect sizes, sample periods, and post-2015 validity.
- Separate what the evidence shows from your inference.

Save your output notes to /Users/michael/Projects/ETF Factor Rotation/research_notes/Small cap screen design/positioning_analysts_attention.md

**As a first step, you must read /Users/michael/Library/Application Support/Claude/local-agent-mode-sessions/skills-plugin/12a927b0-83dc-47b2-8871-edf37ec7130c/fcb33469-21d2-4fcb-95de-3eb32b3c2765/skills/deep-research/references/researcher.md for instructions on how to conduct research.**
agents.report:
Notes are saved at `/Users/michael/Projects/ETF Factor Rotation/research_notes/Small cap screen design/positioning_analysts_attention.md`.

Most figures come from paper abstracts, working-paper drafts and search excerpts, not the published tables; where drafts disagree, both numbers are in the notes. Almost no paper isolates the $250M-$1B band or tests anything net of a 1% round trip at 1-5 sessions, so the role assigned to each signal is my judgment from gross effect sizes.

**Main conclusion:** after a 1% round trip, almost none of these signals is a stand-alone trade at 1-5 sessions. They are useful as triggers that put a name on the list, or as conditioning for a catalyst-driven idea.

**Signals that clear the cost bar on the evidence**
- **First coverage of a neglected name:** +4.86% at announcement (Demiroglu & Ryngaert), and initiations beat ordinary recommendations by 1.02 points (Irvine). The drift after the open is unmeasured, and the book enters in regular hours only.
- **Schedule 13D:** about 7-8% over the 20 days either side of the filing, with a run-up before the filing and no reversal over the next year (2001-2006 sample). A 13G is worth about 0.6%; I found nothing showing a short-horizon reaction to 13F filings.
- **Retail attention peaks (short side):** top Robinhood buys returned -4.7% over 20 days, and social-media attention predicts a negative next-day return. Best used as a veto on longs, since these names are the hardest to borrow.
- **Squeeze unwind (short side):** squeezes fade in about seven trading days. I found no evidence that "high short interest plus good news" works as a long screen.

**Signals that have decayed or are too small**
- **Post-revision drift:** on average zero since 2003 (Altınkılıç, Hansen & Ye); what remains is in very low-priced, thinly traded names. Older work does show slower pricing with less coverage (Gleason & Lee), which supports the book's bet in direction only.
- **Daily short volume:** abnormal short-term flow predicted nothing in 2010-2015 once the data were public. I would not build a trigger on it.
- **Short interest, days-to-cover, borrow fee:** these work at a month or longer (days-to-cover about 1.2% a month long-short). The borrow-fee edge is mostly paid away in the fee itself, so they serve as conditioning and a short-side gate.
- **Broad retail order imbalance:** halved after 2016 and survives only in small caps, at 0.1-0.3% a week long-short.
- **Index effect:** the S&P 500 addition effect fell from 7.4% to under 1%. Russell migrations show about a 1.2% run-up and 0.95% reversal over 20 sessions, measured at the $5.8B boundary, which is irrelevant to this book.
- **IPO lockup expiry:** -1.5% over three days in 1988-1997; I found no peer-reviewed US confirmation after 2015, only a weaker student-level estimate.

**Dated item:** Russell now reconstitutes twice a year. Preliminary lists came out 2026-11-13 and the first December reconstitution takes effect after the close on 2026-12-11. The bottom of the Russell 2000 is about $144M, and S&P 600 additions need $1.2B or more, so additions are mostly above the book's range.

**Gaps the report writer should know about**
- No post-2015 test of analyst drift or short-interest predictability in this size band.
- No study of the lower Russell 2000 boundary.
- Several magnitudes I recalled but could not confirm are listed under Gaps in the notes, not as findings.
- Quantpedia, S3, Ortex and the S&P index-effect research were not reviewed; only Alpha Architect and Dimensional were.

I ran about 40 searches and fetches against the guide's limit of 15, because the brief covered nine question areas.

agents.brief:
Research how an event-driven candidate screen for a small discretionary long/short equity book should be designed: how to combine event triggers, how to rank candidates, how many to pass to research, how LLMs can be used for triage, and how to measure whether a screen is working with a small sample.

Context: an automated system trades (in a shadow run, no orders yet) US companies worth $250M to $1B (no biotech, banks or REITs, about 425 names), long and short against IWM (the Russell 2000 ETF), holding 1 to 5 sessions, regular hours only, roughly 1% round-trip cost. Three passes run each trading day (about an hour after the open, midday, after the close). In each pass a rule-based screen picks up to 20 candidates (currently: earnings reactions, large unexplained moves on heavy volume, insider buying), one LLM research agent per candidate reads the news and filings, and an LLM judge gives every candidate a verdict (take or pass), a direction, a conviction (1-5) and a rank; every verdict is scored afterward against IWM at holds of 1-5 sessions whether taken or not. The bet is that thin analyst coverage means news is priced slowly. A recent midday pass found only 1 candidate. The first review of results is in about three weeks.

Objective: a dense, sourced account of best practice and evidence for designing the screen-then-research funnel, ending in concrete design options.

Key questions:
- LLMs reading news to predict short-horizon returns: Lopez-Lira & Tang "Can ChatGPT forecast stock price movements?" and follow-ups (2023-2026) — effect sizes, that the effect is concentrated in small caps and negative news, how fast it decays, results after costs, look-ahead/memorization critiques (e.g. Glasserman & Lin; Sarkar & Vafa), results with newer models. Evidence on LLM agents doing fundamental/event research (e.g. Kim/Muhn/Nikolaev on financial statement analysis; papers on LLM earnings-call analysis). What this implies for using a cheap LLM pass over ALL headlines/8-Ks for the universe as the screen itself (an "everything with news today" triage) instead of price thresholds.
- Event-driven and news-based quant strategies in practice: how do practitioners (RavenPack research, Refinitiv/LSEG MarketPsych, Bloomberg event-driven feeds, Wolfe/Deutsche quant notes, academic "news analytics" literature) score news novelty, relevance and sentiment and combine with price reaction? Evidence that novelty (first report vs repeat; Tetlock "All the news that's fit to reprint") and "fresh vs stale" news matters for continuation vs reversal.
- Combining signals: is a composite score (event type × surprise size × volume × coverage × liquidity) better than separate setups with quotas? Evidence on conditioning variables that amplify under-reaction: low analyst coverage, low institutional ownership, low attention days (Fridays, busy news days; Hirshleifer/Lim/Teoh; DellaVigna & Pollet), high idiosyncratic volatility, illiquidity. Which conditioning variables should rank candidates in a thin-coverage small-cap book?
- Trigger design: price-triggered (a move happened, find out why) vs information-triggered (a filing/press release appeared, regardless of price move). Evidence that under-reaction is largest when the initial price response is SMALL relative to the news (so price-move thresholds may screen out the best under-reaction cases). 
- Funnel sizing: how many candidates per day is sensible for a universe of ~425 names; base rates of material events per small-cap per year (8-Ks per firm-year, press releases, earnings days); precision/recall trade-off of loose vs strict thresholds when research capacity is cheap (LLM agents) but judge attention is limited; evidence on decision quality vs number of options considered.
- Statistics of evaluation with small samples: how many scored verdicts are needed to detect a rank-return relationship of plausible size (e.g. information coefficient 0.03-0.10) or a take-vs-pass spread of ~50-100 bp with daily idiosyncratic volatility of 3-4% in small caps; power calculations; overlapping holds and same-day clustering (need for date-clustered standard errors); multiple-testing cautions when tuning thresholds (Harvey/Liu/Zhu; Bailey & López de Prado deflated Sharpe); how to A/B two screen versions in a shadow run (e.g. record both the strict and loose screens' names and compare).
- Market-regime handling: on broad selloff days should thresholds be relative to sector/peer moves rather than only the index? Evidence on beta/sector-adjusting abnormal returns in event studies for small caps (market-model vs size/industry-matched benchmark).
- Universe hygiene: standard filters to exclude closed-end funds, SPACs, ADRs, limited partnerships, units/warrants/preferreds, recent IPOs, shell companies (CRSP share codes 10/11 equivalents using free data such as Nasdaq screener fields, SEC SIC codes, company names).

Suggested sources:
- Academic papers (SSRN, arXiv q-fin, NBER, JF, JFE, RFS) from 2019-2026 on LLMs and news analytics in finance; classic event-study methodology (MacKinlay; Kothari & Warner); backtest-overfitting literature.
- Practitioner white papers (RavenPack, Man AHL, AQR, Two Sigma, Alpha Architect, Quantpedia).
- Read the papers or their abstracts/tables, not blog summaries; check surprising claims against a second source.

Constraints:
- US small caps, 1-5 session horizon, an individual's budget. Give numbers (effect sizes, sample sizes needed) wherever possible and show the arithmetic for power calculations.
- Separate what the evidence shows from your inference.

Save your output notes to /Users/michael/Projects/ETF Factor Rotation/research_notes/Small cap screen design/screen_design_ranking_evaluation.md

**As a first step, you must read /Users/michael/Library/Application Support/Claude/local-agent-mode-sessions/skills-plugin/12a927b0-83dc-47b2-8871-edf37ec7130c/fcb33469-21d2-4fcb-95de-3eb32b3c2765/skills/deep-research/references/researcher.md for instructions on how to conduct research.**
agents.report:
The notes file is complete against the brief and saved at `/Users/michael/Projects/ETF Factor Rotation/research_notes/Small cap screen design/screen_design_ranking_evaluation.md`. It covers all eight key questions plus a closing section of design options, each with takeaway, cited findings, inferences and gaps. The power arithmetic is my own, worked from standard formulas.

**Key findings**

- **LLM news signal is real but too small on its own.** Lopez-Lira and Tang (v6, Oct 2025; headlines after the model's cutoff) find about 34 bp of long-short drift on day one and 19 bp on day two, then nothing. It is concentrated in small stocks and negative news, and the Sharpe fell from 6.54 (2021 Q4) to 1.22 (early 2024). The strategy is unprofitable at 20 bp round-trip, so at this book's 1% cost an LLM pass works as triage and ranking, not as a signal.
- **Earnings reactions need conditioning.** In that sample earnings headlines had the biggest first-day move and about zero drift; insider-transaction headlines had the most drift.
- **One well-known paper is withdrawn.** Kim, Muhn and Nikolaev (GPT-4 beats analysts on financial statements) was pulled in Feb 2025 after a co-author could not replicate it.
- **In-window LLM backtests are untrustworthy.** Models recall pre-cutoff values, and date instructions and name-masking do not prevent it, so the triage prompt should be tuned forward in shadow only.
- **"Unexplained moves" are the reversal case.** Chan and Savor find that moves with new information continue, while moves with no identifiable news reverse; Tetlock finds the same reversal after stale news. The research agent should label each name new / stale / none.
- **A price gate removes the best under-reaction cases.** Low-attention events show a weaker first reaction and larger drift (Friday earnings: 15% lower immediate response, 60% larger delayed). The supported design is information-triggered entry, with the price move used as a feature (sign, and size relative to the news).
- **Funnel arithmetic (mine).** For 425 names I estimate roughly 20 8-Ks a session and about 7 earnings reports a session on average (heavily seasonal). A 3-standard-deviation move gate yields only about 1 to 5 names a day, which matches the one-candidate midday pass; a 2-standard-deviation gate yields about 19.
- **Three weeks cannot settle edge.** Detecting a rank-return correlation of 0.05 needs about 3,100 scored verdicts, and 0.10 needs about 780. With 300 to 900 verdicts the smallest detectable value is 0.09 to 0.16, and same-day clustering roughly doubles or triples the requirement. A 100 bp take-vs-pass spread at a 1-session hold needs about 1,070 verdicts if takes are 10% of them.
- **The bar the judge must clear.** To cover 1% costs the top of the ranked list needs a rank-return correlation near 0.10 at 3 to 5 session holds, about three times what average headline drift implies.
- **Multiple testing.** Trying 20 threshold variants and keeping the best gives a t-statistic of about 1.9 by luck alone.
- **Selloff days.** Moves should be measured against beta-adjusted sector peers in units of the stock's own volatility; on a day IWM (the Russell 2000 ETF) falls 3%, a beta-1.8 name shows a spurious −2.4% "abnormal" move against the index alone.

**Design options in the file**

- **A, minimal:** keep the current triggers, lower the move gate to 2 standard deviations on a sector-adjusted basis, and add the new / stale / none label.
- **B, recommended:** an information-triggered loose gate, with a cheap LLM triage that scores and logs every item, a unit-weight composite rank, and the top 20 going to research. It runs in shadow beside the current screen and is compared on the names only the loose gate admits.
- **C, maximal:** a daily triage record for all 425 names, to reach a usable sample fastest.

The file also sets out an evaluation protocol to fix before the first review.

**Gaps flagged in the file**

- No reliable 8-K or press-release count per firm-year for this size band; the fix is to count directly from the free EDGAR bulk file for the 425 names.
- No test of models newer than GPT-4 on post-cutoff news drift.
- Several papers were confirmed from abstracts or secondary summaries only, each marked where it appears. Published event-study power tables could not be read.
- No public evidence on MarketPsych or Bloomberg event feeds, or sell-side quant notes.
- Token cost of the triage and short-borrow availability were not priced.

agents.brief:
Research the evidence on price, volume and news-conditioned move signals as predictors of short-horizon (1 to 5 trading session) returns in US small caps: when does a large daily move continue, and when does it reverse?

Context: this feeds the design of a candidate screen for a discretionary long/short swing book. The book trades US companies worth $250M to $1B (no biotech, banks or REITs, about 425 names), long and short against IWM (the Russell 2000 ETF), holds 1 to 5 sessions, enters in regular hours only (about an hour after the open, at midday, or at the next open), pays roughly 1% round-trip in spread. Today the screen flags a "news move": no earnings report, but the stock moved at least 5% against IWM, at least 1.5 of its typical daily ranges (ATR), on at least twice its 20-day average volume. A research agent then reads the news to find out why and a judge decides long or short. On a recent day 74 of 425 names moved 5%+ against IWM but only 1 cleared all three bars.

Objective: a dense, sourced account of what predicts continuation vs reversal after a large one-day (or intraday) move in small, thinly covered stocks, with effect sizes, cost-adjusted results and recent-period validity, so the screen can be tuned (thresholds, what to add, what to drop) and so the judge knows the base rates.

Key questions:
- Short-term reversal (Jegadeesh 1990; Lehmann; Nagel "Evaporating liquidity"; Avramov/Chordia/Goyal): how strong is the 1-5 day reversal in small/illiquid stocks, how much is bid-ask bounce, and does it survive costs?
- News vs no-news moves: Tetlock ("Does public financial news resolve asymmetric information?"), Chan (2003) "Stock price reaction to news and no-news", Savor (2012) "Stock returns after major price shocks: the impact of information", Jiang/Li/Wang "Pervasive underreaction: evidence from high-frequency data", Boudoukh et al. "Which news moves stock prices?" — do moves WITH identifiable news continue and moves WITHOUT news reverse? Effect sizes at 1-5 days, by size.
- High-volume return premium (Gervais/Kaniel/Mingelgrin) and volume shocks: does abnormal volume predict next-week returns, in which direction, in small caps? Llorente/Michaely/Saar/Wang on volume and return autocorrelation (informed vs liquidity trading).
- Overnight gap vs intraday move: do gaps continue or fade in small caps? Overnight/intraday return decomposition (Lou/Polk/Skouras) relevance.
- Large-drop "overreaction" literature (Bremer & Sweeney; Cox & Peterson; Atkins & Dyl): bounce after big one-day declines — real after bid-ask?
- Analyst coverage and the speed of news incorporation (Hong/Lim/Stein "Bad news travels slowly"): size of slow-diffusion effect in low-coverage names, at what horizon.
- Peer/industry lead-lag: do small caps drift after a large peer's or customer's news (Cohen & Frazzini "Economic links"; Hou "Industry information diffusion"; Menzly & Ozbas)? At a 1-5 day horizon?
- 52-week-high proximity, short-term momentum (Medhat & Schmeling "Short-term momentum": high-turnover stocks continue, low-turnover reverse) — implications for a volume filter.
- Does scaling a move by the stock's own volatility (ATR/sigma) matter vs raw percent? What thresholds does the literature use?
- Market-wide selloff days: are idiosyncratic moves on such days less informative?
- Recent-period (2015-2026) and post-decimalization evidence; retail-era effects.

Suggested sources:
- Academic papers (SSRN, NBER, JF, JFE, RFS, RAPS). Read the papers or their abstracts/tables, not blog summaries; check surprising claims against a second source.
- Practitioner summaries (Quantpedia, Alpha Architect, AQR) for tradability.

Constraints:
- US equities; focus on small caps and 1-5 session horizons. Give effect sizes in bp/percent, sample periods, and whether results hold post-2015 and after costs of ~1% round-trip.
- Separate what the evidence shows from your inference.

agents.report:
The notes file is complete against the brief and saved at `/Users/michael/Projects/ETF Factor Rotation/research_notes/Small cap screen design/price_volume_news_moves.md`. It has 11 sections, one per key question, each with Takeaway, Cited Findings, Inferences and Gaps.

In this pass I filled the 52-week-high question, added a small-stock magnitude for the high-volume premium, added Lehmann's weekly reversal figures and the "weekly momentum" follow-up, and added one line on Hou.

**What the evidence shows**
- **News vs no-news is the best-supported split.** Five independent data sets agree that large moves with identifiable news continue and moves without it reverse.
  - Boudoukh et al. (S&P 500, 2000-2009): about 20 bp per day continuation after identified-news extreme moves, about 16 bp per day reversal after no-news ones, and zero when a story exists but has no classifiable event.
  - Pritamani and Singal: about +2% / -1.7% over 20 days when news and a volume increase coincide.
  - Tetlock: ten-day reversal is 38% lower on news days, and small, illiquid stocks show high-volume continuation only on news days.
- **Plain reversal is real but not tradable at a 1% cost.** Nagel finds 0.30% per day at closing prices but 0.18% at quote midpoints, so roughly half is bid-ask bounce. Avramov, Chordia and Goyal conclude profits are below costs. Reversal is faster and stronger in volatile names, over within about two weeks in high-turnover names, and rises with the VIX.
- **The bounce after a 10%+ drop does not hold up in small stocks.** For small non-optionable Nasdaq stocks (1996-2004), day +1 is +0.81% at closing prices but -0.36% at bid-ask midpoints.
- **Volume has no single sign.** The high-volume premium is about 0.35% at one day to 0.94% at twenty days in small stocks, on old NYSE data. For small, illiquid stocks a high-volume move reverses unless it comes with news.
- **Medhat and Schmeling's short-term momentum does not support chasing high-volume small-cap moves.** It is a one-month effect and strongest in the largest, most liquid stocks.
- **Retail-attention fades are the largest recent effect.** Top Robinhood herding stocks return -4.7% abnormal over 20 days; daily top winners and losers underperform by about 1.6-1.7% the next month.
- **Slow effects are context only.** Analyst coverage, peer and customer lead-lag, and 52-week-high proximity are monthly-horizon effects, not shown to work at 1-5 days.

**My inferences for the screen (marked as such in the file)**
- Make the ATR-scaled bar primary and raise the raw floor toward 7-10%, since expected drift on a 5% move is roughly at cost.
- Soften the 2x volume bar; nothing supports 2x specifically, and volume does not set direction.
- Have the research agent separate an identifiable event from commentary only and from nothing.
- Add an attention-spike flag, and measure the move against the stock's industry and against IWM scaled by the stock's beta (how much it normally moves with IWM).
- Record whether the move was overnight or intraday.

**Gaps that remain**
- No refereed post-2015 study covers $250M-$1B US stocks at 1-5 days net of realistic costs for any of these effects.
- Large overnight gaps split by news, and volatility-scaled versus raw thresholds, have no direct tests.
- No direct test exists of how informative single-stock moves are on market-wide selloff days.
- Some figures come from abstracts or secondary summaries, each labelled in the file: Savor's per-horizon numbers, the Jiang/Li/Wang sample and drift size, Jegadeesh's spread, and Hou's and Menzly/Ozbas's magnitudes.
- Medhat and Schmeling's "strongest in the largest, most liquid stocks" wording is from my recollection of the published abstract and is not flagged as such in the file; check it before relying on it.

Research the evidence on earnings-related signals for predicting short-horizon (1 to 5 trading session) stock returns in US small caps.

Context: this feeds the design of a candidate screen for a discretionary long/short swing book. The book trades US companies worth $250M to $1B (no biotech, banks or REITs, about 425 names), long and short against IWM (the Russell 2000 ETF), holds 1 to 5 sessions, enters in regular hours only (it can enter the morning after a report, about an hour after the open, at midday, or at the next open), pays roughly 1% round-trip in spread. The bet is that thin analyst coverage means news is priced slowly. Today the screen flags a name that reported since yesterday's close and moved at least 3% against IWM and one typical daily range.

Objective: a dense, sourced account of which earnings-related signals have real evidence of predicting returns over the next 1-5 sessions (not just 60-day drift), how large the effects are, whether they survive costs in small/illiquid names, and whether they still hold in recent years (2015-2026).

Key questions:
- Post-earnings-announcement drift (PEAD): how much of it arrives in the first 1-5 days after the announcement-day reaction? Is it stronger in small caps and low-analyst-coverage names? Has it decayed (e.g. Martineau "Rest in Peace PEAD", Chordia et al., McLean & Pontiff on post-publication decay)? What survives in microcaps/small caps after trading costs?
- Which measure of surprise predicts best at short horizons: SUE vs analyst consensus, the announcement-day abnormal return (EAR, Brandt et al.), revenue surprise, guidance changes, combined EAR+SUE? What about names with no or 1-2 analysts where there is no consensus?
- Does the announcement-day reaction continue or reverse over days 2-5? Does it depend on volume, on gap vs intraday move, on whether the move was large (overreaction), on after-hours vs next-day?
- Guidance raises/cuts, pre-announcements and profit warnings: short-horizon drift evidence.
- Conference-call tone / text signals / LLM reads of earnings releases: evidence of 1-5 day predictability.
- Earnings announcement premium (pre-announcement run-up) and whether entering BEFORE a report has evidence.
- Asymmetry: do bad-news reactions drift more than good-news ones in small caps (short side), given borrow constraints?
- Practical thresholds used in the literature (decile cuts, minimum abnormal return) that could translate into screen rules.

Suggested sources:
- Academic papers (SSRN, NBER, Journal of Finance, JFE, RFS, Journal of Accounting Research, The Accounting Review): Bernard & Thomas, Brandt/Kishore/Santa-Clara/Venkatachalam (EAR), Chan/Jegadeesh/Lakonishok, Martineau (2022), Hirshleifer/Lim/Teoh (distraction), DellaVigna & Pollet (Friday), Hou/Xue/Zhang replication, Novy-Marx & Velikov (costs), Meursault et al. (PEAD.txt), recent 2022-2026 papers on PEAD in microcaps.
- Practitioner research (AQR, Alpha Architect, Quantpedia, Research Affiliates) summarizing whether it's tradable.
- Read the papers themselves or their abstracts/tables, not just blog summaries; check surprising claims against a second source.

Constraints:
- US equities only; focus on small caps ($250M-$1B) and short horizons of 1-5 sessions. Clearly separate evidence that is about 60-day drift from evidence about the first week.
- State sample period for each result and say explicitly whether it holds post-2015.

The notes are saved at `/Users/michael/Projects/ETF Factor Rotation/research_notes/Small cap screen design/earnings_signals.md`, organised by the eight key questions. The web-search budget ran out before a few follow-ups could be run, so several items rest on abstracts or search summaries only; each is labelled in the file.

**What the evidence shows**

- **Drift in days 2-5:** it survives only in the bottom NYSE size quintile, which I believe covers most of a $250M-$1B book, though I could not verify the breakpoint. Martineau (2022, data to 2019) finds about 10 bps per surprise-decile step over days 2-5 since 2011, and nothing after day 5. Outside that quintile, 60-day drift has been insignificant since 2006.
- **Size of the edge against costs:** my arithmetic from that coefficient is about 0.9% top-to-bottom decile, or roughly 0.45% per position, against a 1% round trip. Novy-Marx and Velikov show costs take about two-thirds of the gross PEAD spread; Chordia et al. put it at 70-100% in illiquid stocks.
- **Best surprise measure:** the benchmark-relative announcement move holds up better than SUE after costs (net 0.34% a month vs 0.26%). The two are independent, and requiring both roughly doubles the 60-day spread. For names with no analysts, the year-over-year earnings change is the measure that still predicts in 2016-2019.
- **Entry timing:** the EPS number is priced by the open. Wu et al. (2006-2023) find entering at 8:45 AM CT the morning after and exiting at the close loses 0.5% a day after spreads; that test is value-weighted and covers the first session only.
- **Call content:** this is the one piece with recent evidence of slow pricing. Transcript sentiment entered at the next open spread 153 bps in 2024-2025 (S&P 1500, mostly large and mid caps, 1 bp cost assumed). In the bottom size quintile, call content continues and press-release wording reverses over days 2-61.
- **Volume:** high unexpected volume on the reaction day predicts higher later returns (about 1.4% over three months) regardless of the news sign, so it helps longs more than shorts.
- **Entering before a report:** the announcement premium was about 61 bps a month in 1973-2004, was not concentrated in small stocks, and is reported as gone in the US (the decay finding is from a search summary only).
- **Short side:** the evidence does not show a larger short-side drift, and nothing nets out borrow fees.
- **Thresholds:** the literature uses prior-quarter quintile or decile ranks, not fixed percentages. Extreme-quintile announcement moves average roughly ±9% against benchmark, so the screen's 3% cut admits a wide middle band the papers find little in.

**Gaps**

- No study tabulates days 1-5 drift for $250M-$1B names or for 2020-2026.
- No US study splits days 2-5 returns by gap versus intraday move, or by size of the earnings-day move.
- No days 1-5 evidence on guidance changes or profit warnings in the US.
- The NYSE 20th-percentile breakpoint level, the McLean-Pontiff decay figure, and the Michaely et al. rebuttal of the Friday effect were not verified.

Research the evidence on corporate events and filings (other than earnings reports) as predictors of short-horizon (1 to 5 trading session) stock returns in US small caps.

Today the screen flags insider buying (officers/directors buying $100,000+ in a week on Form 4, or two insiders and $50,000) and unexplained large moves on heavy volume.

Objective: a dense, sourced account of which corporate events have real evidence of predicting returns over the following 1-5 sessions (and, separately, over the following month), with effect sizes, whether they survive costs in small names, and whether they still hold in recent years (2015-2026). Cover both long and short setups.

Which purchases are informative (opportunistic vs routine per Cohen/Malloy/Pomorski; cluster buys; CEO/CFO vs directors; size relative to salary/holdings; small-cap vs large)? Is most of the return in the first days or spread over 6-12 months? Insider sales as a short signal?

- M&A: acquirer reaction drift, target rumor.
- CEO/CFO departures, auditor resignations, restatements, late filings (NT 10-K/10-Q), delisting notices, going-concern language: short-side evidence.
- Dividend initiations/cuts, special dividends, spin-offs.
- Short-seller reports (activist shorts) on small caps: day 1-5 continuation?

agents.report:
The notes are saved at `/Users/michael/Projects/ETF Factor Rotation/research_notes/Small cap screen design/corporate_events.md`, but they are incomplete in places. The web search budget ran out and several fetches failed, so some topics rest on abstracts or search summaries. Each finding is marked "(read)" or "(summary)", and each section has a Gaps list.

**What has post-event drift you can catch entering at the next open**
- **Credible activist short reports:** about -8% on the day, then a further 13-14% over days 2-60 in two independent samples (2006-2011 and 1996-2018). Reports that cause no day-one move still drift -13%. A quarter to a third of targets get delisted, and borrow is the constraint.
- **Late-filing notices (NT 10-K / NT 10-Q):** -2% to -3% at filing, then about -5% over days 3-62, and -7% to -10% when the stated reason is not an accounting one. The sample is 2000-2008 only.
- **Hedge fund 13D filings:** about 3.2% run-up before, 2.0% on days 0-1, and roughly 2 more points by day 20, with no reversal (2001-2006). Later evidence suggests the filing is priced faster now.
- **Fades:** merger-rumour targets gain 4.3% on the day and give back 1.4% over ten sessions, or 2.7% over twenty when the rumour is wrong. Filing-day moves driven by retail attention reverse by about a quarter over days 4-8.

**Insider purchases (the current screen flag)**
- The reaction is about 2% over the 5 days starting at the filing (2003-2022, over 97,000 filings), and that figure includes the gap you cannot catch.
- Prices start moving within seconds of the filing, so net of 1% cost a 1-5 session hold on the average purchase is near break-even.
- More of the return comes over 30-60 days: 3.4% over 60 days, and 2-6% over 30 days in a 2018-2024 microcap sample.
- Filters with support: non-routine buyers, a second insider buying within days, CFO buyers, purchases not following the company's own acquisition, and stocks far below the 52-week high.
- Dollar size and title had weak support in the studies that tested them.
- Insider sales are not a usable short signal: about -0.3% at filing, and weaker since the 2022 rule change.

**Where the edge is in the announcement jump, not after**
- Overnight offerings, convertibles, PIPEs, ATM programs and shelves show no supported day 1-5 continuation to short.
- Buyback authorizations react about 2% on the day, with nothing afterwards until completion news; the long-run drift has faded since about 2003.
- Restatements and delisting notices are priced around the filing.
- Dividend changes and spin-offs have only old or disputed drift evidence.

**8-K item types**
- Average signed reactions for items 1.01, 5.02, 7.01 and 8.01 are under 1%, so the item code is a prompt to read the filing, not a signal.
- Distress items (acceleration of debt, exit costs, impairments) drift -1% to -2.5% over 30-90 days and work better as a veto on longs.
- A negative 8-K paired with an unrelated upbeat press release the same day is priced more slowly. That is the closest evidence to the "8-K without a press release" question; no paper tests that case directly.

**Main gaps**
- Almost no study reports days 1-5 separately or restricts to $250M-$1B; most drift windows are 30 sessions or longer.
- Nothing usable was found on special dividends, post-2000 tender offers, ATM announcement returns outside REITs, day-level returns after overnight offerings, the Niessner paper, or practitioner insider research (2iQ, Verity).
- Post-2015 evidence is thin for 13D filings, late-filing notices and rumours.
- Minus signs in two extracted tables (Brendel-Ryans, Bartov-Konchitchki) were restored from the surrounding prose.

agents.brief:
Research the data sources available in late 2026 to an individual (non-professional, US-resident) trader for building an event-driven candidate screen on US small-cap stocks: what exists, what it costs, how fresh it is, what the terms allow, and what free versions are good enough.

Context: an automated research system screens about 425 US companies worth $250M to $1B three times a day (about 10:30 AM, 2:00 PM and 5:30 PM Eastern) for events worth researching, then an LLM research agent reads up on each candidate. Today it uses only free sources: Yahoo Finance (daily bars, quotes, analyst counts, earnings dates), Nasdaq's public screener and earnings calendar JSON, OpenInsider (Form 4 purchases; it fails sometimes), and an Interactive Brokers (IBKR) paper/live account through IB Gateway for quotes (the owner has an IBKR Pro account with a US equities market-data subscription). SEC EDGAR refused the script's requests because it sent no contact email in the User-Agent. The owner is willing to hear about paid sources but wants cost and a free alternative stated up front. Machine-readable access (API, RSS, bulk file) from a Python script on a Mac matters; scraping fragile HTML is a last resort.

Objective: a sourced catalogue, by signal type, of the best data source options with price (per month, as currently listed), latency/freshness, coverage of small caps, access method, rate limits, licensing limits for personal use, and a recommended pick plus a free fallback for each.

agents.brief:
Research the evidence on INTRADAY and opening-session technical signals for US small-cap stocks: what in the first minutes/hours of trading (or the overnight gap) predicts the rest of the day and the next 1 to 5 sessions.

Context: this feeds the design of a candidate screen for a discretionary long/short swing book. The book trades US companies worth $250M to $1B (no biotech, banks or REITs, about 425 names), long and short against IWM (the Russell 2000 ETF), holds 1 to 5 sessions, enters in REGULAR HOURS ONLY at two live points — about 10:30 AM Eastern (one hour after the open) and about 2:00 PM Eastern — or at the next session's open after an evening pass. Round-trip cost is roughly 1% in spread; entries hit the bid/ask (no resting orders). An LLM research agent reads the news on each screened name before a judge decides. The owner has an Interactive Brokers account with real-time US equity data, so minute bars, pre-market prints and relative volume by time of day are available. The owner wants to know whether technical signals deserve a bigger role in the screen, especially for the 10:30 AM and 2:00 PM passes.

Objective: a dense, sourced account of which intraday/opening signals have credible evidence, with effect sizes, cost-adjusted results, recent-period validity, and a judgment for each of: screen trigger / ranking input / entry-timing rule / veto / drop.

Key questions:
- "Stocks in play" and opening-range breakouts: Zarattini, Barbon & Aziz (2024) "A profitable day trading strategy for the U.S. equity market" (5-minute ORB on stocks with high relative volume: universe filters, reported returns/Sharpe, cost assumptions, how much depends on relative volume and on small caps) and Zarattini & Aziz's other ORB/VWAP papers (QQQ/TQQQ); independent replications or critiques. Does opening relative volume (first 5-30 minutes vs its average for that time of day) identify names whose move continues that day and over following days?
- Intraday momentum: Gao, Han, Li & Zhou (2018) "Market intraday momentum" (first half-hour predicts last half-hour, in ETFs) and single-stock versions; Baltussen, Da, Lammers & Martens (hedging demand); Heston, Korajczyk & Sadka (intraday periodicity: same half-hour continuation across days); does a stock's direction at 10:30 AM predict the rest of the day in small caps?
- Overnight vs intraday: Lou, Polk & Skouras "A tug of war"; Hendershott, Livdan & Rösch; Berkman et al. (2012) "Paying attention: overnight returns and the hidden cost of buying at the open" (retail-attention stocks open high and reverse intraday — size in small/hard-to-value stocks); Aboody et al. overnight returns as sentiment (high overnight return stocks underperform later); Bogousslavsky "The cross-section of intraday and overnight returns". Implication for: entering at the open vs waiting an hour; fading vs following a gap.
- Opening gaps on news vs no news in small caps: gap-and-go vs gap-fade base rates; how much of an earnings/news reaction is in the gap vs first hour vs rest of day (e.g. Jiang, Likitapiwat & McInish on after-hours earnings; Michaely, Rubin & Vedrashko; Grégoire & Martineau "How is earnings news transmitted to stock prices?"; Wu et al. on trading the morning after). For a book that cannot trade pre-market, what does the evidence say about entering one hour after the open on an overnight news gap: is there continuation left, in which cases (first-hour holds the gap / closes above VWAP / fills half the gap)?
- VWAP and intraday trend state: any evidence that price above/below VWAP or holding the opening range at 10:30 AM/midday predicts the close or next days for single stocks.
- Closing-strength signals: close location within the day's range (closing near the high/low) after a news move as a predictor of next-day continuation — relevant to choosing between a 2:00 PM entry and next open; "strong close" literature; last-half-hour returns and MOC imbalance effects in small caps; overnight drift after strong closes.
- Time-of-day liquidity/spread patterns in small caps: when are spreads narrowest (U-shape; first 30 minutes widest)? Implication for the 10:30 AM and 2:00 PM entry times at ~1% cost; evidence on small-cap effective spreads by time of day.
- Intraday reversal after extreme opening moves; halts (LULD) and post-halt continuation/reversal in small caps.
- Multi-day follow-through from day-one intraday pattern: does a news day that trends all session (open near low, close near high) continue more over days 2-5 than one that gaps and fades? Any evidence, academic or careful practitioner.
- After data-snooping and realistic small-cap costs (hitting bid/ask), which of these are credible?

Suggested sources:
- Academic papers (SSRN, NBER, JF, JFE, RFS, JFQA, Journal of Financial Markets). Read the papers or their abstracts/tables, not blog summaries; check surprising claims against a second source.
- Careful practitioner research (Concretum Research/Zarattini, Quantpedia, Alpha Architect); treat un-refereed backtests skeptically and say so.

Constraints:
- US equities; small caps ($250M-$1B) where the paper allows; say explicitly when evidence is from ETFs, large caps or other markets. Give effect sizes, sample periods, post-2015 validity and cost assumptions.
- Mark each finding as read from the paper or from a summary. Separate what the evidence shows from your inference.
- You have a limited web-search budget: prioritize (1) Zarattini et al. stocks-in-play ORB, (2) overnight/intraday and open-entry cost papers, (3) gap/news transmission and morning-after entry, (4) close-location and multi-day follow-through, and write notes to the file as you go so nothing is lost if you are cut off.

agents.report:
Notes are saved to `/Users/michael/Projects/ETF Factor Rotation/research_notes/Small cap screen design/technical_signals_intraday.md`. The file has ten sections, one per key question, each finding tagged by how it was sourced, and a judgment table in section 10.

**Bottom line:** technical signals deserve a bigger role for finding names in play, not for direction. Every refereed intraday effect is 3–13 basis points a day against the book's 100 bp round-trip cost.

Times below are Central, as in the file (the brief's 10:30 AM and 2:00 PM Eastern passes are 9:30 AM and 1:00 PM CT).

Papers read in full: Zarattini-Barbon-Aziz, Lou-Polk-Skouras, Aboody et al., Baltussen-Da-Soebhag, the SEC limit-up/limit-down white paper, and a Bogousslavsky–Collin-Dufresne draft. Most others are abstract or summary only and tagged as such.

- **Stocks in play (Zarattini, Barbon, Aziz 2024):** the useful result is the sorting variable, not the breakout rule.
  - The 5-minute breakout on all liquid stocks earns 3.2% a year (Sharpe 0.48); restricted to the top 20 by opening relative volume it earns 41.6% (Sharpe 2.81).
  - The 30- and 60-minute versions earn only 2.3% and 4.1% a year, so the same-day continuation is over before a 9:30 AM CT entry.
  - It models only a $0.0035/share commission, requires 1M+ shares a day, has no out-of-sample period, and is un-refereed.
  - By my arithmetic the book's spread is about 2.5R against a reported edge of 0.08–0.38R.
  - **Role:** opening relative volume as screen trigger and ranking input; breakout entry rule dropped.

- **Intraday momentum:** this is an index effect. Across single stocks the sign flips: stocks down on the day bounce in the last half hour (13 bp a day in the smallest fifth, 1993–2024) and give it back the next day. **Role:** drop "direction at 9:30 AM CT" as a signal.

- **Overnight versus intraday:** each component persists in its own session and is offset in the other. Aboody et al. find a 1.76-point weekly overnight spread but only 0.06–0.26 points close-to-close. **Role:** a gap alone is neither a fade nor a follow signal; longs wait an hour, and shorts on attention-driven gap-ups are better entered at the open (small effect).

- **News gaps:** the earnings reaction is in the opening price on average. Wu et al. (2006–2023) find that entering at 8:45 AM CT and holding to the close loses about 0.5% after spreads. A 9:30 AM CT entry on a news gap is therefore a bet on days 2–5, not on the afternoon.

- **VWAP, opening range held, close location, day shape:** no credible single-stock evidence. VWAP has only un-refereed index-ETF backtests; late-day moves revert. **Role:** record and test on the book's own data, no role yet.

- **Spreads and halts:** spreads and volatility are highest at the open and decay over 30–60 minutes, and volatility pauses cluster in the first 15–20 minutes in smaller stocks with prices reverting afterward. Both entry times sit in the cheap part of the day; avoid starting positions in the last 30 minutes.

**Gaps that matter:**
- I found no time-of-day spread table for $250M–$1B stocks; the book's own recorded bid/ask at each pass would answer this.
- I found no study of days 2–5 returns sorted on gap size, first-hour behaviour or day shape for small caps.
- The Jiang-Li-Wang drift magnitudes were not obtained, so "follow a news gap" leans on the daily-horizon evidence in the adjacent notes.
- Most samples exclude or thinly cover the book's size range, though I did not check this against NYSE size breakpoints.
- The Berkman et al. open-price figures conflict between excerpts (+10/−7 bp versus +13/−13 bp).

agents.brief:
Research the evidence on classic technical-analysis signals computed from DAILY price and volume bars as predictors of short-horizon (1 to 5 trading session) returns in US small caps.

Context: this feeds the design of a candidate screen for a discretionary long/short swing book. The book trades US companies worth $250M to $1B (no biotech, banks or REITs, about 425 names, typical daily range 3-7%), long and short against IWM (the Russell 2000 ETF), holds 1 to 5 sessions, pays roughly 1% round-trip in spread. An LLM research agent reads the news on each screened name and a judge decides direction. Earlier research for this project already covered: short-term reversal (Jegadeesh, Nagel, Avramov et al.), news vs no-news moves (Chan, Savor, Tetlock, Boudoukh), the high-volume return premium (Gervais et al.), Medhat & Schmeling short-term momentum, and large one-day-drop bounces. Do NOT repeat those; this task is the rest of the technical toolkit. The owner specifically wants to know whether technical signals deserve a bigger role in the screen (as a trigger that puts a name on the list, as a ranking input, or as a filter/veto on a news-driven idea).

Objective: a dense, sourced account of which daily-bar technical signals have credible out-of-sample evidence at 1-5 day (and separately 1-4 week) horizons in small, volatile US stocks, with effect sizes, cost-adjusted results, recent-period (2015-2026) validity and data-snooping status, and a judgment for each of trigger / ranking input / veto / drop.

Key questions:
- Moving-average and trend rules on individual stocks: Brock/Lakonishok/LeBaron; Sullivan/Timmermann/White and Bajgrowicz & Scaillet on data snooping and costs; Park & Irwin survey; Han, Yang & Zhou (2013) "A new anomaly: the cross-sectional profitability of technical analysis" (MA timing strongest in high-volatility, small stocks — effect size, horizon, after costs, follow-ups and critiques); Han, Zhou & Zhu (2016) "A trend factor" (multi-horizon MA signals; performance in small caps; post-publication); Avramov, Kaplanski & Subrahmanyam "Moving average distance as a predictor of equity returns"; Detzel, Strauss, Zhou.
- Machine-read price patterns: Jiang, Kelly & Xiu "(Re-)Imag(in)ing Price Trends" (CNN on 5/20/60-day OHLCV chart images predicting 5-day returns; reported Sharpe; that it is strongest in small stocks; turnover and cost results; what the CNN keys on — e.g. close relative to the recent range); Murray, Xia & Xiao "Charting by machines"; Lo, Mamaysky & Wang on chart patterns; Gu, Kelly & Xiu and later ML papers on which price-based features matter at short horizons (short-term reversal, max return, turnover, volatility).
- Breakouts and highs: 52-week-high and new-high breakouts at short horizons (George & Hwang; Huddart, Lang & Yetman "Volume and price patterns around a stock's 52-week highs and lows" — volume and returns right after a breakout through the 52-week high/low); 20-day/55-day channel (Donchian) breakouts on single stocks; breakouts with vs without volume expansion; volatility-contraction-then-expansion setups (NR7, Bollinger squeeze) — any refereed evidence.
- Oversold/overbought oscillators on single stocks: RSI(2)/RSI(14), Bollinger band extremes, consecutive down days, distance below a moving average — is this anything more than short-term reversal, and does it survive in small caps after costs? Connors-style practitioner results and independent replications.
- Relative strength: 1-month and 3-12 month relative strength as a CONDITIONING variable for a 1-5 day trade (does a news-driven move in the direction of the prior trend continue more than one against it?); residual/idiosyncratic momentum (Blitz, Huij & Martens); industry momentum at weekly horizon; interaction of prior trend with post-earnings drift (e.g. George, Hwang & Li on 52-week high and PEAD; Chan/Jegadeesh/Lakonishok).
- Volatility and lottery features as vetoes: MAX effect (Bali, Cakici & Whitelaw), idiosyncratic volatility puzzle (Ang et al.), high recent turnover — do names that have just had extreme up days underperform over the next days/weeks (a veto on chasing longs / a short setup)? Size of effect in small caps, and borrow caveats.
- Volume-based technicals beyond the high-volume premium: on-balance volume/accumulation, volume dry-up before moves, relative volume as "in play" indicator; any evidence.
- Support/resistance and round numbers/anchoring (Osler; Bhattacharya, Holden & Jacobsen "Penny wise, dollar foolish"; nominal price anchors) at short horizons.
- Seasonality usable at 1-5 days in small caps: turn-of-month, day-of-week, pre-holiday, month-end/quarter-end window dressing, tax-loss selling into December and the January rebound in small-cap losers (timely: it is late November) — current evidence.
- Overall: after data-snooping corrections and ~1% round-trip costs, which technical signals are credible for $250M-$1B names? Where do authors find technicals work BEST (high volatility, low coverage, high information uncertainty — e.g. Zhang 2006 "Information uncertainty and stock returns"; Han/Yang/Zhou)? That is precisely this book's universe, so be specific.

Suggested sources:
- Academic papers (SSRN, NBER, JF, JFE, RFS, JFQA, Management Science, Journal of Banking & Finance). Read the papers or their abstracts/tables, not blog summaries; check surprising claims against a second source.
- Practitioner research and replications (Quantpedia, Alpha Architect, AQR, Robeco, Concretum, CSSA, Quantified Strategies — treat un-refereed backtests skeptically and say so).

Constraints:
- US equities; small caps; 1-5 session horizon with 1-4 week results noted separately. Give effect sizes (bp/percent, t-stats), sample periods, whether results hold post-2015 and after ~1% round-trip costs.
- Mark each finding as read from the paper or from a summary. Separate what the evidence shows from your inference.
- You have a limited web-search budget: prioritize the highest-value questions first (Han/Yang/Zhou; trend factor; Jiang/Kelly/Xiu; breakouts/52-week high short-horizon; MAX/lottery veto; prior-trend conditioning; December tax-loss), and write notes to the file as you go so nothing is lost if you are cut off.

agents.report:
Notes are saved at `/Users/michael/Projects/ETF Factor Rotation/research_notes/Small cap screen design/technical_signals_daily.md` (10 sections, about 57 KB). Every finding is tagged READ, SUMMARY or MEMORY, and each section has Takeaway / Cited Findings / Inferences / Gaps.

**Bottom line:** no daily-bar technical signal has evidence of a stand-alone, cost-covering edge at 1-5 sessions in $250M-$1B names. Gross effects are real and largest in small, volatile, low-coverage stocks, but the book's roughly 1% round trip exceeds them. Technicals earn a modestly bigger role in three narrow places.

- **Trigger:** the first cross of a 52-week high or low on abnormal volume. Huddart, Lang & Yetman find a volume spike lasting weeks and positive returns after either event, largest in week one and in small stocks. It is an attention event, not a direction signal.
- **Ranking input:** two have support.
  - Trend agreement with the news: with moving-average distance (21-day over 200-day average), high-distance stocks drift after good news and low-distance stocks do not (t = 4.61; difference t = 2.37). The 52-week-high anchoring work points the same way.
  - On no-news names only, a reversal score refined by where the close sat in its recent range and by rising volume, which is what the Jiang-Kelly-Xiu chart model keys on.
- **Veto (soft):** don't chase an extreme one-day gain with no real news, and don't bottom-fish a name with repeated large down days without a news reason. Top-decile maximum-daily-return stocks lose about 1.0% the next month (Bali, Cakici & Whitelaw) and ranked daily winners/losers about 1.6% (Kumar, Ruenzi & Ungeheuer). That is only 0.25-0.4% per five sessions, so it is not a short trigger.
- **Drop:**
  - Single-stock moving-average crosses: classic rules fail false-discovery tests and costs, and were significant for about 3% of individual US stocks in 1990-2004.
  - RSI and Bollinger extremes: no refereed evidence; they restate short-term reversal.
  - Donchian, NR7 and squeeze setups, on-balance volume and accumulation: no refereed evidence found either way.
  - Round numbers: a penny-scale, one-day effect.
  - Turn of month: "significant only for large and liquid stocks".

**Key numbers read from the papers:**

| Signal, 5-day hold, 2001-2019 (Jiang-Kelly-Xiu tables) | All stocks, equal-weight | Largest 500 |
|---|---|---|
| Chart model (5-day image) | 83% a year, Sharpe 7.15 | 12% a year, Sharpe 1.02 |
| Trend factor (Han-Zhou-Zhu) | 59% a year, Sharpe 2.92 | 4% a year, Sharpe 0.22 |
| One-week reversal | 53% a year, Sharpe 2.84 | -5% a year, Sharpe -0.30 |
| 12-month momentum | 2% a year, Sharpe 0.07 | 5% a year, Sharpe 0.19 |

- The chart model was fixed in 2000 and turns over 619-690% a month; the authors say the weekly version is "mostly accessible to investors who behave as market makers."
- Momentum (winners minus losers) earns 0.63% a month in the lowest-volatility quintile and 2.63% in the highest (Zhang 2006), which is why continuation after news should be strongest in this universe.

**Seasonality for late November/December:** year-end selling of small losers and an early-January rebound is documented and strongest in stocks institutions don't trade, but that sample is 1999-2005. Post-2010 evidence is thin and second-hand, so I put it as context for the judge, not a screen rule.

**Gaps the report writer should know about:**
- Han-Yang-Zhou's and the trend factor's own cost, size and turnover tables were paywalled; those numbers come from a digest and abstracts. Han-Yang-Zhou times volatility-decile portfolios, not single stocks.
- Huddart's week-one magnitudes (about 0.6% after highs, about 5% after lows in the smallest quartile) are second-hand; the 5% figure looks inflated.
- George, Hwang & Li's magnitudes were not obtainable.
- Nothing re-tests any of these signals on 2020-2026 data, isolates the $250M-$1B band, or nets out short-borrow costs.
- No study measures the trend-conditional news drift over days 1-5; the documented drift runs over weeks to months.

The notes close by suggesting the retained features be recorded beside each night's verdicts and scored before they influence the screen; that is my suggestion, not something the owner asked for.

agents.brief:
Run an empirical study on this project's own data: in our small-cap universe, what happens over the next 1 to 5 sessions after the kinds of days our screen flags, and how do different thresholds change the number and quality of candidates?

Context: the repo at /Users/michael/Projects/ETF Factor Rotation holds a "small-cap book" in shadow run (no orders). Its universe is journal/smallcap/universe.json (about 425 US names worth $250M-$1B, each with symbol, name, sector, industry, cap, dollar_volume, analysts). The screen is src/factor_rotation/smallcap/screen.py (read its docstring and `numbers`, `candidates`): it flags (a) an earnings reaction — reported since yesterday's close and moved >=3% against IWM and >=1.0 typical daily ranges (14-day ATR as % of prior close); (b) a "news move" — no report, moved >=5% against IWM, >=1.5 ranges, on >=2x the 20-day average volume; (c) insider buying. The book holds 1-5 sessions against IWM (long stock/short IWM or the reverse), enters either at the next session's open (night pass) or intraday about 10:30 AM ET / 2:00 PM ET at the live price. Round-trip cost is roughly 1% (100 bp). On 2026-11-20 midday, 74 names were down 5%+ against IWM but only 1 passed all three bars. Daily bars are loadable with `from factor_rotation import bars; bars.load(symbols)` (a DataFrame with symbol, date, open, high, low, close, volume; check how much history it holds — it may be only a few months to a couple of years). If history is short, pull longer daily history yourself with yfinance (it is installed in the project's uv environment; use `uv run python` from the repo root; pull 3-5 years of adjusted daily bars for the universe plus IWM and cache them as parquet in your scratch folder). Past earnings dates: yfinance `Ticker.get_earnings_dates(limit=...)` gives historical dates with timestamps for many names (rate-limit yourself; about 500 calls is the practical ceiling, cache the results); Nasdaq's calendar via `factor_rotation.smallcap.sources.earnings(day)` gives one day at a time.

Objective: measured answers, from this universe's own price history, to the questions below, written up as dense notes with tables. This is evidence to sit beside a literature review, so be careful about methodology and candid about limitations.

Key questions:
1. Event counts: per trading day, how many names clear the news-move bar at a grid of thresholds (excess move 3/5/7%; ranges 0.75/1.0/1.5/2.0; volume 1.0/1.5/2.0/3.0x)? Median, 10th and 90th percentile per day. Same for the earnings-reaction bar. What grid point yields about 5-10 and about 10-20 candidates a day?
2. After a large relative move (non-earnings day): mean and median return against IWM from the NEXT OPEN over holds of 1,2,3,4,5 sessions, measured in the direction of the move (positive = continuation, negative = reversal), split by: up vs down move; size of move in ranges (1-1.5, 1.5-2, 2-3, 3+); volume ratio bucket (<1, 1-2, 2-3, 3+); gap share (how much of the move was the opening gap vs intraday); analyst count (<=2, 3-5, 6+); dollar-volume tercile; whether IWM itself moved more than 1.5% that day. Report N, mean, median, hit rate, t-stat using date-clustered standard errors (or at least averaging by date first), and the value after 100 bp of cost.
3. After earnings days: same analysis in the direction of the announcement-day reaction — does the reaction continue over days 1-5 from the next open in this universe? Split by reaction size, volume, analyst count, up vs down.
4. Does a stricter bar actually select better outcomes (larger absolute subsequent relative moves, i.e. more "something to be right about"), or just fewer names? 5. Peer effect: when one name in an industry (use the universe's industry field) has an earnings reaction of 2+ ranges, do the other names in that industry drift in the same direction over the next 1-5 sessions?
6. Is scaling by the stock's own ATR better than a raw percent threshold at separating continuation from reversal?

The sample is five years of Yahoo daily bars (2021-06-01 to 2026-11-19) for today's 425 names, with 5,229 usable earnings reaction days. Results are in basis points against IWM (the small-cap ETF), entered at the next open and held 1 to 5 sessions, as `score.py` does.

## Findings

1. **Counts.** At today's bars the screen finds a median of 2 news moves a day (10th–90th percentile 1–5) and 1 earnings reaction (0–9), 4 together (1–15), over the last 12 months.
   - Volume is the bar that binds: of non-earnings names moving 5%+ against IWM, 14% pass 2x volume, 21% pass 1.5 ranges, 7% pass both.
   - About 5–10 news candidates a day: 5% / 1.0 ranges / 1.5x volume (median 7) or 5% / 1.5 / 1.0x (median 6).
   - About 10–20 a day: 5% / 1.0 / 1.0x (median 14) or 3% / 0.75 / 1.5x (median 12).
   - The 2026-11-20 observation reproduces: 72 names down 5%+ in my partial bar, median ATR 10.4%, so the median move was 0.75 ranges. The one name at 1.5 ranges was HQL, a closed-end fund.

2. **Non-earnings moves.** A 5%+ move with no report has no drift on average (N = 12,447). The subset the screen selects (1.5+ ranges, 2x+ volume, N = 1,839) reverses: −41 bp after one session, −70 after two, −88 after five (t −3.6, −4.3, −3.4).
   - Up moves on heavy volume carry it (−97 bp at two sessions, t −4.5); moves on under 2x volume do nothing.
   - This is the only result that survives a Bonferroni correction (5 of 463 tests, all this finding).
   - Fading it nets −12 bp after the 100 bp cost, so it is a base rate, not a trade.

3. **Survivorship check.** I ran the same bar on 600 names now just outside the band ($100M–$250M and $1B–$3B), using Nasdaq's calendar for all 1,354 sessions.
   - The up-move reversal holds there at a third to a half smaller: −40 bp at two sessions outside the band, −57 bp pooled (t −3.6).
   - The in-band down-move reversal does not hold. Names now below the band continued falling after heavy-volume drops (+87 bp, t +2.7).

4. **Earnings.** There is no reliable drift from the next open: +17 bp at three to four sessions (t about 1.1), and the sign flips between years. The continuation happens on the reaction day itself. Entering at that day's open in the gap's direction made +52 bp by the close (t +3.2), mostly on down gaps; that result was found after looking and rests on open prints.

5. **Stricter bar.** It selects moves more unusual for the stock, not more room. The mean absolute five-session move is 731 bp for names passing the news bar and 770 bp for 5%+ movers that fail it. Every flagged group needs about 56–58% directional accuracy to clear cost at five sessions; unflagged names need 61%.

6. **Peers.** They move with the reporter the same day (+39 bp, t +7.1) and do not drift afterwards.

7. **ATR versus raw percent.** Neither predicts direction. Ranges isolates the reversal pocket (3+ ranges: −134 bp at three sessions); raw percent picks volatile names with about 40% more raw room.

8. **Hygiene.** 59 names should come out: 32 closed-end funds, 17 business development companies, 4 REITs, 2 pharma, and one each of royalty trust, bank, crypto-treasury vehicle and de-SPAC shell. Another 25 are flagged but kept. Removing them barely changes any result; all analyses were run on the clean set.

9. **Intraday (optional).** Sixty sessions of 30-minute bars are inconclusive, and the window was an unusually trending earnings season.

- **Survivors only.** Today's membership is applied to the past. The check in item 3 covers the news-move result; the earnings and peer results were not re-run on outside names.
- **Earnings dates.** Yahoo misses about 12% of reports and is a session off for roughly one in eight to one in five. A coverage rule kept the misses out of the non-earnings sample (zero leaks in a 26-session check against Nasdaq). Mis-timing remains in the earnings sample and flatters continuation there.
- **Today's attributes.** Analyst counts and industries are today's values.
- **Not tested.** Insider buying, and intraday entries beyond the 60-session sample.

The study is done and the notes are saved at `/Users/michael/Projects/ETF Factor Rotation/research_notes/Small cap screen design/own_data_technicals.md`. The short answer: technical signals do not earn a role as a trigger or a ranking input, and at most two narrow flags are worth showing to the judge.

## What was run
- **Sample:** signal days 2022-06-01 to 2026-11-19 (1,123 sessions), 366 names after the sibling's hygiene list, 309,946 eligible name-days, median 263 names a day. Entry at the next open, exits at the close 1/2/3/5 sessions later, stock less IWM. Halves split at 2024-08-22.
- **Second sample:** I added an approximately point-in-time $250M-$1B sample (336,542 name-days), built from the sibling's extra pull of 612 names now just outside the band. Past market value is today's value scaled by the price ratio, so it is approximate and still has no delisted names.
- **Data:** nothing was downloaded. I copied the sibling's cached files read-only and wrote nothing in its folder.
- **Checks:** one signal and one forward return were recomputed from the raw bars and matched.

## Findings
- **Standalone signals (186 definitions, 744 tests per sample):** there is no long side anywhere, and nothing covers the 100 bp round trip. Trend state, moving-average timing, 21/63/126-day relative strength, close location, MAX, volatility and calendar effects give 5-session spreads of 0-30 bp with |t| under 2.
- **No oversold bounce from the next open:** RSI(2) under 10, new 20-day lows and the worst 5-day losers lose a further 10-20 bp next session. The bounce happens overnight (+5 to +8 bp) and is given back during the session.
- **The one family that passes:** a new 55-day closing high on 2x volume, not near earnings (2,310 events), loses 52 bp per date next session (t -4.1) in the band sample and 44 bp (t -3.0) point-in-time. It is a short-side fade worth under half the cost, with borrow untested. The 3-5 session part does not hold up: -101 bp at 5 sessions in the band sample, -8 bp point-in-time.
- **Conditioning on a big-move day (11,412 non-earnings events):** with or against the 50/200-day trend, 63-day relative strength, volatility contraction, and MAX or volatility state separate nothing. All states together explain 0.1-0.5% of variance, and a score fitted on the first half fails on the second.
- **Two extension effects hold in both samples and both halves:**
  - An up move that closes at a new 55-day high does 85-88 bp worse over 3 sessions than an up move inside its range (t -3.6 and -3.7).
  - A down move in a name already more than 2 ATR below its 50-day average keeps falling next session, by 45-53 bp per date (t 3.5 and 3.6).
- **Composite on the holdout:** top-minus-bottom tenth at 5 sessions is -41 bp (t -1.5) in the band sample and -37 bp (t -1.3) point-in-time, so it has the wrong sign.

## Survivorship is material
Applying today's universe to the past biases the band sample, and this affects the sibling study too.
- **Baseline drift:** today's band members lost 13 bp per 5 sessions to IWM. Names now $1B-$3B gained 5 bp, names now $100M-$250M lost 63 bp, and the point-in-time sample is at +2 bp.
- **A pure artifact:** sorting by past dollar volume gives a -127 bp spread (t -6.5) in the band sample and +2 bp point-in-time.
- **The sibling's headline:** up moves on the current news bar reverse 98 bp per date at 5 sessions in the band sample, but only 6 bp (t -0.1) point-in-time. The next-session fade of about 44 bp (t -2.3) survives; the multi-day part does not.

## Recommendation for the screen
- **Trigger:** no.
- **Ranking input:** no.
- **Veto:** not as a hard rule. The two extension effects are base rates of 30-85 bp, below the cost on their own, and could be shown to the judge beside each candidate as facts.
- **Entry timing:** after a high-attention day the stock gains 5-45 bp overnight and gives it back open-to-close, so a next-open long gets the losing half. Daily bars cannot test whether a later entry avoids this.

## Limits
- One definition per signal with no parameter search; 4.4 years in one regime.
- Every consistent result is on the short side, and borrow is not modelled.
- Yahoo opening prints for thin names may be poor.
- A placebo of 400 random signals passes the |t| > 3, both-halves bar 0.5-1% of the time against the universe and 2.5-4% against IWM.

The notes file is about 237 KB, mostly tables. Scripts and outputs are in `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-michael-Projects-ETF-Factor-Rotation/4f1b8889-0d21-4ce9-af55-2bf1952b498c/scratchpad/smallcap_technicals/`: `01_build_features.py` through `06_build_notes.py`, `tech_common.py`, `notes_template.md`, and the `out/` folder. I saved the report to `/Users/michael/Projects/ETF Factor Rotation/reports/Small cap screen design.md` (about 5,400 words, built from all ten notes and the two own-data studies).

**Main finding.** The screen should put names on the research list mainly because something was disclosed, not because the price spiked. It should keep a looser price route beside that, rank everything in one list, and print a few base-rate facts beside each name. The best-supported result across the literature is that big moves with identifiable news keep going and moves without news fade. No daily or intraday technical signal covers a 1% round trip on its own, and on the book's own data a composite of the best technical signals failed when tested on the second half of the data it wasn't built on.

**How the two own-data studies fit together (the cautious reading leads the report).** The first study's headline was that big up moves on heavy volume with no report reverse about 88 bp over five sessions. That mostly comes from testing today's universe on the past. In the roughly point-in-time sample the same event gives:
- -44 bp the next session (t -2.3)
- -49 bp at three sessions (t -1.3)
- -6 bp at five sessions (t -0.1)

The next-session fade of roughly 25-50 bp survives every check, mostly after a close at a new high. It happens between the open and the close, after a 29-43 bp overnight gain. It is well under the 1% cost, so it goes in front of the judge as a base rate, not as a trade. The first study's earnings results were never re-run point-in-time, so how much survivorship inflates them is unknown.

**Proposed screen, with starting thresholds:**
- **Clean the universe:** drop the 59 funds, BDCs, REITs and other non-operating names, and add simple rules to keep them out.
- **Measure moves against the stock's beta to IWM** (the Russell 2000 ETF the book hedges with). Scoring stays against IWM.
- **Earnings:** every report since the last pass, with no move bar. The 4:30 PM CT pass also takes reports released after that day's close, tagged as an experiment.
- **News moves:** 5% beta-adjusted, 1.0 typical range, 1.5x volume. That gives a median of 8 a day instead of 2.
- **Insider buying:** read Form 4s straight from SEC EDGAR instead of OpenInsider, with the bar lowered to $50k from one insider, or two insiders and $25k.
- **New filing route:** activist 13D stakes, late-filing notices (NT 10-K / NT 10-Q), and distress 8-K items 1.03, 2.04, 2.05, 2.06, 3.01 and 4.02.
- **New analyst route** (lowest priority): analyst actions on names with 0-2 analysts.
- **Ranking:** one list in three tiers (filings, then earnings, then price movers) replaces the current round-robin. Keep the cap of 20 per pass and show the list to the judge in shuffled order.
- **Repeat rule:** a name judged in the last three sessions can come back if a new filing or report arrives.
- **Facts beside each candidate:** two warnings for the judge, not hard bans. An up move closing at a new 55-day high usually loses 30-45 bp the next session. A drop to a new 55-day low, or more than 2 ATR below the 50-day average, usually keeps falling 25-50 bp the next session. Borrow status for any short, and the Russell reconstitution taking effect after the close on 2026-12-11.

**Decisions for you:**
- **EDGAR contact email (required):** a real address, an alias is fine, kept in the local `.env` and never in the repo or on the public dashboard. The filing, insider and earnings-timing routes don't work without it.
- **Paid data:** none recommended now. Revisit after two weeks of the free feeds; the first candidates would be IBKR Benzinga $35/month, FMP Premium $69/month and Massive Starter $29/month.
- **Thresholds:** each one is set up as a yes/no in a table in the report.

**What three weeks can show.** About 150-300 scored verdicts by around 2026-12-11. That can only detect a rank correlation of about 0.16 or more, while about 0.10 is needed to pay costs. Backtest two candidate-screen routes of this project's small-cap book on its own universe, using SEC EDGAR filing timestamps so there is no look-ahead: (1) the FILING route and (2) the INSIDER-BUYING route. The question: do these events, mechanically and before any human/LLM judgment, predict returns against IWM over the next 1-5 sessions (and 10/20 for context) in US companies worth $250M-$1B, and does any part of that survive a ~1% (100 bp) round-trip cost?

## Context
- Repo: /Users/michael/Projects/ETF Factor Rotation. The small-cap book (shadow run, no orders) trades US operating companies worth $250M-$1B (no biotech, banks, REITs, funds), long or short against the same dollars of IWM (the Russell 2000 ETF), holding 1-5 sessions. Passes run at 9:30 AM CT (10:30 AM ET), 1:00 PM CT (2:00 PM ET) and 4:30 PM CT (5:30 PM ET); the morning and midday passes enter at the live price, the night pass at the next session's open.
- Read these first: src/factor_rotation/smallcap/screen.py (module docstring, `insider_groups`, `candidates`) and src/factor_rotation/smallcap/edgar.py (event definitions, `events`, `parse_form4`, `purchases`), and the design report reports/Small cap screen design.md (sections on the proposed screen). The routes as built:
  - FILING: an initial Schedule 13D (form "SCHEDULE 13D" or older "SC 13D"; not amendments), NT 10-K or NT 10-Q, or an 8-K carrying item 1.03, 2.04, 2.05, 2.06, 3.01 or 4.02.
  - INSIDER: Form 4, transaction code P (open-market purchase, acquired), by an officer or director (a holder who is only a 10% owner doesn't count), within 5 sessions: one insider >= $50,000, or two or more insiders together >= $25,000; triggered on the filing that makes the group qualify.
- Universe: journal/smallcap/universe.json (366 names, each with symbol, cik, sic, cap, industry, analysts). A wider set of about 612 names now just outside the band ($100M-$250M and $1B-$3B) was pulled by an earlier study for a rough point-in-time check: see research_notes/Small cap screen design/own_data_technicals.md and own_data_study.md for how it was built, and the cached data under /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-michael-Projects-ETF-Factor-Rotation/4f1b8889-0d21-4ce9-af55-2bf1952b498c/scratchpad/smallcap_study/data/ (multi-year Yahoo daily bars as parquet for the universe, the adjacent names and IWM; read-only — copy what you need, never write there). Earlier findings to keep consistent with: survivorship bias from applying today's universe to the past was material for some results; the approximate point-in-time sample is the more conservative read.

## Data access
- Use the project's own EDGAR client so you never handle the SEC contact address: `from factor_rotation.smallcap import edgar` then `edgar._get(url)` (it reads SEC_USER_AGENT from .env itself, rate-limits to 8/s and retries). Do NOT read, print, echo or copy .env or the SEC_USER_AGENT value anywhere; do not set your own User-Agent for sec.gov. Run Python with `uv run python` from the repo root.
- Filing history: `edgar.company(cik)` returns only the SEC's "recent" block (about the last 1,000 filings). For older filings, the submissions JSON (https://data.sec.gov/submissions/CIK##########.json) lists extra pages under filings.files (e.g. CIK##########-submissions-001.json at https://data.sec.gov/submissions/) — fetch those to cover 2021-2026. acceptanceDateTime is UTC.

Check which is feasible; be gentle with the SEC (stay at or under 8 requests/second, cache all downloads in your scratch folder).
- Prices: reuse the cached Yahoo bars; pull missing ones with yfinance only if needed (batch, sleep between batches).

## Method
- Sample: 2021-06 to 2026-11 (match the cached bars). Main sample = today's 366 names. Robustness = the approximate point-in-time sample (today's band plus the adjacent names, kept on dates when their approximate past market value was $250M-$1B, as the earlier technicals study did), and say how results differ.
